summary: Sauti arrives at the Naimisha forest, is welcomed by the sages, and is asked what he will tell them. They choose the history composed by Vyasa.
Sauti bows to the supreme being and describes the world's creation from a cosmic egg, the lineage of gods and sages, and the many ways the epic is studied.

Vyasa has composed the epic but has no one to write it. Brahma tells him to call on Ganesha, who agrees to write it if Vyasa never pauses. Vyasa agrees on condition that Ganesha understand each verse first, and ties knots of hard verses to slow him.
Sauti compares the epic to a lamp, a sun and a tree, and sums up its contents book by book. He names how Vyasa fathered Dhritarashtra, Pandu and Vidura and later had the story recited.
Sauti gives the size of the epic in verses and in what worlds it is known. He tells briefly of the Pandavas' birth, arrival at Hastinapura and early life.
The Pandavas win Draupadi and the Rajasuya sacrifice. Duryodhana is humiliated at their hall, gets the dice game arranged, and the great war follows. Dhritarashtra starts to speak to Sanjaya.

Dhritarashtra lists, one by one, the events that told him his side would lose, from Arjuna's winning Draupadi to Aswatthaman's night attack. After each he repeats that he had no hope of success. He ends by mourning Gandhari and the few survivors.
Dhritarashtra wishes to die. Sanjaya comforts him with the example of kings of the past, who also died, and with the teaching that Time creates and destroys all things.
Sauti explains the merit of hearing and reciting the epic, and why it is called the Mahabharata: the gods weighed it against the four Vedas and it was heavier.
A short closing line: penance, study and the pursuit of wealth are harmless unless misused.

The sages ask about Samanta-panchaka. Sauti tells how Parashurama made lakes of blood there and how the Kuru battle was later fought on the same ground. He also defines an Akshauhini and says how many days each general led the Kaurava army.
Sauti begins the table of contents and lists, in order, the sub-books of the epic. He says the eighteen books are condensed from Vyasa's longer plan and starts with the first book, Adi Parva.
Contents of Adi Parva's remaining parts, then of the Sabha, Vana (Aranyaka), Virata, Udyoga and Bhishma books, each with its main events.
Contents of the Drona, Karna, Shalya, Sauptika and Stri books: the war's later days, Abhimanyu's death, Karna's fall, Duryodhana's defeat, the night massacre, and the women's lament.
Contents of the Shanti, Anushasana, Aswamedhika and Asramavasika books: Yudhishthira's grief, Bhishma's teachings, the horse sacrifice, and Dhritarashtra's retreat to the forest.
Contents of the last books: the Yadavas' destruction in Mausala, the Pandavas' final journey, and Yudhishthira's ascent to heaven. A note on the supplement, the Harivamsa.
Sauti closes the contents section with the merit of the Bharata and the benefit of hearing it.
The curse on Janamejaya's family. The king's brothers beat Sarama's pup, Sarama curses them, the king seeks a priest and picks Somasrava, and the tale turns to Ayoda-Dhaumya's pupil Aruni.

Aruni plugs a broken water channel with his own body and is named Uddalaka. Upamanyu, sent to herd cows, is stripped by his teacher of every food source until hunger drives him to eat a poisonous plant and blinds him.
Dhaumya finds blind Upamanyu in a dry well and tells him to pray to the divine twin physicians, the Aswins. Upamanyu begins a long hymn about time, the year as a wheel, and the universe.
The hymn ends and the Aswins appear. Upamanyu refuses their cake until he offers it to his teacher. Pleased by his loyalty, they restore his sight and promise him golden teeth.

Upamanyu is praised by his teacher. Then Veda's story: he serves Dhaumya patiently, becomes a teacher himself, and leaves his pupil Utanka in charge of the house, where Utanka refuses to do wrong when the women ask him to.

Utanka is thanked by Veda and sent to ask his teacher's wife for a gift. She asks for Queen Paushya's earrings. On the road a strange man on a huge bull makes Utanka eat the bull's dung. Utanka then asks King Paushya for the earrings and cannot find the queen.

Paushya says Utanka is ritually unclean; Utanka washes properly and the queen gives the earrings with a warning about Takshaka. A quarrel over unclean food leads to mutual curses. On the road a beggar steals the earrings, turns into Takshaka, and flees underground, where Indra's thunderbolt helps Utanka dig after him.

In the world of serpents Utanka praises the snake chiefs but does not get the earrings. He sees two women weaving, a twelve-spoked wheel and a man with a horse, and is told to blow into the horse. Fire pours out, Takshaka panics and returns the earrings.

Utanka rides the horse and reaches his teacher's house just in time, and is blessed. His teacher explains the strange sights (night and day, the year, Indra and the rain god, Agni, and nectar in the bull's dung). Angry at Takshaka, Utanka goes to Hastinapura to see Janamejaya.

Utanka tells Janamejaya that Takshaka killed his father Parikshit and should be burned in a snake sacrifice. The king is enraged, asks his ministers how his father died, and is overcome with grief. The chapter ends.
Sauti asks the sages what they want to hear. They say Saunaka, their chief, should be present first. When Saunaka has finished his duties and taken his seat, he begins to speak.
Saunaka asks for the history of the Bhrigu race. Sauti lists the line from Bhrigu to Chyavana, Pramati, Ruru and Sunaka. Saunaka asks why Chyavana got his name.
The Rakshasa Puloma, who had once been promised the same woman, finds her alone at the hermitage, abducts her, and asks Agni whether she is truly Bhrigu's wife.
Agni, afraid of both a lie and Bhrigu's curse, admits she was first chosen by the Rakshasa but was properly married to Bhrigu with fire rites.

The Rakshasa carries Puloma away as a boar, and her baby falls out and burns him to ashes. Brahma comforts her and names her tear-river. Bhrigu learns Agni gave her away and curses him to eat all things.
Agni defends himself, then goes into hiding and all sacrifices stop. The gods take the problem to Brahma, who limits the curse. Agni returns and the rites resume.
Closing line: the seventh section ends.
Descent from Chyavana to Ruru. The story of Pramadvara's birth and upbringing, her betrothal to Ruru, her death from snakebite, and the grief of the sages.
Ruru's grief in the forest, the heavenly messenger's offer, and Dharma's consent to revive Pramadvara with half of Ruru's life.
Pramadvara wakes, the two marry, and Ruru begins killing snakes. He meets a Dundubha snake and raises his staff to strike it.
Ruru explains his vow, the snake pleads for its kind, Ruru spares it, and the snake reveals it is a cursed sage.
The story of the curse on Sahasrapat, his release at the sight of Ruru, and his lesson that Brahmanas must be gentle and not kill.
Ruru asks for the Astika story, the sage disappears, and Ruru's father relates it.
Saunaka's questions and Sauti's promise to tell the Astika story as he heard it from his father.
The wandering ascetic Jaratkaru finds his ancestors hanging in a pit, eaten away by a rat, because he has no descendants.
The ancestors urge him to marry. He promises to wed only a bride of his own name offered as alms.
Jaratkaru's search, Vasuki's offer of his sister of the same name, and the marriage.
Why Vasuki married his sister to the sage, the birth of Astika, and a summary of how Astika saved the snakes and freed his father's ancestors.
Saunaka's request. The story of Kadru and Vinata, their boons from Kasyapa, the eggs, Vinata's mistake and Aruna's curse, and Garuda's birth.
Closing line: the sixteenth section ends.
The sisters see Uchchaihsravas, the question about the churning, and the gods' assembly on Mount Meru where the churning is advised.
Preparations: Mandara is uprooted, placed on the tortoise, and used as a churning staff with Vasuki as rope. The churning begins and creates chaos.
The gods tire and Narayana renews their strength. Treasures rise from the ocean, the poison Kalakuta is swallowed by Siva, and Narayana, as an enchantress, takes the nectar.
Closing line: the eighteenth section ends.
The gods drink the nectar, Rahu is beheaded, and the battle against the Asuras begins and is turned by Vishnu's discus.
The Asuras hurl mountains but are driven into the earth and sea. The gods return Mandara and give the nectar to Narayana.
The wager of the sisters, Kadru's trick, her curse on her own sons, and Brahma's approval of it.
The sisters' journey and a long poetic description of the ocean.
The snakes decide to obey Kadru and turn into black tail hairs. The sisters cross the ocean.
Vinata loses the wager and is enslaved. Garuda hatches and terrifies the gods, who are reassured by Agni and then praise Garuda until he calms down.
Closing line: the twenty-third section ends.
Garuda reduces his size and carries Aruna to the east. Saunaka asks why Surya was angry.
Surya's anger at the gods after Rahu's enmity, the panic of the world, and Brahma's remedy of making Aruna his charioteer.
Kadru commands Vinata to carry her to the Nagas' island, Garuda carries the snakes toward the sun, and Kadru prays to Indra for help.
Indra covers the sky with clouds and a great rain falls. The snakes and their mother reach Ramaniyaka.
The snakes land on the island and enjoy it. Garuda learns why they are enslaved and asks the snakes the price of freedom. They demand amrita.
End of the closing line of the twenty-seventh section.
Vinata's advice about Brahmanas and her blessing, and Garuda's attack on the Nishada fishermen.
The Brahmana escapes from Garuda's throat. Garuda meets his father Kasyapa and asks for more food.
Kasyapa tells the story of the brothers cursed to be an elephant and a tortoise, blesses Garuda, and Garuda picks up both and lands on a giant banyan whose branch breaks.
Garuda saves the Valakhilya sages, receives the name Garuda, and Kasyapa asks the sages to let go of the branch.
Garuda drops the branch on an empty mountain and eats the elephant and tortoise. Omens appear in heaven, Vrihaspati explains them, and Indra and the gods prepare to defend the nectar.
Saunaka's questions, and the story of how Indra mocked the Valakhilyas and they began a sacrifice to create a rival to him.
Kasyapa mediates: the new Indra will be a bird king and his son. Vinata conceives and bears Aruna and Garuda.
Closing line: the thirty-first section ends.
The battle of Garuda against the gods and Yakshas, and his quenching of the fire around the nectar.
Closing line: the thirty-second section ends.
Garuda gets past the wheel and snakes, takes the nectar, meets Vishnu and gets boons, is struck by Indra's thunderbolt and sheds a feather, and Indra offers friendship.
Closing line: the thirty-third section ends.
The friendship of Garuda and Indra, Garuda's boast, and the plan to return the nectar. Garuda asks that snakes be his food.
The snakes lose the nectar, their tongues split, Garuda frees his mother, and the story ends with its benefit.
Saunaka's request and Sauti's introduction to the list. The list begins with Sesha, Vasuki and others.
First part of the list of snake names.
Second part of the list of snake names.
Last names, and Sauti's remark that the rest are countless.
Sesha's penances and his talk with Brahma, in which he says he wants to avoid his brothers.
Sesha asks only for virtue. Brahma tells him to support the earth, and he slides under it and holds it.
Brahma praises Sesha as Dharma himself and gives him Garuda as helper.
Vasuki's council: his speech, the many proposals of the snakes to stop Janamejaya's sacrifice, and his rejection of them.
Elapatra recalls what Brahma told the gods: Astika, son of Jaratkaru and Vasuki's sister, will stop the sacrifice. He advises Vasuki to prepare.
Vasuki raises his sister, the gods plead for him to Brahma, Brahma confirms the plan, and Vasuki sets snakes to watch the sage.
Saunaka asks about the name Jaratkaru and Astika's birth.
Vasuki's waiting, and the tale of Parikshit hunting a deer, meeting the silent sage Samika, and placing a dead snake on his shoulder. Samika's son Sringin comes home.
Krisa taunts Sringin about his father's dead snake.
Sringin hears the story of the king and the snake from Krisa and curses the king.
Sringin tells his father, who criticises him and explains the value of kings.
Sringin insists on his curse; Samika counsels forgiveness and sends a disciple, Gaurmukha, to warn the king.
Gaurmukha's message, the king's regret, his fortified tower, and Kasyapa meeting Takshaka on the road.
The tree test: Takshaka burns a banyan with a bite, and Kasyapa revives it.
Takshaka buys Kasyapa off, sends disguised snakes with fruit to the king, and bites the king when he puts a worm from the fruit on his neck.
The death of Parikshit, the crowning of Janamejaya, and his marriage to Vapushtama.
Jaratkaru meets his ancestors in the pit, offers his merit, and they explain the rope, the rat and their plight.
Jaratkaru reveals who he is to his ancestors.
He agrees to marry on his conditions, searches in vain, calls aloud in the forest, and Vasuki brings his sister.
Vasuki's offer, the marriage and its agreement, the conception, and the sunset dilemma while the sage sleeps.
She wakes him, he is offended and leaves, with a prophecy about the son.
The sage leaves for penance.
She tells her brother about the sage's departure, and Vasuki is reassured by his words.
The birth and upbringing of Astika.
Saunaka's request. Janamejaya's question to his ministers and their account of Parikshit's reign.
Janamejaya asks for the full story of his father's death. The ministers describe the hunt and the dead snake.
The ministers tell how the sage was insulted, how his son Sringin cursed the king, and how Takshaka killed the king after Kasyapa was paid off.
Janamejaya asks his ministers for every detail, grieves, and declares his resolve to avenge his father on Takshaka.
Janamejaya decides on a snake-sacrifice, the priests explain it, the platform is built, and a builder warns of obstruction, so the king bars entry to all.
The priests start the sacrifice, and countless snakes of every kind fall into the fire.
Saunaka asks about the priests, Sauti names them, and the snakes continue to fall into the fire while Takshaka seeks Indra's protection.
Vasuki, grieving over the destruction of his race, calls his sister and asks her to send her son Astika to stop the sacrifice.
Jaratkaru tells Astika that Kadru cursed the snakes to burn in the sacrifice, and that the gods asked Brahman how to undo the curse.
Brahman says a Brahmana born of Jaratkaru will save the snakes, Jaratkaru reveals her son's role, and Astika promises to stop the sacrifice.
Astika gets past the doorkeepers and enters the sacrificial compound, where he honours the king, priests, and sacred fire.
Astika praises the sacrifice and its priests with a long string of comparisons, and the king, noticing signs around him, addresses them.
Janamejaya offers Astika a boon, but the Sadasyas and the Hotri say Takshaka has not yet arrived, and the king urges the priests to finish the rite.
The priests and the Suta Lohitaksha say Takshaka is hiding with Indra, and the Hotri's libations force Indra to release him toward the fire.
Takshaka is about to fall into the fire when Astika asks that the sacrifice end, and the king offers gold and cattle instead.
Astika refuses all gifts and asks only for the end of the sacrifice, and the assembly presses the king to grant it.
Sauti names the principal snakes from several families, and says the rest are too many to count, all burned in the fire.
Sauti adds that many other huge and powerful snakes were burned in the great sacrifice.
The king grants Astika's boon, ends the sacrifice, rewards the priests, and sends Astika home to his family.
The snakes thank Astika and promise safety to anyone who remembers his deed, and Astika later goes to heaven.
Sauti closes the story, saying the recital is a charm against fear of snakes, and that he passes on Pramati's tale to Ruru.
Saunaka asks for Vyasa's history, Sauti explains what Vyasa recited, and Sauti agrees to tell the Mahabharata from the start.
Vyasa is introduced and welcomed with honour, and Janamejaya asks him about the Kurus, the Pandavas, and the cause of their war.
At Vyasa's command, Vaisampayana begins the full recital of the history to the king and the assembly.
Vaisampayana explains why the Pandavas were driven out, with Duryodhana's plots: poison, drowning, and a lac house at Varanavata that Vidura had warned them about.
The Pandavas escape the lac house, win Draupadi, settle Khandavaprastha, and are sent into exile after a dice game, and then the war ends the rivalry.
Janamejaya asks for the full recital, and Vaisampayana agrees and describes the Mahabharata's size, merits, author's purpose, and range of subjects.
Indra blesses King Uparichara Vasu with a crystal car, a garland and a pole, and Vasu starts a festival in Indra's honour.
Vasu's sons found kingdoms, his children are born from a river and a mountain, and Vasu sends his seed to his wife Girika through a hawk.
The hawk drops the seed, a fish swallows it, and from the fish come the twins Matsya and Satyavati, the girl later courted by the sage Parasara.
Satyavati, freed from her fishy smell, bears Vyasa, who arranges the Vedas, and the text lists the births of Bhishma, Vidura, the Pandavas, the Kauravas and their allies.
The text says hundreds of thousands of kings fought in the great battle, and it names only the principal ones.
Vaisampayana says that the Kshatriyas were restored after Parasurama, the earth prospered, and then Asuras were reborn as kings who oppressed the world, so the earth went to Brahman for help.
Brahman tells the gods to be born on earth, and Indra goes to Narayana, who agrees to be incarnated.
Vaisampayana says the gods were reborn among royal and Brahmarshi families and slew the Danavas and Rakshasas, then begins the genealogy that Janamejaya requested.
He recites the lines of Kasyapa's children and says that the account brings long life, progeny and fame to those who read it.
Vaisampayana names Brahman's sons and their lines, including the Rudras, Daksha's daughters, the Vasus, Dharma's sons, and the Adityas, with Kasyapa as father of gods and Asuras.
He traces the Bhrigu descendants, including Sukra, Chyavana, Aurva and Parasurama, and lists the animals and beings born of Tamra, Krodha, Surabhi and others.

Vaisampayana names the earthly rebirths of Asuras, Danavas and other beings, from kings like Jarasandha to heroes like Bhishma, Drona and Duryodhana, and Janamejaya asks for the sons of Dhritarashtra.
Vaisampayana lists Dhritarashtra's children, then explains how the Pandavas, Draupadi, Abhimanyu and Karna were born as portions of gods and other beings.
Janamejaya asks for the Kuru line from its beginning, and Vaisampayana starts with King Dushmanta and describes his prosperous, virtuous reign.
Dushmanta marches into the forest with a great army and hunts until the forest is emptied of its animals.
Dushmanta crosses a barren plain, reaches a beautiful forest by the Malini, and resolves to visit the hermitage of Kanwa.
He enters the hermitage with only his minister and priest, and is amazed by the chanting and learning of its Brahmanas.
In the empty hermitage Dushmanta meets Sakuntala, who says she is Kanwa's daughter, and he questions her about her birth.
Sakuntala starts to explain her birth, quoting her father's account of Indra's fear of Viswamitra and his sending of Menaka to tempt him.
Kanwa's account continues with the union of Viswamitra and Menaka, the abandoned infant guarded by vultures, and her adoption by Kanwa.
Dushmanta proposes a Gandharva marriage and argues for it from the rules of marriage, and Sakuntala agrees on condition that her son becomes heir.
They marry, Dushmanta promises to send an escort, and Kanwa, returning home, approves the union and blesses the coming son.
Sakuntala asks Kanwa for a boon that the Paurava monarchs stay virtuous and keep their thrones.
Sakuntala brings her son to Dushmanta and asks him to honour his promise, but he denies knowing her, and she answers with a long speech on a father's duty and on truth.
A voice from heaven declares the boy to be Dushmanta's son, the king names him Bharata and installs him as heir, and the text describes Bharata's conquests and sacrifices.
Vaisampayana recites the genealogy from Daksha through Manu, Pururavas and Nahusha to Yayati, who exchanges his old age for Puru's youth and returns it again.
Yayati crowns Puru, goes to the mount of Bhrigu, and after long years of asceticism dies and ascends to heaven with his wives.
Janamejaya asks about Yayati's marriage, and the gods send Kacha to Sukra to learn the reviving science, and Kacha becomes his disciple.
Kacha serves Sukra and Devayani for five hundred years, the Danavas kill him, Sukra revives him, and they kill him again.
Kacha is hidden inside Sukra's stomach, is brought out by a rip in his belly, and revives Sukra, who then curses wine-drinking Brahmanas.
Kacha, after a thousand years of study, takes his leave to return to heaven.
Devayani asks Kacha to take her hand, he refuses, and each curses the other.
Kacha returns to heaven, and the gods praise his deed and grant him a share in sacrificial offerings.
Indra's trick sets off the quarrel between Devayani and Sarmishtha, Sarmishtha throws Devayani into a well, and Yayati finds her and asks who she is.
Yayati lifts Devayani out and returns to his capital, and Devayani's father Sukra is told of the insult and soothes her.
Sukra urges forgiveness over anger, and Devayani refuses, saying she will not stay among those who speak ill of good behaviour.
Sukra, angered at the insult, prepares to leave the Asuras, and Vrishaparvan begs him to stay and offers him all the Asura wealth.
Devayani demands that Sarmishtha and a thousand maids attend her, and Vrishaparvan orders Sarmishtha to comply.
Sarmishtha agrees to become Devayani's attendant and to follow her wherever she is given away, and Sukra returns to the Asura capital.
Devayani and Sarmishtha meet Yayati in the woods, and he asks their names and their stations.
Devayani chooses Yayati, he resists on grounds of caste, Sukra arrives and gives Devayani to him, and absolves him of the sin of a mixed marriage.
Yayati marries Devayani with the proper rites, receives Sarmishtha and the maids, and returns to his capital.
Yayati installs Devayani and Sarmishtha, Devayani bears a son, and Sarmishtha, anxious to have a child, approaches the king with her request.
Yayati yields to Sarmishtha, and she bears a son.
Devayani learns of Sarmishtha's child and is told a Rishi is the father, then finds Sarmishtha's three sons with Yayati in the woods and learns the truth.
The boys run to their mother, Devayani accuses Sarmishtha, and she leaves for her father Sukra, who curses Yayati with decrepitude.
Yayati begs Sukra to remove the curse, and Sukra says he can pass it to a son willing to take it.
Yayati asks Yadu and Turvasu to exchange youth for his old age, and both refuse and are cursed.
Yayati asks Drahyu and Anu, who refuse and are cursed, and then Puru agrees and takes the decrepitude.
Yayati enjoys Puru's youth for a thousand years, renounces desire, returns the youth, and, after the four orders object, is backed by the people in crowning Puru.
Puru is crowned, Yayati goes to the forest, and the peoples descended from his sons are named.
Yayati withdraws to the forest, ascends to heaven and is hurled down, and Janamejaya asks for the whole story, which Vaisampayana agrees to tell.
Yayati dwells in heaven, and Indra asks him what he said to Puru when he gave up the kingdom.
Yayati recites his counsel to Puru on kingship, forgiveness and speech.
Indra tells Yayati he must fall for disregarding others, Yayati asks to fall among the virtuous, and as he falls the royal sage Ashtaka welcomes him.
Yayati, falling from heaven, introduces himself, speaks on destiny and humility, and recounts his stay in the heavens and his fall.
Ashtaka asks why Yayati was cast out, and Yayati describes the earth-hell of self-praise and the sufferings of rebirth.
Ashtaka asks how fallen beings are reborn, and Yayati explains rebirth from a subtle seed through the womb.
Yayati lists the seven gates to heaven and says vanity destroys them.
Ashtaka asks how the four stages of life should be lived, and Yayati outlines the duties of each, then the number of kinds of Munis.
Yayati explains what a Muni is, wherever he lives, and describes the silent, detached ascetic.
Ashtaka asks whether the ascetic or the knower reaches Brahman first, and Yayati says the wise do, and then reveals that he is falling to the earth-hell.
Ashtaka offers Yayati the regions he has earned, Yayati refuses, and Pratardana asks whether he too has regions.
Pratardana offers his worlds, and Yayati refuses, saying a king should not take another's merit.
Vasumat asks for heavenly worlds, offers them to Yayati, and proposes that he buy them, which Yayati declines.
Sivi offers his worlds too, Yayati refuses, and Ashtaka says they will descend if Yayati does not take them.
Yayati says he will take only what he has earned, and the others point him to five golden cars.
The company sets out for heaven together, and Ashtaka asks why Sivi has gone ahead, and Yayati explains and identifies himself.
Vaisampayana closes the episode, saying Yayati ascends to heaven, rescued by his descendants.
Vaisampayana traces Puru's line through Dushmanta and Bharata to Samvarana, whose defeat by the Panchalas is reversed by Vasishtha, and on through Kuru, Pratipa and Santanu.
Vaisampayana says many more excellent monarchs were born in the lines of Bharata and Manu.
Vaisampayana starts the genealogy from Daksha and Aditi and runs through Yayati and the descendants of Puru to Tansu.
The genealogy passes through Ilina and Dushmanta to Sakuntala and her son Bharata, with verses on Dushmanta's descendants.
The name of Bharata is explained, and the line runs through Hastinapura and its kings to Santanu.
The text traces the line from Santanu through Bhishma, Satyavati's sons and Pandu's curse to the Pandavas, their marriages, and the rebirth of Parikshit, and ends with the recital's benefits.
Mahabhisha is cursed for staring at Ganga, asks to be reborn to Pratipa, and Ganga agrees to bear the Vasus, cursed by Vasishtha, as her children.
Ganga comes to Pratipa as a maiden, is refused and offered as a wife to his son, agrees on conditions, and Santanu later meets and asks to marry her.
Ganga marries Santanu under conditions, drowns their sons one by one until the king protests, and leaves after revealing who she is, giving the eighth child to Santanu to rear.
Santanu asks why the Vasus were cursed, and Ganga describes Vasishtha's asylum and the cow Nandini, and how the Vasus, led by Dyu, stole her.
Vasishtha curses the Vasus, softens the curse for Dyu, Ganga disposes of the children, and she leaves with her son while Santanu returns home.
Santanu's virtues and peaceful reign are praised, and Ganga presents his grown son Devavrata, whom Santanu makes heir.
Santanu meets the fisherman's daughter, the fisherman demands a pledge about her son, and Devavrata goes to win her for his father.
Devavrata renounces the throne and vows celibacy, the fisherman gives his daughter, and Devavrata is named Bhishma and granted the choice of his death.
Santanu's sons are born to Satyavati, Santanu dies, Chitrangada is killed by a Gandharva, and Bhishma installs Vichitravirya.
Bhishma wins the Kasi princesses by force, defeats the kings and Salya, lets Amba go, and marries Ambika and Ambalika to Vichitravirya, who dies of consumption.
Satyavati asks Bhishma to raise children on his brother's widows, and Bhishma refuses on grounds of truth and his vow.
Bhishma tells Satyavati of Parashurama's destruction of the Kshatriyas and the story of Utathya's son Dirghatamas, born blind, and of his marriage and quarrel with his wife.
Dirghatamas is cast into the Ganges, rescued by King Vali, and fathers sons, and Bhishma concludes that the line may be continued by Brahmanas' seed.
Bhishma proposes a paid Brahmana, Satyavati reveals that Vyasa, her son by Parashara, can serve, and Bhishma approves and calls Vyasa.
Vyasa agrees on condition of a year's vow and warns of his looks, and Satyavati persuades the princess of Kosala to accept him.
The three widows bear Dhritarashtra, who is blind, Pandu, who is pale, and Vidura, born of a maidservant, each as Vyasa has foretold.
Janamejaya asks about Dharma's curse, and Vaisampayana tells how the sage Mandavya was impaled as a thief and was visited by sages in bird form.
Mandavya forgives the king, questions the god of justice, learns that his offence was a child's, and curses Dharma to be born as Vidura.
The Kuru land prospers, Bhishma raises the three princes, Pandu becomes king, and Bhishma turns to Vidura for counsel.
Bhishma proposes marriages, Vidura defers, and Gandhari is married to Dhritarashtra, blindfolding herself out of devotion.
Pritha receives Durvasa's mantra, summons the Sun, and bears Karna, who is abandoned and raised by Radha and her husband, gives his armour to Indra, and is named Karna.
Kunti chooses Pandu at her father's assembly, and the couple is married and goes to Hastinapura.
Bhishma wins Madri for Pandu from Salya with gifts, Pandu marries her, and he conquers many kingdoms and returns in triumph.
Pandu shares his wealth with the family and performs sacrifices, retires to the woods with his wives, and Bhishma arranges Vidura's marriage.
Gandhari's boon and two-year pregnancy lead to a lump of flesh, which Vyasa divides into parts that are kept in pots of butter to mature.
Duryodhana is born with ominous signs, Dhritarashtra asks who should be king, and Vidura's advice to cast off the eldest is refused, and the hundred sons, a daughter and Yuyutsu are born.
Janamejaya asks how Duhsala was born, and Vaisampayana explains that the extra part of the lump, set aside for Gandhari's wish, became her daughter.
Janamejaya asks for the sons' names in birth order, and Vaisampayana recites them, adding that they were skilled warriors and that Duhsala was married to Jayadratha.
Janamejaya asks about the Pandavas, and Vaisampayana begins with Pandu shooting a deer in the forest, which turns out to be a sage in animal form, who cries out like a man.
Pandu defends the killing, and the dying sage answers that the timing was the crime and curses Pandu to die when desire takes him.

Pandu vows to renounce desire and the world, and his wives insist on sharing his forest life. He gives away his wealth, and his attendants carry the news back to Hastinapura, where Dhritarashtra grieves.
Pandu travels with his wives through a series of named mountains and lakes in the Himalayas, reaching the Hundred-Peak mountain where he continues his austerities.
Pandu asks to go with the sages to Brahma's gathering. They warn him that the northern heights are too dangerous, and he answers that he is sonless and has not repaid his debt to his ancestors.
The sages foresee a blessed son for Pandu, and Pandu, recalling his lost power to beget children, asks Kunti to have sons by another man.
Kunti tells Pandu she will accept only him, then recounts the story of Vyushitaswa and his widow Bhadra, whose promised offspring came from the dead king's body, and asks Pandu to do likewise.
Pandu argues from old precedents that wives should bear children at their husband's command, and Kunti recalls the mantra Durvasa once gave her to call a god.
Pandu chooses Dharma, the god of justice, as the father, and Kunti agrees to call him.
Kunti calls Dharma and Vayu, who father Yudhishthira and Bhima. Pandu then decides to win Indra's favour through a year of severe austerity, and Kunti keeps her own vow.
Indra promises Pandu a son and fathers Arjuna, and the gods and celestial beings gather to celebrate. When Pandu asks for more children, Kunti refuses.
Madri asks Pandu for children, Pandu asks Kunti to help, and Kunti tells Madri to call a god, so Madri bears twins to the Ashvins.
The five sons are named and grow up on the mountain, and Kunti later refuses Pandu's request for more children.
Pandu forces himself on Madri in a spring grove and dies in the act. Kunti and Madri argue over who will follow him in death, and Madri makes her case.
Madri ascends her husband's funeral pyre.

The sages bring Pandu's family to Hastinapura, where the court and citizens gather. The eldest sage presents the five sons, explains their divine births and asks for the funeral rites, and then the sages vanish.
Dhritarashtra orders a royal funeral, and Vidura and Bhishma carry out the rites by the Ganga, where the bodies are burned while the people weep.
The Kurus perform the water rite, and the people mourn for twelve days with the Pandavas.
After the funeral, Vyasa warns that the age is declining, and Satyavati retreats to the forest to die. The Pandava boys grow up, and Bhima proves stronger than the Kaurava boys in play.
Duryodhana, jealous of Bhima, poisons his food and throws him into the Ganga, but Bhima sinks to the Naga realm, where the serpents' venom cancels the poison and he revives.
The Naga king's kin give Bhima nectar that makes him very strong, and he drinks eight jars of it.
The Kauravas return without Bhima, and Yudhishthira and Kunti, alarmed, ask about him; Kunti fears Duryodhana has killed him.
Vidura advises Kunti not to accuse Duryodhana, and to protect her other sons.
Bhima wakes, returns from the Naga realm and tells his brothers what happened; Duryodhana tries poison again, and Yuyutsu warns the Pandavas.
Duryodhana and his allies keep plotting, but the Pandavas bear it on Vidura's advice, and Dhritarashtra sends the princes to Kripa to learn arms.
Janamejaya asks about Kripa's birth, and Vaisampayana traces the twins to Saradwat and a nymph sent by Indra, and tells how Santanu adopted them and Saradwat trained Kripa.
Bhishma hires Drona to teach the princes, and Vaisampayana traces Drona's birth from Bharadwaja's seed, his friendship with Drupada, and the birth of his son Aswatthaman.
Drona goes to Rama, Jamadagni's son, who has given away all his wealth, and receives all of his weapons and knowledge of arms.
Drona reminds Drupada of their friendship, Drupada mocks his poverty and rejects him, and Drona leaves for Hastinapura.
Drona lives in Kripa's house, and when the princes lose a ball in a well, he recovers it with blades of grass before they know who he is.
Drona retrieves a ring, the princes report to Bhishma, and Drona tells how Drupada scorned him; Bhishma then welcomes him as teacher.
Bhishma honours Drona, and Drona teaches the princes, with Arjuna excelling; Karna, backed by Duryodhana, opposes Arjuna, and Ekalavya is refused as a pupil.
On a hunt, a dog leads the princes to Ekalavya, who shows great skill; Drona then asks for his right thumb as fee, and Ekalavya gives it.
Drona rates the princes' skills, then tests them with a mock bird, and each pupil reports seeing more than the target and is sent aside.
Arjuna alone passes Drona's aiming test, and later he saves Drona from a crocodile and receives the Brahmasira weapon.
Drona asks the king's permission for a public display, the arena is prepared, and on the day the princes show their skill, ending with Bhima and Duryodhana entering with maces.
The crowd divides between Duryodhana and Bhima partisans, Aswatthaman restrains the maces, and Drona presents Arjuna, whose display of weapons wins delight.
As the show is nearly over, a thunder-like sound comes from the gate, and Duryodhana and his brothers rise in haste.
Karna enters the lists and challenges Arjuna, but Kripa asks for his lineage, and Duryodhana makes him king of Anga.
Karna is crowned king of Anga, and he and Duryodhana embrace in friendship.
Karna's charioteer father Adhiratha comes to the arena, Bhima mocks Karna as a charioteer's son, and Duryodhana defends him at length. The day ends with the crowd dispersing.
Drona sends the princes against Drupada as his fee; the Kauravas are routed, and the Pandavas advance, and Bhima cuts down Drupada's elephants.
Arjuna defeats Drupada's general Satyajit, seizes Drupada himself, and holds back Bhima from killing the Panchala people; the princes bring the captive to Drona.
Drona humbles Drupada, gives him half his kingdom and asks for friendship, and Drupada resolves to find a son who can defeat Drona; Drona keeps Ahicchatra.
Dhritarashtra names Yudhishthira heir apparent, and the Pandavas grow in skill; Drona reminds Arjuna of his promised fee, and the Pandavas conquer many kingdoms, which leaves Dhritarashtra uneasy.
Dhritarashtra asks Kanika whether to make peace or war with the Pandavas, and Kanika gives a long list of ruthless principles of statecraft.
Kanika tells the fable of the jackal and the deer, then offers more advice on deceit and spies and urges the king to guard against the Pandavas.

Vidura learns of the plot to burn Kunti and her sons, provides a boat for their escape, and the house of lac burns; Janamejaya asks for the full story, and Vaisampayana turns to the citizens' talk of Yudhishthira as king.
Duryodhana, distressed by the citizens' support for Yudhishthira, urges Dhritarashtra to act before the kingdom passes to Pandu's line.
Duryodhana urges that the Pandavas be sent to Varanavata; Dhritarashtra hesitates, citing Pandu's virtue and the elders' disapproval, and Duryodhana argues the elders will not oppose it.
Duryodhana wins the people over, Dhritarashtra's councillors praise Varanavata to the Pandavas, and the Pandavas set out after receiving the elders' blessings.
Duryodhana instructs Purochana to build an inflammable house in which to burn the Pandavas, and Purochana sets off at once.
The Pandavas take leave of the elders and citizens, and Vidura secretly warns Yudhishthira in code that the house is a trap.
Kunti asks what Vidura said, Yudhishthira explains the warning, and the Pandavas set out for Varanavata.
The Pandavas are welcomed and lodged in Purochana's house; Yudhishthira realises it is a trap set by Duryodhana, and he tells Bhima to stay calm and plan a secret escape.
A miner sent by Vidura warns of the fire and digs a secret tunnel under the house while the Pandavas feign contentment.
After a year of calm, the Pandavas choose their moment; on the feast night Bhima sets the house on fire, and the family escapes through the tunnel while the citizens watch the blaze.
Vidura's agent meets the Pandavas by the Ganga, shows them a boat, proves his trustworthiness with Vidura's coded words, and ferries them across.
The people of Varanavata find the burnt house and blame Duryodhana, and Dhritarashtra mourns the Pandavas and orders their rites, while Vidura does not weep.
The Pandavas cross the Ganga and reach a dense forest, exhausted, and Yudhishthira asks Bhima to carry them on.
Bhima carries his family through the forest, fetches water for the thirsty Kunti, laments their hardship, and keeps watch while they sleep.
Hidimva sends his sister to fetch the sleepers, but she falls in love with Bhima and offers to help him; Bhima refuses to abandon his family.
Bhima tells the Rakshasa woman that he will not wake his family and that Rakshasas cannot match his strength.
Hidimva comes down from his tree, sees his sister's infatuation, and rushes to kill her, but Bhima stops him.
Bhima challenges Hidimva alone, the two wrestle, and their struggle wakes the Pandavas.
Kunti questions Hidimva, and the brothers wake to see Bhima fighting; Arjuna urges haste, and Bhima kills the Rakshasa.
The Pandavas set out with their mother, followed by Hidimva's sister.
Yudhishthira stops Bhima from harming Hidimva's sister, who begs to marry him; Bhima agrees to stay with her until she bears a son, and Ghatotkacha is born.
Hidimva and her son Ghatotkacha take their leave of the Pandavas.
The Pandavas wander disguised through the lands, meet Vyasa, and are led to Ekachakra, where Vyasa predicts a great future for Yudhishthira.
The Pandavas agree to wait for Vyasa, and he goes back to his home.
The Pandavas live by alms at Ekachakra; while Bhima is at home, Kunti hears a Brahmana household wailing and asks Bhima to help.
The Brahmana, his wife, son and daughter lament their helplessness and speak of dying together.
The Brahmana's wife offers to go to the Rakshasa in his place, and the couple weep together in silence.
The daughter urges her parents to sacrifice her, the little son makes them smile, and Kunti steps forward to speak to them.
Kunti asks the cause of the Brahmana's grief, and he explains the tribute owed to the Rakshasa Vaka and his plan to go with his family.
Kunti offers one of her sons, the Brahmana refuses to let anyone die for him, Kunti promises her son's strength, and Bhima agrees to go.
Yudhishthira objects to Kunti's plan to send Bhima to the Rakshasa; Kunti defends it by pointing to Bhima's strength and the debt owed to the Brahmana.
Yudhishthira approves of the plan, and Bhima takes the tribute to Vaka's forest, where a long fight breaks out.
Bhima makes Vaka's kin promise to stop eating men, the townspeople find the body, and the host Brahmana credits an unnamed Brahmana with the killing to protect the Pandavas.
The Pandavas stay on at Ekachakra, Janamejaya asks what they did next, and a visiting Brahmana tells them of distant lands and of Draupadi's birth.
The Pandavas ask the Brahmana for the details of the births and of the broken friendship, and he begins his account of Draupadi's birth.
The Brahmana narrates Drona's birth, his boyhood friendship with Drupada, Drupada's scorn, and the Pandavas' capture of Drupada as fee.
Drupada courts the sages Yaja and Upayaja to get a Drona-slayer, and Yaja's sacrifice produces Dhrishtadyumna and Krishna, and Drona trains the prince.
Kunti proposes leaving Ekachakra for Panchala, and Yudhishthira agrees but asks whether his younger brothers will consent.
The Pandavas set out for Panchala, and Vyasa visits them to foretell Draupadi's marriage to all five brothers, then departs.
The Gandharva Angaraparna bars the Pandavas at the Ganga; Arjuna defeats him with a fiery weapon, and Yudhishthira orders mercy at his wife's plea.
The grateful Gandharva offers Arjuna a science of illusion and horses in exchange for his fire weapon, and explains why he rebuked the Pandavas.
Arjuna asks about the name Tapatyas, and the Gandharva tells how the Sun chose King Samvarana for his daughter Tapati, and how the king came upon her in the hills.
Samvarana declares his desire and asks Tapati's name, but she vanishes, and the king wanders in grief.
Tapati reappears, the king declares his passion, and Tapati tells him to ask her father, the Sun, for her hand.

Samvarana is revived and worships the Sun, Vasishtha wins Tapati for him, and when a drought strikes Vasishtha brings the couple home and the rains return; the Gandharva then explains why Arjuna is called Tapatya.
Arjuna asks about Vasishtha, and the Gandharva describes his power and urges the Pandavas to appoint a learned priest.
Arjuna asks about the feud, and the Gandharva tells how Viswamitra, after a visit to Vasishtha's hermitage, coveted the wish-granting cow Nandini and offered a kingdom for her.
Viswamitra seizes Nandini by force, and Vasishtha, bound by his forgiving vow, leaves the cow to resist for herself.
Nandini routs Viswamitra's army with barbarian troops from her body, and Viswamitra renounces power and becomes a Brahmana through austerity.
Kalmashapada and Shakti clash on a forest path; Shakti curses the king, Viswamitra possesses him with a Rakshasa, and the king's cook serves human flesh to a Brahmana, who curses him again.
The possessed king devours Shakti and the other sons, and Vasishtha tries to kill himself by several means, all of which fail.
Vasishtha tries to end his life in rivers, learns from Adrisyanti that she carries Shakti's child, and frees Kalmashapada, who asks for an heir, which Vasishtha grants.
Parasara is born, calls Vasishtha father, and resolves to destroy the world; Vasishtha begins to dissuade him by telling the story of the Bhrigus and the Kshatriyas.
The Bhrigu woman tells the Kshatriyas that her son blinded them; Aurva restores their sight but resolves on destruction, until the Pitris beg him to restrain his wrath.
Aurva defends his wrath, the Pitris suggest he cast it into the sea, and Aurva does so, which Vasishtha offers as a lesson to Parasara.
Parasara begins a sacrifice to destroy the Rakshasas in revenge; the sages urge him to stop, and he ends the rite and casts its fire into the north.
Arjuna asks about the queen's union with Vasishtha, and the Gandharva tells of the Brahmani's curse and the king's repentance and request for an heir.
Arjuna asks the Gandharva for a priest; the Gandharva names Dhaumya, whom the Pandavas install before setting out for the Swayamvara.
On the road the Pandavas meet Brahmanas bound for Drupada's Swayamvara, who describe Draupadi and invite them along, and Yudhishthira agrees.
The Pandavas enter Panchala unrecognised, Drupada announces the contest with a stiff bow, and the Swayamvara begins before a great crowd of kings.
Dhrishtadyumna names the Kaurava princes, Karna and a long list of kings and Yadavas who have come to compete for Draupadi.
The princes try the bow and fail one after another; Karna draws it, but Draupadi rejects him as a charioteer's son, and Arjuna steps forward when the rest give up.
Arjuna, in Brahmana disguise, strings the bow and shoots the mark, and wins Draupadi, to the joy of the gods and the crowd.
The rejected kings rush at Drupada, Bhima and Arjuna face them, and Krishna identifies the brothers to Balarama.
Arjuna and Bhima fight off the kings, Arjuna duels Karna and Bhima tosses Shalya; Krishna persuades the kings to withdraw, and Kunti worries at home.
The brothers present Draupadi to Kunti, who is alarmed by her own words, and Yudhishthira resolves that Draupadi shall be the common wife of all five.
Krishna and Balarama visit the potter's house, and Krishna greets Yudhishthira and praises the brothers' escape.
Dhrishtadyumna hides in the potter's house and overhears the Pandavas, and in the morning he reports to Drupada, who asks who won his daughter.
Dhrishtadyumna reports the contest and the night at the potter's house, Drupada's priest asks the strangers who they are, and Yudhishthira answers and the feast is announced.
The invitation comes, the party rides to the palace, and Drupada's display and the meal show the guests' royal bearing to Drupada and his son.
Drupada asks who they are, Yudhishthira reveals the Pandavas' identity and their escape from Varanavata, and Drupada promises support and asks Arjuna to take Krishna's hand.
Yudhishthira proposes that Krishna be shared by all five brothers, Drupada objects, Yudhishthira defends it by his mother's command, and Vyasa arrives as the matter is being discussed.
Vyasa asks for the company's views; Drupada and Dhrishtadyumna object, and Yudhishthira defends the match with precedent and his mother's command.
Kunti voices her worry about untruth, and Vyasa says he will explain the custom only to Drupada, taking him aside to begin.
Vyasa tells the story of Yama's pause in killing, Indra's humbling by Mahadeva, the curse that sends five Indras into the world of men, and the birth of Krishna and Valadeva.
Vyasa names the brothers as the former Indras and Draupadi as Sri, grants Drupada divine sight, and tells the story of a maiden who asked Mahadeva for five husbands.
Drupada accepts Vyasa's account, Vyasa names the day, and the wedding is held with Dhaumya presiding, followed by Drupada's gifts and the Pandavas' settling in Panchala.
Drupada's women greet Kunti, Kunti blesses Krishna, and Hari (Krishna) sends the newly married Pandavas a great store of gifts.
News of the marriage spreads, the kings blame Bhishma and Dhritarashtra, Duryodhana returns dejected, and Vidura tells Dhritarashtra the Pandavas are alive and allied with Drupada.
After Vidura leaves, Duryodhana and Karna press Dhritarashtra to act against the Pandavas in private.
Dhritarashtra asks for his son's plans in private, and Duryodhana sets out a list of ways to ruin the Pandavas, ending by asking Karna's opinion.
Karna rejects Duryodhana's subtle plans and urges open war on Drupada, Dhritarashtra praises him but asks the elders to advise, and the king gathers his ministers.
Bhishma opposes any quarrel with the Pandavas, appeals to the king's good name, and urges that half the kingdom be given to them.
Drona backs Bhishma and proposes a diplomatic mission; Karna mocks the elders with a tale about kingship and fate, and Drona rebukes him.
Vidura defends the elders, argues the Pandavas are invincible and rightful heirs, and urges the king to make peace with them and win Drupada as an ally.
Dhritarashtra accepts the counsel and sends Vidura to bring the Pandavas home, and Vidura delivers gifts and the request to Drupada.
Drupada gives his consent on condition that the brothers, Rama and Krishna all agree, and Vasudeva supports their return.
The Pandavas enter Hastinapura to a joyful welcome, Dhritarashtra sends them to Khandavaprastha, and they build Indraprastha, which attracts many people.
The Pandavas settle at Khandavaprastha, and Krishna returns to Dwaravati with Rama.
Janamejaya asks about the Pandavas' conduct, Narada visits and warns them of discord, and Yudhishthira asks for the tale behind the warning.
Narada recounts the brothers' birth, their penance on the Vindhya mountains, the gods' attempts to break them, and Brahma's boon that only each other can slay them.
The brothers conquer heaven and the lower worlds, then order the slaughter of sacrificers and Brahmanas, which ruins religion and daily life on earth.
The gods appeal to Brahma, Viswakarman creates Tilottama, she walks round the assembly, and then leaves to tempt the brothers.
Narada tells how the brothers fell out over Tilottama and destroyed each other, and the Pandavas make a rule about Draupadi on his advice.
Arjuna breaks the rule to recover a Brahmana's cattle, Yudhishthira tells him he has no fault, and Arjuna insists on exile to keep his word.
Arjuna obtains Yudhishthira's leave and sets out for the forest for twelve years.
Arjuna leaves for the forest with a retinue of Brahmanas and ascetics and reaches the source of the Ganga, where he thinks of settling.
At the Ganga's source, Ulupi pulls Arjuna into her Naga palace, persuades him to yield, and grants him invincibility in water.
Arjuna visits holy sites, reaches Manipura, and marries Chitrangada on her father's terms, then goes on his way after she bears a son.
Arjuna visits the shunned sacred waters, wrestles a crocodile at Saubhadra, and the freed Apsara begins to explain her curse.
Varga recounts the Brahmana's curse and pardon and Narada's advice, Arjuna frees the Apsaras, and he visits Chitrangada and his son before moving on to Gokarna.
Arjuna tours the western holy places, meets Krishna at Prabhasa and on Raivataka, and is welcomed into Dwaraka, where he stays with Krishna.
The Raivataka festival opens, Arjuna sees Bhadra and asks Krishna for her hand, and the plan to carry her off with Yudhishthira's assent is set.
Arjuna carries off Subhadra, the Yadava court sounds the alarm, and Valadeva rages at the insult while the others await Krishna's word.
Vasudeva defends the abduction, Arjuna marries Subhadra, the Vrishnis bring gifts to Indraprastha, and Abhimanyu and Draupadi's five sons are born and trained.
Yudhishthira's prosperous rule is described, Arjuna and Krishna set out for a summer outing on the Yamuna, and a radiant Brahmana approaches them as they talk.
Agni asks Arjuna and Krishna to help him burn Khandava, and the narrator tells the story of King Swetaki, whose sacrifice ended up making Agni sick.
Agni, surfeited from twelve years of butter, is told by the Creator to eat the forest's creatures, but the forest dwellers repeatedly put his blaze out.
Brahma sends Agni to Arjuna and Vasudeva, and Arjuna lists the weapons he needs for the task.
Agni summons Varuna, Arjuna and Krishna receive celestial weapons and a car, and Agni blazes around the forest.
Arjuna and Krishna cut down creatures fleeing the burning forest, the gods appeal to Indra, and Indra's rain struggles against the fire.
Arjuna blocks Indra's rain, Aswasena escapes, and the gods join the fight, which Arjuna and Krishna win before Indra's mountain is shattered.
The creatures of Khandava are slaughtered as the gods retreat, Arjuna shields the Asura Maya from Agni, and Agni burns the forest for many days.
Agni spares six of the forest's dwellers, named as Aswasena, Maya and four birds.
Janamejaya asks why the birds survived, and Vaisampayana tells how Mandapala, denied heaven, fathered sons as a bird and then praised Agni.
Agni, pleased with the praise, agrees to spare Mandapala's sons while burning the forest.
The fire approaches, Jarita laments, her chicks urge her to save herself, she proposes a mouse's hole, and the chicks refuse.
Jarita insists the hole is safe, the chicks refuse and urge her to save herself, and she leaves them as the fire approaches.
The four brothers speak in turn about wisdom, the eldest's duty, and the approaching fire.
Each brother sings a hymn of praise to Agni and asks for protection.
Agni, mindful of his promise to Mandapala, agrees to spare the birds, and Drona asks him to consume the creatures that trouble them.
Mandapala worries aloud to Lapita, the two quarrel over his divided attention, and he finds his sons safe but cold toward him.
Mandapala and Jarita quarrel, he cites Arundhati's jealousy, and the sons finally come forward to greet and worship him.
Mandapala reassures his sons, Agni is satisfied, Indra grants boons to Arjuna and Krishna, and Arjuna, Krishna and Maya rest by a river.
The Adi Parva closes, followed by a licence notice from the Project Gutenberg edition.
Maya, rescued by Arjuna, offers to do something in return, and Arjuna sends the offer on to Krishna.
Krishna asks Maya to build a grand hall for Yudhishthira, and Maya is honoured and begins construction on a large plot.
Krishna's farewells at Khandavaprastha, his ride out with the Pandavas, and his arrival at Dwaraka, followed by Yudhishthira's return to his capital and Krishna's welcome at home.
Maya sets out for the treasures, describes the sacred mountain site, recovers the club and conch, and builds the palace for the Pandavas, which he reports complete in fourteen months.
Yudhishthira enters the new hall after feeding Brahmins and giving gifts, and the sages, kings, princes and celestial musicians gather to attend him.
Narada arrives at the assembly, is welcomed by the Pandavas, and begins his long list of questions to Yudhishthira about kingship and the fruits of learning, wealth and marriage.
Narada asks about trade, artisans, the army's skills, public welfare and the care of the needy, and Yudhishthira vows to follow his advice.
Yudhishthira replies briefly to Narada's counsel, asks whether he has seen a finer hall, and Narada offers to describe the halls of the gods, which Yudhishthira asks him to do.
Narada describes Indra's assembly hall, its size and splendour, and the gods, sages, Gandharvas and Apsaras who attend Indra there.
Narada describes Yama's hall, a place of comfort, where many dead kings and sages, sannyasis, musicians and Yama's officers attend the god of justice.
Narada describes Varuna's hall in the waters, its gem trees and birds, and the snakes, demons, rivers, seas and mountains who worship Varuna there.
Narada describes Kuvera's hall, its beauty and its attendants, including Shiva and Parvati, and closes by announcing the description of Brahma's hall.
Narada tells how he reached Brahma's hall with the sun god's help, describes the beings who attend Brahma there, and says Yudhishthira's hall is the finest on earth.

Yudhishthira asks about Harishchandra and Pandu, Narada recounts Harishchandra's Rajasuya and relays Pandu's request, and Narada leaves for Dwaravati while Yudhishthira begins to consider the sacrifice.
Yudhishthira describes his peaceful reign and reflects on the Rajasuya, his ministers urge him to proceed, and he sends for Krishna and asks for his counsel.
Krishna surveys the kings who support Jarasandha, recounts the Yadavas' flight from Mathura and their new city, and says the Rajasuya requires Jarasandha's defeat.
Yudhishthira voices his doubts about Jarasandha, Bhima urges action, and Krishna argues that Jarasandha's captives must be freed and the sacrifice pursued through war.
Yudhishthira says he is afraid for his brothers and Krishna and asks that the plan be given up, and Arjuna replies that valour requires them to fight.
Krishna urges a secret attack on Jarasandha, Yudhishthira asks about him, and Krishna begins the story of Jarasandha's miraculous birth through the sage's mango and the Rakshasa woman Jara.
Jara explains that she is a household goddess who was pleased by worship and gave the child to the king, and the king names the boy Jarasandha and raises him.
The sage foretells Jarasandha's greatness, Vrihadratha retires and dies, and Jarasandha's power grows until the Yadavas hold back from fighting him.
Krishna proposes a duel with Jarasandha, Yudhishthira sends the three off with his blessing, and they journey in disguise across many rivers and lands to the city of Magadha.
Krishna shows Arjuna the city of Girivraja, the three break the Chaityaka peak and enter the city in disguise, and Jarasandha questions them and receives Krishna's explanation.
Jarasandha protests his innocence, Krishna accuses him and reveals their identity, Jarasandha accepts the challenge, and the duel is set with Bhima as the fighter.
Bhima and Jarasandha wrestle with bare arms for about two weeks, and when Jarasandha tires, Krishna urges Bhima to strike and Bhima resolves to kill him.

Rama laments and vows vengeance, wipes out the warriors, and retires to Mahendra; he then appears to Yudhishthira and his brothers and honours the Brahmanas.
Yudhishthira visits sacred places along the coast, fasts at Prabhasa, and is met by the Vrishnis, who weep at the Pandavas' condition.
Janamejaya asks about the meeting, and Valarama laments the Pandavas' suffering and attacks the Kuru elders and Duryodhana.
Satyaki urges war, Krishna explains Yudhishthira's pride, and Yudhishthira sends the Vrishnis home and proceeds to the Payosini.
Lomasa describes the sacrifices on the Payosini and the holy sites near the Narmada, and Yudhishthira asks about Chyavana and Indra.
Sukanya blinds Chyavana, the army is afflicted, and Saryati gives his daughter to the sage.
The Ashvins tempt Sukanya, restore Chyavana to youth, and Chyavana promises to make them Soma-drinkers.
Chyavana officiates for Saryati, Indra opposes the offering to the Ashvins, and Chyavana summons the demon Mada.
Indra accepts the Ashvins' right to Soma, Chyavana scatters Mada, and Lomasa lists the holy places for Yudhishthira to visit.
Yudhishthira asks about Mandhata, and Lomasa recounts his unusual birth, his rule, and the sacrifices and rain he brought, before Yudhishthira turns to Somaka.
Jantu is stung, Somaka laments his single son, and he asks the priest for a rite to get a hundred sons.
The priest proposes that Jantu be the sacrificial victim, with the smoke of his fat to bring the sons.
The sacrifice of Jantu and the birth of a hundred sons, followed by the priest's punishment in hell and Somaka's choice to share it.
Somaka and the priest work off their sins and are freed, and Lomasa recommends six nights of self-control at this hermitage.
Lomasa names the sacred sites along the Yamuna and in the Kuru field, Yudhishthira bathes, and he says he can see Arjuna from there.
Lomasa names a series of sacred sites, from the Saraswati to Lopamudra's place, and ends with the tale of Usinara and the hawk and pigeon.
The hawk demands the pigeon, Usinara refuses to give it up, offers his own flesh in its place, and is then honoured by Indra and Agni.
Lomasa introduces Swetaketu's hermitage and Ashtavakra's story, Yudhishthira asks about his deformity, and Lomasa explains the curse, Kahoda's drowning, and the journey to Janaka.
Ashtavakra argues his way past the gatekeeper, answers Janaka's riddles, and is admitted to meet Vandin.
Ashtavakra challenges Vandin, and the two trade numbered verses until Ashtavakra completes the last and wins the debate.
Vandin is revealed as Varuna's son, Kahoda is restored, and Ashtavakra's crooked body is straightened in the Samanga.
Lomasa names the sacred sites, then tells how Yavakri sought Vedic learning by severe penance and how Indra tried to dissuade him.
Indra grants Yavakri his boons, and Bharadwaja warns his son against pride, citing the fate of Medhavi.
Yavakri's advances, Raivya's anger, the two beings made from his hair, Yavakri's flight from water to water, and his death at his father's fire room.
Bharadwaja returns, learns of his son's death from the Sudra, laments, curses Raivya, and burns himself on a fire.
Paravasu kills Raivya by mistake, Arvavasu takes on the penance, Paravasu accuses him and has him driven from the sacrifice, and the gods reward Arvavasu and restore the dead.
Lomasa names the mountains they have passed, describes the sites ahead, and asks for protection; Yudhishthira tells his brothers to guard Krishna and the twins and to be careful.
Yudhishthira asks Bhima to turn back, Bhima refuses and offers to carry the others, Draupadi says she can go on, and Lomasa says the mountain requires austerity.
The party is welcomed by Suvahu, leaves their servants with him, and sets out for the Himalayas; Yudhishthira laments Arjuna's absence and plans the journey to Gandhamadana.
Lomasa describes the sacred sites and Naraka's bones, then tells Yudhishthira how the sunken Earth was raised by Vishnu in the form of a boar.
The gods praise Vishnu and return home, and the Pandavas set out again along the path Lomasa showed them.
The Pandavas travel toward Gandhamadana, are caught in a dust storm and heavy rain, take shelter apart, and regroup when the weather calms.
Draupadi collapses, the brothers gather round, Yudhishthira laments his fault, the Brahmins restore her, and Bhima calls on Ghatotkacha to help carry the party.
Ghatotkacha and other Rakshasas carry the party to the hermitage of Nara and Narayana, where the sages welcome Yudhishthira and the Pandavas settle in.
Draupadi asks for more lotuses, and Bhima climbs the mountain, startling the animals; footnotes 1 and 2 follow.
Footnotes 2 to 4 explain a sacrifice, the Viswedeva offering, and the dakshina gift.
Footnotes 5 and 6 explain disinterested action and a yoga that renounces motive.
Footnotes 7 to 9 explain a breath-based yoga, the groups of gods, and an order of celestials.
Footnotes 10 and 11 explain the celestial flowers and the ascetic powers such as Anima and Laghima.
Footnotes 12 to 14 explain Vishnu's bow, a set of sacrificial terms, and Dhritarashtra's epithet.

Footnotes 20 and 21 give symbolic meanings for thunder, lightning and cloud.

Footnotes 32 and 33 cover Vandin's sixth sense and Ashtavakra's eighth element.

Vandin's claim about bondage to happiness and misery, with footnotes 37 and 38 on the twelve virtues and the path to release.
