Headings introduce the next part of the text, then Bhima fights animals and reaches a lake, and Hanuman warns him to turn back.
Bhima demands passage, Hanuman refuses and feigns weakness, Bhima fails to move his tail, and Hanuman begins his account of Rama and Sita.
Hanuman recounts Rama's alliance with Sugriva, the search for Sita, the defeat of Ravana, and Rama's return home, and explains why he blocks the path.
Hanuman declines to show his earlier form and describes the four yugas, from the perfect Krita age to the declining Kali age, before telling Bhima to return.
Bhima asks to see Hanuman's true form, Hanuman enlarges himself, and Bhima praises him; Hanuman warns against rash action and lectures on class duties and kingship.
Hanuman shrinks and embraces Bhima, offers to punish the Kauravas, and promises to help in battle by roaring from Arjuna's flagstaff before he vanishes.
Bhima walks on through the forest, reaches a river full of Saugandhika lotuses, and feels his errand is close to done.
Bhima finds Kuvera's lake, drinks its water, and is questioned by the armed Rakshasas who guard it.
Bhima states his errand and refuses to ask Kuvera's permission, then fights and defeats the Krodhavasas, who report to Kuvera, who allows him to take the lotuses.
Portents appear, Yudhishthira sets out with the others to find Bhima, they find the slain Yakshas, Yudhishthira rebukes Bhima, and the garden warders are pacified.
Yudhishthira lists the holy places visited and asks how to reach Kuvera's abode; an aerial voice gives the route, and Dhaumya advises following it.
Jatasura seizes the Pandavas and Draupadi; Yudhishthira and Sahadeva confront him; Bhima arrives, rebukes him, kills him after a long fight, and is praised.
Yudhishthira recalls Arjuna's promised return and leads the company toward Sweta, passing Vrishaparva's hermitage and then through the Gandhamadana forest to Arshtishena's hermitage.
Arshtishena questions Yudhishthira about his duties and warns the Pandavas not to go beyond Kailasa, asking them to wait there for Arjuna.
Janamejaya asks about the Pandavas' stay, and Vaisampayana tells how Draupadi urges Bhima to clear the summit, where he fights and kills Maniman.
Yudhishthira scolds Bhima, the fleeing Rakshasas report to Kuvera, who rides to the summit, is grateful to Bhima, and says he has been freed from a curse.
Yudhishthira asks why Agastya cursed Kuvera, and Kuvera recounts how Maniman insulted the sage at Kusasthali and was cursed to die at a mortal's hands.
Kuvera advises Yudhishthira on patience and restraint, praises Arjuna, blesses the brothers and leaves, and the dead Rakshasas are removed from the summit.
Dhaumya names the regions of the cosmos and explains how the sun and moon move around Meru, bringing the seasons.
The Pandavas pass a month on Gandhamadana, longing for Arjuna, who has spent five years in Indra's heaven and now comes back with the celestial weapons.
Arjuna arrives in Indra's chariot, honours his elders, gives Draupadi jewels, and tells of what he learned in heaven.
Indra comes to the Pandavas, is honoured by Yudhishthira, and tells him he will rule the earth.
Yudhishthira asks how Arjuna gained the weapons, and Arjuna describes his penances, his fight with a boar and a hunter, and Shiva's gift of the Pasupata weapon.
Arjuna recounts the gods' visit and Indra's invitation, his time learning arms in heaven, Indra's request that he destroy the Nivata-Kavachas, and the gods' gifts before he sets out.
Arjuna reaches the ocean, Matali drives him into the Danava city, and the Nivata-Kavachas come out to fight while sages gather to watch.
The Nivata-Kavachas attack, Arjuna and Matali scatter them with arrows and trampling, Arjuna breaks their weapons with Indra's missile, and they turn to illusion.
The Danavas unleash rock showers, floods, fire, wind and darkness; Arjuna counters them with Indra's weapons, and Matali falters until Arjuna steadies him.
Arjuna defeats the hidden Nivata-Kavachas with Indra's thunderbolt, enters their city, and learns from Matali that it once belonged to Indra.
Arjuna sees Hiranyapura, learns of its boons, attacks and destroys it with Rudra's weapon, and returns to Indra, who praises him.
Indra blesses Arjuna and sends him back; Arjuna returns to his brothers, who rejoice, and promises to show the weapons the next morning.
Arjuna displays his celestial weapons, nature trembles, Narada warns him to use them only for a worthy cause, and the gods depart, leaving the Pandavas in the forest with Krishna.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did, Vaisampayana describes their time in Kuvera's realm, Bhima urges action against Duryodhana, and the brothers take leave of the mountain.
The Pandavas travel back through several regions, spend a year in the Visakhayupa forest where Bhima is seized by a snake, and reach the Saraswati and Dvaitavana in the twelfth year.
Janamejaya asks about Bhima's fear, and Vaisampayana describes Bhima's hunting and his capture by a huge snake in a cave.
Bhima questions the snake, which reveals itself as the cursed king Nahusha, and Bhima accepts his fate; Yudhishthira, sensing ill omens, goes out and finds him caught by the snake.
Yudhishthira offers other food, the snake sets its terms, and Yudhishthira answers its opening questions about who a Brahmana is and what should be known.
The snake and Yudhishthira discuss caste and conduct, and the snake accepts it cannot eat Bhima; a section heading closes the chapter.
Nahusha teaches Yudhishthira about virtue, rebirth, and how the senses, mind and soul perceive things.
Nahusha explains mind and intellect, admits he was ruined by prosperity, recounts Agastya's curse, and returns to heaven; the Brahmanas then admonish Bhima.
The rainy and autumn seasons pass by the Saraswati, and the Pandavas go into the Kamyaka forest at the start of the dark fortnight.
Krishna arrives at Kamyaka, greets the Pandavas, and offers to help them regain the kingdom; Markandeya and Narada join them, and Yudhishthira asks about action and fate.
Markandeya explains how a person's deeds follow him through rebirth, and how the wise attain the highest good.
Markandeya tells how a Haihaya prince killed a sage by mistake, how the sage was restored by his father Tarkshya, and why Brahmanas fear no death.
Atri seeks wealth from King Vainya, a quarrel with Gautama over the king's status is settled by Sanatkumara in the king's favour, and Atri receives great gifts.
Saraswati, asked by Tarkshya about virtue, lists the rewards of study, gifts and offerings, and Tarkshya asks for the rules for keeping the sacred fire.
Manu rescues a fish, is warned of a flood, survives in a boat tied to a horned fish, and is told that Brahma will recreate the world through him.
Yudhishthira asks Markandeya to explain the causes of things; Markandeya describes the yugas, the destruction of the world, and his vision of the boy-god who holds the universe.
Narayana reveals his identity and his power; Markandeya recognises Janardana, now Krishna, and the Pandavas bow down and are consoled.
Yudhishthira asks what the Kali age will bring; Markandeya describes the decline of virtue, social disorder and omens, and the coming of Kalki, who restores order.
Markandeya describes Kalki's restoration of order and gives Yudhishthira his closing counsel on kingship, which Yudhishthira promises to follow.
The Pandavas and their companions are filled with joy and wonder at Markandeya's teaching.
Markandeya tells of King Parikshit's marriage and the frog-king's revelation, then of Sala's theft of the Vami horses from Vamadeva and Sala's death at the hands of Rakshasas.
Dala aims a poisoned arrow at Vamadeva, which kills his son instead, and after the queen's plea he returns the horses to the sage.
Yudhishthira asks about Vaka's long life and his meeting with Indra; Indra visits Vaka and asks about the sorrows of the immortal, which Vaka describes.
Indra asks about the joys of a deathless life, Vaka praises a simple, honest meal shared with guests, and Indra returns to heaven.
Suhotra and Sivi refuse to yield the road, Narada quotes verses on goodness and humility, and Suhotra gives way out of honour.
Yayati, son of Nahusha, gives a thousand cows to a Brahmana who asked for them for his teacher, saying he never boasts of or regrets a gift.
Seduka sends a Brahmana to Vrishadarbha for steeds, the king whips him, and then gives him the whole day's revenue as amends.
Agni, as a pigeon, flees to King Sivi, pursued by Indra as a hawk; Sivi cuts his own flesh to match the pigeon's weight, and the gods reveal themselves and promise him a son.
Narada names the kings who will fall from heaven and the reasons, and says he himself will fall because he is not equal to Sivi, whose self-sacrifice was a test by Vidhatri.

Indradyumna, fallen from heaven, is passed from Markandeya to the owl, the crane and the tortoise, who recalls his sacrifices; a heavenly car takes him back, and Markandeya notes that Krishna once raised Nriga.
Yudhishthira asks about charity, Markandeya lists futile gifts and lives and names the deserving recipients, with food the greatest gift, and Yudhishthira asks about the road to Yama.
Markandeya describes the road to Yama's realm and its rewards, then teaches on honouring Brahmanas, gifts of cows, purity, and the superiority of knowledge over outward austerity.
Yudhishthira asks about meritorious charity, and Markandeya explains the times and seasons when gifts earn the greatest merit.
Yudhishthira asks about the king's changed name, and Markandeya starts the tale with the sage Utanka, who wins Vishnu's favour and hears that a future king will kill the demon Dhundhu.
Markandeya lists the kings from Sasada to Kuvalaswa, whose father retires, and Utanka persuades the king to stay and deal with the demon Dhundhu.
Vrihadaswa hands the task to his son and leaves, Yudhishthira asks about Dhundhu's ancestry, and Markandeya tells of the cosmic flood and the demons Madhu and Kaitabha whom Vishnu beheads.

Dhundhu gets his boon and attacks, the king's sons are burned until the king's water quenches the fire, Dhundhu is killed with the Brahma weapon, and the king is renamed Dhundhumara with three surviving sons.
Yudhishthira asks about women's virtue and the duties of sons and Kshatriyas, and Markandeya explains parents' hopes for children and how a wife earns heaven.
Kausika kills a crane in anger, and while waiting for alms at a housewife's door he is kept waiting; she explains her devotion to her husband and sends him to a fowler in Mithila.
Dismissed by the housewife, Kausika goes home and reproaches himself.
Kausika reaches Mithila and finds the fowler selling meat, who hears the fowler's account of his trade, the duties of each class, and the signs of true virtue.
The fowler explains that his trade follows from his karma, argues that all life involves harm, and asks Kausika what he thinks of this state of affairs.
The fowler teaches that karma governs fortune and disease and that the soul is reborn according to its deeds, and Kausika asks how the soul is eternal and what the senses are.
The fowler traces the slide from learning into sin, contrasts the wise man, and starts to outline the elements, qualities and principles of Brahma.
The fowler lists the qualities of the five elements, then argues that subduing the senses, like a charioteer taming his horses, is the path to spiritual light.
The fowler defines tamas, rajas and sattwa by their marks and says that good qualities can raise a man's standing regardless of birth.
The fowler explains the vital airs and the soul, then urges the overcoming of anger and greed and the practice of renunciation as the path to liberation.
The fowler shows the Brahmana his home and parents, whom he honours as his highest gods and serves with daily devotion.
The fowler urges the Brahmana to go home to his parents, then tells how he came to be a fowler after accidentally wounding a sage while hunting.
The sage's curse is softened, the Brahmana praises the fowler's teaching on character and contentment, and he goes home to his parents, closing the story for Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira asks about the fire-god's withdrawal and the birth of Kumara, and Markandeya tells how Agni returned to his place after Angiras persuaded him.
Markandeya lists Angiras's children by Subha, starting with his son Vrihaspati and several daughters, each named for a quality.
Markandeya traces the fire-deities descended from Vrihaspati, each named for a sacrificial role, with Swaha's three sons linked to the three qualities.
A being from Uktha's penance, marked with five colours, creates the fire of the manes, day and night, and the sacrifice-obstructing gods who must be appeased.
Markandeya names many fires descended from Tapa and Bhanu and lists the rites needed to correct the sacred fire when it is disturbed.
Markandeya tells how Swaha hid from defilement and how Atharvan restored him, then names the rivers said to be the mothers of the fires.
Indra, seeking a leader for the gods, rescues a woman from the Asura Kesin in the Manasa mountains and drives the Asura off.
Devasena asks for a champion husband, Indra reads omens and wins Brahma's approval, and the fire Adbhuta, aroused by the Rishis' wives, is pursued in disguise by Swaha.
Swaha, disguised as Siva, seduces Agni and casts his seed into a lake, from which the six-faced Skanda is born and displays his power.
The omens follow Skanda's birth, Swaha is revealed as mother, six wives are divorced, Viswamitra performs the rites, and the gods' plot to kill Skanda is set aside as the Mothers adopt him.
Indra advances against Skanda, is driven back by his fire, and then pierces him with the thunderbolt, from whose wound Visakha is born.
The wound yields a host of followers, the Mothers and Sisu are named, and Skanda is called the father of the Kumaras.
Skanda is urged to become Indra, declines, and Indra asks him to lead the gods' forces.
Skanda is anointed commander, honoured as the son of Rudra, and married to Devasena, and the sacred days of his anointing and victory are named.
The cast-off Rishis' wives ask Skanda to adopt them, Indra and Vinata seek honour from him, and the Mothers claim to be his mothers as well.
The Mothers ask Skanda to replace the earlier mother goddesses and to let them devour rivals' children, and Skanda gives them other offspring on condition that they protect children.
Skanda sets the Mothers to afflict children until sixteen, and Markandeya lists the spirits that trouble children and adults.
Swaha asks Skanda to grant her union with Agni, and he links her name to offerings made through Agni.
Brahma sends Skanda to his father, and Markandeya describes the spirits, the bells and banners, and the grand procession of Mahadeva's army.
Skanda is dismissed, omens appear, and the Asuras attack; Indra rallies the gods, and Mahisha seizes Rudra's chariot until Skanda kills him.
Skanda routs the Danavas and is praised by Indra; Markandeya closes the story with a list of Skanda's names and a prayer to him.

Satyabhama asks Draupadi how she wins her husbands' obedience, and Draupadi replies that it comes from humble, dutiful service rather than charms, listing her household duties; Satyabhama then apologises.
Draupadi gives Satyabhama practical advice on winning and keeping her husband's love through devoted service, discretion and good company.
Krishna takes leave of the Pandavas, and Satyabhama comforts Draupadi with news of the Pandava sons in Dwaraka and of their future victory.
Janamejaya asks about the Pandavas in the forest, a Brahmana brings news of their suffering to Dhritarashtra, who laments, and Sakuni reports the king's words to Duryodhana.
Sakuni and Karna urge Duryodhana to go and gloat over the exiled Pandavas, and when they finish they fall silent.
Duryodhana doubts he can win permission to visit the Pandavas, and Karna and Sakuni agree on the cattle-inspection pretext.
Dhritarashtra is asked to permit a cattle-inspection trip, warns of the Pandavas, and grudgingly lets Duryodhana go with a large following.
Duryodhana inspects his cattle and enjoys the woods, then finds the lake at Dwaitavana blocked by Chitrasena's Gandharvas, who spurn his messengers.
The Kuru soldiers attack the Gandharvas and are routed, and Karna fights alone until his chariot is broken and he escapes.
Duryodhana and the Kaurava party are seized by the Gandharvas, and the fleeing soldiers appeal to the Pandavas, while Bhima mocks them and Yudhishthira reproves him.
Yudhishthira urges his brothers to rescue Duryodhana, first by conciliation and then by force if needed, and Arjuna pledges to do so, restoring the Kauravas' spirits.
The Pandavas arm and march out, Arjuna demands Duryodhana's release, the Gandharvas refuse, and battle begins.
Arjuna and the Pandavas defeat the Gandharvas with celestial weapons, and when Chitrasena reveals himself as Arjuna's friend, the fighting stops.
Arjuna and Chitrasena argue over the captives, Chitrasena explains the Kaurava plot, and the Gandharvas and Pandavas take the captives to Yudhishthira.
The Gandharvas depart, Indra revives the slain, Yudhishthira warns Duryodhana against rash acts, and Duryodhana sets off for his capital in shame.
Janamejaya asks about Duryodhana's shameful return, Duryodhana leaves in grief, and Karna comes to comfort him at night, admitting his own flight.
Duryodhana explains to Karna how the Gandharvas captured the Kauravas, how the Pandavas freed them at the soldiers' appeal, and how Chitrasena reconciled with Arjuna.
Duryodhana, ashamed of his captivity, resolves to starve himself, offers the throne to Dussasana, who refuses, and Karna urges the brothers to stop grieving and go home.
Karna urges Duryodhana to rise and stop grieving, warning that a self-starving king would be mocked, and Duryodhana remains resolved to die.
Sakuni and the others fail to change Duryodhana's mind about fasting, and the Danavas summon him through a rite to their nether world, where they flatter him.
The Danavas promise Duryodhana victory, the goddess returns him to his place, and Karna urges him to rise and march back to the city with his army.
Bhishma rebukes Duryodhana and urges peace, Duryodhana laughs at him, and Karna offers to conquer the earth alone, which Duryodhana welcomes.
Karna conquers the kingdoms around, returns to Hastinapura with tribute, and is embraced by Dhritarashtra, who then trusts that the Pandavas have been defeated.
Karna and Duryodhana plan a great sacrifice, the priests advise a different rite, and the work on the sacrificial plough begins.
The sacrifice begins, Dussasana's messenger invites the Pandavas, Yudhishthira declines, and Vidura entertains the guests.
The citizens praise the sacrifice, Karna vows to kill Arjuna, and Duryodhana rules and gives gifts, while the Pandavas grow anxious and plan to leave.
Yudhishthira dreams of the surviving deer begging him to leave, and he moves the Pandavas to the Kamyaka forest out of pity.
The Pandavas endure their exile, Vyasa visits and teaches on asceticism, and then Yudhishthira asks about charity, leading Vyasa to tell the tale of Mudgala.
The story of Mudgala: his generous gift of corn, Durvasa's repeated tests, and the celestial chariot that comes to take him to heaven.
The messenger describes heaven and its drawbacks, Mudgala chooses liberation over heaven, and Vyasa consoles Yudhishthira and departs.
Duryodhana plots against the Pandavas, Durvasa tests and then favours him, and Duryodhana asks him to visit the Pandavas after Draupadi has eaten.
Durvasa visits the Pandavas when Draupadi has eaten; she prays to Krishna, who eats the last grain, and the sages flee, leaving the Pandavas safe.
The Pandavas hunt in Kamyaka, Jayadratha sees Draupadi at the hermitage, and he sends Kotika to ask who she is.
Kotika asks Draupadi who she is and introduces himself and the princes with him, naming Jayadratha of Sauvira as their leader.
Draupadi introduces herself and her husbands, who are away hunting, and invites the visitors to wait for their hospitality before she withdraws.
Kotika tells Jayadratha who Draupadi is, Jayadratha is captivated and goes to the hermitage, and he urges her to abandon the Pandavas and marry him.
Draupadi rebukes Jayadratha, refuses his demands, is seized and dragged to his chariot, and Dhaumya follows the ravisher's army.
The Pandavas return to find Draupadi's maid weeping, learn that Jayadratha has carried her off, and follow the tracks in pursuit.
Jayadratha asks Draupadi to name the Pandavas, she describes each brother and warns him, and the brothers attack the enemy charioteers.
The Pandavas rout the Sindhu army and Jayadratha flees, Yudhishthira asks Bhima to spare him, and Draupadi urges the brothers to pursue and slay him.
Bhima humiliates Jayadratha and Yudhishthira frees him; Jayadratha seeks Shiva's boon, and Shiva recounts Vishnu's incarnations and Arjuna's divine powers.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did next, and Yudhishthira asks Markandeya whether any man has suffered more than he has.
Markandeya describes Rama's loss of Sita, Yudhishthira asks about Rama's family, and Markandeya begins the story of Rama's and Ravana's origins.
Visrava's sons perform penances, Brahma grants them boons, and Ravana defeats Kubera, takes Lanka and the Pushpaka chariot, and comes to terrorise the world.
The gods and sages seek Brahma's help against Ravana, Brahma foretells Vishnu's incarnation, and he orders the gods to beget monkey and bear allies and sends Manthara to sow strife.
Yudhishthira asks about Rama's exile, Markandeya describes Dasaratha's plan and Kaikeyi's demands, the forest life and Dandaka battles, and Surpanakha's complaint to Ravana.
Ravana enlists Maricha, who lures Rama away in deer form; Sita is left alone, and Ravana abducts her while the vulture Jatayu watches.
Jatayu fights Ravana and falls, Sita is carried to Lanka, and Rama and Lakshmana, searching for her, kill a headless Rakshasa who advises them to seek Sugriva.
Rama's journey to Pampa and Rishyamuka, his alliance with Sugriva and the killing of Vali, followed by Sita's state in Lanka and the comfort Trijata gives her.
Ravana visits Sita in the grove, offers her the place of queen, and is refused by her before he goes away.
Lakshmana presses Sugriva to act, the search parties return, and Hanuman reports finding Sita in Ravana's city of Lanka.
The armies assemble and reach the sea, Rama asks the Ocean for a way across, and Nala builds a bridge that carries the army to Lanka; Vibhishana joins Rama, and Angada is sent to Ravana.
Ravana fortifies the city, Angada delivers Rama's challenge and escapes Ravana's men, and then the armies fight at Lanka's walls.
Ravana's invisible demons are exposed and killed, and Ravana opens a general battle in which the chief warriors on each side are paired off.
Prahasta and Dhumraksha are killed, and Ravana wakes Kumbhakarna and sends him out to fight.
Kumbhakarna is struck down by Lakshmana, and his two younger brothers are killed by Hanuman and Nala, while the battle continues.
Ravana urges Indrajit to fight, Indrajit duels with Lakshmana and Angada, and then vanishes and wounds Rama and Lakshmana.
Vibhishana revives the brothers, who gain sight of invisible beings, Lakshmana kills Indrajit, and Avindhya persuades Ravana to spare Sita and go to battle himself.
Ravana's illusions fail, Matali brings Indra's chariot to Rama, and Rama kills Ravana with a Brahma weapon.
Ravana is slain, the gods praise Rama, Sita's purity is affirmed, Rama returns to Ayodhya, and he is crowned and performs the sacrifices.
Markandeya tells Yudhishthira that Rama also suffered, that the Pandavas have strong allies, and that he should not grieve.
Yudhishthira asks about faithful wives, and Markandeya tells how Aswapati's daughter Savitri was born and grew up unmarried.
Savitri sets out with her father's counsellors to travel the holy places and search for a husband.
Savitri names Satyavan as her choice, Narada warns that he will die within a year, Savitri holds to her choice, and her father begins the wedding preparations.
Aswapati asks Dyumatsena for Satyavan's hand, the wedding is held in the hermitage, and Savitri lives there as a devoted wife, still troubled by Narada's warning.
The day of Satyavan's fated death arrives, Savitri completes her fast and insists on following him into the forest, and she goes with him, grieving.
Satyavan falls ill and dies in Savitri's lap, Savitri wins Yama's boons and Satyavan's life back, and the couple starts home through the night.
Dyumatsena searches for Satyavan, the couple returns, Savitri explains her boons, and the sages praise her and leave.
Messengers bring Dyumatsena news of the usurper's death and an invitation to return, he is restored to the throne, and the tale closes with Markandeya's words to Yudhishthira.
Janamejaya asks about Yudhishthira's fear, Vaisampayana explains Indra's plan and Surya's warning, and Karna chooses fame over safety.
Surya presses Karna to refuse the earrings, arguing that fame does not help the dead and that the earrings guarantee his strength against Arjuna.
Karna refuses to give up his vow, Surya advises him to ask Indra for a dart in exchange for the earrings, and Karna waits for Indra.
Janamejaya asks about Karna's earrings, and Vaisampayana begins the story of the Brahmana guest and Kuntibhoja's daughter Pritha.
Kunti promises to serve the Brahmana, her father hands him over to her care, and she waits on him devotedly.
Kunti's service wins the Brahmana's approval, he offers her a boon, and she declines it in favor of a mantra that summons a god.
Kunti tests the mantra on the rising sun, Surya appears and demands her, and she begs him to leave, but he refuses.
Kunti pleads with Surya, consents on condition that her son have armor and earrings, and is made pregnant by Surya while remaining a virgin.
Pritha gives birth in secret, prays over her son, and sends him off in a box on the river Aswa, which drifts to Champa where the child is kept alive.
Adhiratha and Radha adopt the foundling from the river, he is raised as their son, trained as a warrior, and becomes Duryodhana's friend and Arjuna's rival.
Indra begs Karna's armor and earrings, Karna refuses every other gift, and he gives them up in exchange for an infallible dart.
Janamejaya asks where the Pandavas were, and Vaisampayana says they returned to Dwaitavana after finishing their exile.
The Pandavas dwell in Dwaitavana, a deer carries off a Brahmana's fire-sticks, and the brothers chase it in vain and rest under a banyan tree.
The brothers reflect on their misfortunes, Yudhishthira sends them for water, each dies at the lake after drinking without answering, and Yudhishthira goes searching and finds the lake.
Yudhishthira mourns and reflects on his dead brothers, the Yaksha challenges him, and after a long set of answers he chooses Nakula, and all four brothers are restored.
The Yaksha reveals himself as Dharma, Yudhishthira asks for the fire-sticks and a year of concealment, the god grants them, and the brothers return the fire-sticks to the Brahmana.
Yudhishthira asks leave to spend the thirteenth year in disguise, Dhaumya and Bhima encourage him, the Brahmanas depart, and the brothers set out to plan their year.

Janamejaya's question opens the section, and Yudhishthira, back from the asylum, asks his brothers to pick a hiding place; Arjuna names the kingdoms around the Kuru land.
Yudhishthira chooses Matsya and its king Virata, then describes the disguise he will wear as a dice-playing courtier named Kanka, and asks what the others will do.
Bhima describes his cover as a cook and wrestler, Yudhishthira praises Arjuna and asks his role, and Arjuna answers with his own disguise as Vrihannala.
Nakula and Sahadeva each name the work they will do in disguise, and Yudhishthira voices his concern for Draupadi.
Draupadi offers to pass as a hairdresser serving the queen, and Yudhishthira cautions her about her conduct.
Yudhishthira arranges where the household goes, Dhaumya gives his counsel on royal service, and the brothers depart with Draupadi while the servants disperse.
The brothers reach Matsya, carry Draupadi to the city's edge, hide their weapons in a Sami tree, and go in under new names.
Yudhishthira prays to Durga, and the goddess appears to him and promises victory and concealment.
Yudhishthira enters Virata's court, Virata wonders who he is, and Yudhishthira introduces himself as Kanka and asks for a boon.
Virata grants Kanka high status and privileges, and Kanka settles into the court unrecognized.
Bhima arrives as the cook Vallava, Virata is impressed and doubtful, and Bhima is appointed head of the kitchen.
Draupadi wanders the city in disguise, is seen by Queen Sudeshna, and bargains her way into service with conditions.
Draupadi begins living in the city, and no one can tell who she truly is.
Virata meets the cowherd Sahadeva, questions him, and gives him charge of the royal herds.
Sahadeva lives under Virata's protection, unrecognized.
Arjuna enters the court as Vrihannala, Virata offers him high status, Arjuna asks to teach Uttara, and he is tested and placed among the women of the palace.
Nakula enters, impresses Virata with his knowledge of horses, and is appointed to manage the royal stables.
Janamejaya asks what the brothers did, and Vaisampayana describes their hidden service, Bhima's wrestling victory at the festival, and the rewards they receive.
Kichaka becomes infatuated with Draupadi, makes his advances through Sudeshna and then directly, and is repeatedly refused and warned.
Kichaka asks Sudeshna for help, Sudeshna arranges a feast and sends Draupadi, and Draupadi prays for protection before entering Kichaka's presence.
Kichaka tries to seize Draupadi and assaults her in the court, Bhima is held back by Yudhishthira, Draupadi rebukes the court, and she is sent away to Sudeshna.
Draupadi decides that Bhima must avenge her, goes to find him at night, and wakes him to demand action.
Draupadi lists her insults and blames Yudhishthira's gambling, lamenting his fall from the splendour of Indraprastha.
Draupadi lists the humiliating roles of each brother, reports Sudeshna's mockery, and ends her grief-stricken plea.
Draupadi describes her humiliations and her hope for a turn of fortune, and Bhima weeps with her.
Bhima voices his anger and regret, and Draupadi recounts Kichaka's pursuit and her refusals and demands revenge. Bhima then consoles her and turns his thoughts to Kichaka.
Bhima and Draupadi set the trap, and Kichaka comes to the dance hall at night, where Bhima receives him.
Bhima and Kichaka wrestle, Bhima kills him, and the Kichakas' kin prepare to burn Draupadi with the body until Bhima comes to her rescue, uprooting a tree and killing 105 of them.
The narrator tallies the dead and the wonder of the onlookers.
Virata hears the report, sends his message to Draupadi through Sudeshna, Draupadi returns to the city and greets Arjuna and the princesses, and she asks for thirteen more days.
Word of Kichaka's killing spreads, and Duryodhana's spies report their failed search and the chance that Kichaka's death opens up.
Duryodhana orders a renewed search, Karna urges wider spying, and Duhsasana doubts the brothers can be found.
Drona defends the Pandavas' virtue and recommends a new search by holy men.
Bhishma supports Drona's praise of the Pandavas, counsels against spying, and describes the prosperity of the land where Yudhishthira hides.
Kripa agrees with Bhishma but urges Duryodhana to watch the Pandavas, build his strength, and prepare for war or treaty.
Susarman urges an invasion, Karna supports it, and Duryodhana orders a two-pronged raid on Virata's cattle.
The Trigartas seize Virata's cattle, the king arms his forces, and the brothers ride out with the army.
The Matsyas and Trigartas fight a fierce battle at sunset, and the king duels with Susarman until darkness falls.
Virata is captured, Yudhishthira urges Bhima to rescue him, Bhima routs the Trigartas and binds Susarman, and Yudhishthira frees the captive.
Susarman is released, Virata rewards the Pandavas and offers them rule, and the city is told of the victory.
The Kauravas raid Virata's cattle, a cowherd reports to the prince, and the prince is urged to go out and fight.
Uttara calls for a charioteer, Arjuna's plan is relayed through Draupadi, and Draupadi and Uttara debate whether Vrihannala can take the role.
Uttara sends his sister to the dance hall to fetch Vrihannala.
Virata's daughter asks Arjuna to drive, Arjuna protests and pretends to be clumsy, Uttara arms him, and the women send them off with blessings.
Uttara drives toward the Kurus, panics at the sight of their army, flees, and is chased by Arjuna while the Kurus wonder who the charioteer is.
Arjuna catches Uttara, reassures him, and lifts him back into the chariot.
The Kuru leaders see the disguised driver and fear it is Arjuna, Drona reads omens, Karna and Duryodhana argue, and the elders applaud Duryodhana.
Arjuna sends Uttara up the Sami tree to fetch the Pandavas' bows and names the Gandiva among them.
Uttara resists climbing the tree, Arjuna reassures him, and Uttara unwraps the bows and is struck by their brilliance.
Uttara asks whose bows, arrows, quivers and swords these are, describing each in turn.
Arjuna names the Gandiva as his own, traces its divine history, and assigns each of the other weapons to a brother.
Uttara asks where the Pandavas are, and Arjuna reveals his identity and the brothers' disguises, and Uttara asks for proof.
Arjuna gives the meanings of his ten names, and Uttara apologizes and welcomes him.
Uttara offers his services, Arjuna describes his chariot as a fortress and explains his disguise as a vow.
Uttara praises Arjuna and the horses, Arjuna readies himself and sounds the Gandiva, and he answers Uttara's fears.
Arjuna sets up his chariot and sounds the conch, Uttara is frightened, and Drona reads omens of a coming disaster.
Duryodhana argues the Pandavas' year is not over and calls for battle, and Karna dismisses Drona's praise of Arjuna.
Karna boasts that he will defeat Arjuna and invites the Kauravas to watch.
Kripa rebukes Karna's rashness, lists Arjuna's feats, and urges the Kuru warriors to fight together.
Ashvatthaman answers Karna's boast with a sharp rebuke of Duryodhana's dishonest dice victory and a warning about Arjuna.
Bhishma urges the leaders to unite, Ashvatthaman answers with his grievance, Duryodhana asks Drona to forgive, and Drona asks for battle arrangements.
Bhishma calculates the exile's length and advises on the battle, Duryodhana refuses to yield, and Bhishma arrays the army.
Arjuna's chariot advances, Drona recognizes him, Arjuna turns toward Duryodhana, and the Kuru troops are routed as the cattle turn back.
Arjuna turns back to fight, routs several Kuru warriors, and wounds Karna in a long duel that drives him from the field.
Arjuna's onslaught scatters the Kuru army, and Arjuna names the Kuru leaders whom Uttara should approach.
Gods, heavenly kings and sages gather in the sky to watch the battle, and Indra looks on at his son.
Arjuna duels with Kripa, cutting down his weapons and car, and then Kripa is taken away by his men.
Arjuna approaches Drona, respectfully declares his terms, and duels him until Drona withdraws wounded.
Ashvatthaman duels Arjuna, cuts the Gandiva's string, runs out of arrows, and Arjuna turns on Karna.
Arjuna and Karna trade insults before their duel, Arjuna cuts Karna's weapons and wounds him, and Karna flees the field.
Uttara falters, Arjuna reassures him and boasts of his weapons, and Arjuna cuts Bhishma's banner and drives off the Kuru princes who attack him.
The Kuru warriors attack Arjuna together, Arjuna routs them with arrows, and the battlefield turns into a river of blood.
Bhishma and Arjuna duel with celestial and ordinary weapons, the gods praise them, and Arjuna wounds Bhishma and forces him from the field.
Duryodhana and Arjuna trade wounds, Arjuna kills Vikarna's elephant, and Arjuna shames Duryodhana as he flees.
The Kurus rally against Arjuna, Arjuna stuns them with a weapon and his conch, Bhishma counsels Duryodhana to leave, and Arjuna salutes the elders and sounds his conch.
Arjuna spares a band of Kuru soldiers who beg for mercy, tells Uttara to take the credit, and returns to the Sami tree to restore the weapons.
Arjuna asks Uttara to send news ahead of their return, and the party collects their garments and enters the city.
Virata returns, hears that Uttara has gone out with a eunuch as driver, sends troops, and receives news of the victory.
Virata calls for dice, Kanka reluctantly agrees to play, and Virata grows angry at Kanka's praise of Vrihannala.
Virata strikes Yudhishthira with a die, Draupadi catches the blood, and Yudhishthira asks that Uttara enter alone.
Uttara finds Kanka bleeding, Virata admits the blow, Kanka forgives him, and Virata praises his son.
Uttara credits the victory to a celestial youth, Virata asks to honour him, and Arjuna gives the garments to Virata's daughter.
The Pandavas take royal seats in Virata's council, Virata rebukes Kanka, and Arjuna answers with praise of Yudhishthira.
Virata asks who the men are, Arjuna and Uttara identify the brothers and Draupadi and recount Arjuna's feats, and Virata offers his daughter to Arjuna.
Uttara and Virata ask the Pandavas' forgiveness, and Virata makes an alliance and offers his kingdom, which Arjuna accepts for his daughter-in-law.
Virata offers his daughter, Arjuna accepts her for his son, the allies gather and the wedding is celebrated, and the Virata Parva ends.
