The kings assemble in Virata's court and Krishna lays out the Pandavas' case and proposes sending an envoy to the Kauravas.
Balarama proposes a conciliatory envoy to the Kauravas, and Satyaki rises up in anger to answer him.
Satyaki attacks Balarama's plea for peace and declares that the Pandavas must regain their kingdom by force.
Drupada rejects a gentle approach to Duryodhana and calls for allies to be summoned while a priest is sent to Dhritarashtra.
Krishna asks that a peace message be sent to the Kauravas, and Virata sends him home as both camps begin to gather forces.
Drupada gives the priest his instructions, and the priest sets out for Hastinapura with his disciples.
Krishna offers his army or himself to the two rivals, Arjuna picks Krishna, Duryodhana takes the troops, and Balarama refuses to fight.
Arjuna returns to Yudhishthira with Krishna at his side.
Salya marches toward the Pandavas, is entertained by Duryodhana, promises to lead the Kauravas, and then visits Yudhishthira, who asks for his help against Karna.
Yudhishthira asks about Indra's suffering, and Salya tells of the three-headed son, his killing, and the creation of Vritra.
Indra asks for help against Vritra, the gods go to Vishnu, the sages make peace with Vritra, and Indra kills him by a trick and is then left guilt-stricken and hidden.
The gods make Nahusha king, he turns to lust, and he is angered when Indra's queen takes refuge with Vrihaspati.
The gods plead with Nahusha to calm down, Vrihaspati refuses to give Sachi up, and the gods advise her to ask Nahusha for time.
The gods persuade Sachi to go to Nahusha, and he is pleased by her beauty.
Sachi asks Nahusha for time to find Indra, the gods consult Vishnu, Indra cleanses himself by sacrifice and vanishes again, and Sachi calls on Divination.
Divination leads Sachi to the lake where Indra is hidden, and Sachi tells him of Nahusha's threats and asks him to act.
Indra's plan to have Nahusha carried by sages is carried out, and Vrihaspati sends Agni to search for Indra.
Agni refuses to enter the waters, saying water would put him out.
Agni finds Indra in the lotus, and Vrihaspati explains to Indra how Nahusha came to power.
The guardian gods agree to help Indra, who rewards them with domains and shares of sacrifice.
Agastya greets Indra, tells how Nahusha was cursed for his insults, and the gods and other beings rejoice.
Indra returns to power, Salya encourages Yudhishthira with Indra's story, and Salya agrees to undermine Karna before leaving for Duryodhana.
The armies of the Pandavas and Kauravas gather, and the Kaurava forces spread across the land around Hastinapura.
Drupada's priest, received at the Kaurava court, argues that the Pandavas have a right to their inheritance and asks for peace.
Bhishma and Karna answer the priest, Bhishma rebukes Karna, and Dhritarashtra decides to send Sanjaya to the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra tells Sanjaya how to greet the Pandavas, praises them, lists their allies, and expresses fear of their anger.
Sanjaya greets Yudhishthira, who asks after the Kaurava household and reminds the Kauravas of the Pandavas' feats, concluding that peace is hard to reach.
Sanjaya tells Yudhishthira that Dhritarashtra regrets the Pandavas' treatment, praises their heroes, and asks Yudhishthira to hear Dhritarashtra's message.
Yudhishthira asks for Dhritarashtra's message, and Sanjaya pleads for peace, arguing that war would bring ruin on both sides.
Yudhishthira prefers peace, blames Dhritarashtra and Duryodhana for the crisis, and asks only for Indraprastha as his share.
Sanjaya urges Yudhishthira to give up war, arguing that virtue, a good name and the lives of the elders matter more than the kingdom.
Yudhishthira argues that duty can shift in hard times and asks Krishna to judge whether he is right to refuse the terms and fight.
Krishna defends the Pandavas' right to act, recalls the Kaurava wrongs, and says he will go to Hastinapura himself to seek peace.
Sanjaya takes his leave, Yudhishthira praises him and sends greetings to a long list of Kaurava figures, and the final demand goes to Duryodhana.
Yudhishthira sends Sanjaya back with a final message to Dhritarashtra, Bhishma, Vidura and Duryodhana, asking for peace on modest terms.
Sanjaya reports to Dhritarashtra, passes on Yudhishthira's greetings, then rebukes the king for his unjust policy and asks to be excused until morning.
Dhritarashtra summons Vidura, who reproaches him for wronging the Pandavas and then gives a long discourse on wisdom, folly and forgiveness, urging him to return their share.
Dhritarashtra asks for advice, and Vidura warns against unjust aims and unchecked senses and urges him to let Yudhishthira rule.
Vidura tells the story of Virochana and Sudhanwan and Prahlada's judgment, then teaches that a lie for land brings ruin.
Vidura gives a further list of virtues, vices and good conduct, and ends by urging Dhritarashtra to trust the Pandavas.
Vidura tells the sage's tale, explains what makes a family noble, and urges Dhritarashtra to restrain his greed and make peace with the Pandavas.
Vidura lists foolish conduct and the vices that shorten life, then gives long advice on servants, counselors and household conduct.
Vidura warns against a rupture with the Pandavas and names the five kinds of strength, with intellect the greatest.
Vidura gives rules on guests, household, secrets and ministers, and warns Dhritarashtra that he has handed power to Duryodhana and cast off the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra says that destiny rules men, and Vidura gives long counsel on abandoning Duryodhana and protecting the Pandavas, which Dhritarashtra refuses.
Vidura gives a long moral discourse urging Dhritarashtra to restore Yudhishthira, and Dhritarashtra admits he is pulled toward Duryodhana and says destiny rules.
Vidura says he cannot teach further and names the sage Sanatsujata as the better teacher for Dhritarashtra's doubts.
Dhritarashtra asks how to meet the sage, and Vidura summons him to explain the king's doubts.
Dhritarashtra asks whether death can be avoided, and Sanatsujata explains that ignorance is death and that knowledge and self-control are the way to immortality.
Dhritarashtra asks whether ritual or renunciation brings liberation, and Sanatsujata teaches that knowledge is superior and that true Brahmins do not display their learning.
Dhritarashtra asks about silence and whether the Vedas free a person who sins, and Sanatsujata says that unrestrained living cannot be saved by the Vedas alone.
Sanatsujata explains that asceticism is successful when it is free from faults, and he lists the faults that spoil it.
Sanatsujata explains the six kinds of renunciation, the virtues of self-restraint and self-knowledge, and that there is one Brahman, known within oneself.
Dhritarashtra asks for more on Brahman, and Sanatsujata says it is reached through restraint and disciplined study.
Sanatsujata describes the disciple's service to a teacher and the steps of brahmacharya, and then says that Brahman has no visible form.
Sanatsujata lists faults and virtues, the signs of true friendship, and the teaching that knowledge of Brahman, not sacrifice alone, leads to liberation.
Sanatsujata teaches in a long hymn about the primal Seed, the Self in all beings, and the knower who is untouched by deeds.
The night passes, the kings assemble in the hall, and Sanjaya returns from the Pandavas and prepares to deliver their message.
Sanjaya relays Arjuna's defiant reply to Duryodhana, naming the Pandava heroes, predicting Duryodhana's repentance, and warning of the destruction of the Kauravas if they fight.
Bhishma tells the story of Nara and Narayana to warn Duryodhana, Karna boasts in reply, and Drona urges peace while the Kauravas lose hope.
Dhritarashtra asks about Yudhishthira and the Pandava forces, and Sanjaya describes their joyful gathering before he falls senseless.
Sanjaya recovers and names the Pandava warriors and allies one by one.
Dhritarashtra describes his terror of Bhima and his despair at the coming ruin of his sons.
Dhritarashtra despairs of victory against Arjuna, recalls his past triumphs, and sees omens of the destruction of the Kurus.
Dhritarashtra admits the Pandavas are too strong and urges the Kauravas to consider peace to avoid the ruin of the Kurus.
Sanjaya rebukes Dhritarashtra for backing his sons, reminds him of Arjuna's feats and the Pandavas' allies, and tells him that his grief is too late.
Duryodhana recalls the Kaurava elders' pledge, boasts of his mace and of the Kaurava champions, and claims superior numbers before asking Sanjaya for more news.
Duryodhana asks about the Pandava preparations, and Sanjaya reports their confidence and describes Arjuna's magical chariot and horses.
Sanjaya lists the Pandava allies and their assigned opponents, Dhritarashtra despairs, and Duryodhana insists on war.
Sanjaya reports Dhrishtadyumna's vow to fight and his message that the Kauravas should surrender the kingdom.
Dhritarashtra pleads for peace, Duryodhana refuses, and Dhritarashtra disowns him and foresees the Kuru army's ruin.
Sanjaya reports to Dhritarashtra on his visit to Krishna and Arjuna and the message they sent to the Kurus.
Dhritarashtra weighs the two armies, judges the Pandavas stronger, and voices his fear to Duryodhana.
Duryodhana, angry at his father, boasts of his own power and predicts the Pandavas' defeat, then asks about Yudhishthira's war plans.
Karna boasts of his Brahma weapon and vows to defeat the Pandavas, Bhishma rebukes him, and Karna lays down his weapons.
Duryodhana boasts he will defeat the Pandavas, and Vidura answers with a long teaching on self-restraint.
Vidura tells a parable about quarrelling birds and a story of hunters who died seeking honey, then urges peace with the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra pleads with Duryodhana to heed the elders and make peace, listing the Pandava champions he would face.
Sanjaya passes on Arjuna's reply to the Kaurava kings and says he has delivered the message.
After the kings leave, Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya privately about the two armies, and Vyasa and Gandhari are called to hear the answer.
Sanjaya presents Krishna as the supreme Lord, whose power outweighs the universe and who will bring about the Kauravas' downfall.
Dhritarashtra asks how Sanjaya knows Krishna, Sanjaya explains his faith, and Dhritarashtra urges Duryodhana to seek Krishna's protection.
Duryodhana refuses to submit to Krishna, Dhritarashtra and Gandhari rebuke him, and Vyasa urges the king to heed Sanjaya.
Sanjaya says a person with an uncontrolled mind cannot know Krishna and urges the king to subdue his senses through wisdom.
Sanjaya explains many names of Krishna and their meanings, then predicts that Krishna will come to stop the Kurus' destruction.
Dhritarashtra praises Krishna at length, envies those who can see him, and places himself in his hands.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna for help, laying out the Pandavas' grievances and the miseries of poverty and dishonour.
Yudhishthira argues against war and asks Krishna's counsel, and Krishna agrees to go to the Kuru court despite Yudhishthira's fears.
Krishna says Kshatriyas must fight rather than beg, lists the Kauravas' crimes, and says he will try for peace but expects war.
Bhima urges Krishna to speak mildly to Duryodhana, warns of ruin for the family, and asks the elders to mediate.
Krishna laughs at Bhima's softened tone and reminds him of his wrath and his oath to kill Duryodhana.
Bhima boasts of his strength, says he feels no fear, and claims he is holding back only for the sake of the Bharatas.
Krishna explains that his harsh words were meant to test Bhima, promises to seek peace, and says he will drive Arjuna's chariot if war comes.
Arjuna asks Krishna to try for peace while recalling Duryodhana's crimes and doubting that he will deal fairly.
Krishna says human effort and fate both matter, promises to do his best, and doubts Duryodhana will yield.
Nakula says circumstances have changed and advises Krishna to speak mildly, then threaten, when he meets the Kurus.
Sahadeva and Satyaki call for war against Duryodhana, and the assembled warriors roar their approval.
Draupadi, weeping, recounts her humiliation and urges Krishna to punish the Kauravas, and Krishna comforts her with a vow of victory.
Arjuna and Yudhishthira send Krishna off on his mission to Hastinapura, and Krishna sets out amid omens and blessings.
Krishna sets out for Hastinapura with an escort, and omens mark his journey; he spends the night at Vrikasthala.
Dhritarashtra orders a lavish welcome for Krishna, Duryodhana prepares pavilions, and Krishna passes them by.
Dhritarashtra tells Vidura he plans lavish gifts and a grand welcome for Krishna.
Vidura tells Dhritarashtra his lavish hospitality is a deception and urges him to make peace with the Pandavas.
Duryodhana refuses to honour Krishna and proposes to imprison him, while Bhishma and Dhritarashtra object.
Bhishma, furious at Duryodhana, rises and leaves the court.
Krishna enters Hastinapura to a crowd's welcome, is honoured by Dhritarashtra, and then visits Vidura.
Krishna visits Pritha, who grieves for her sons and sends them messages urging courage, and Krishna comforts her.
Krishna takes his leave of Pritha and sets out for Duryodhana's mansion.
Krishna visits Duryodhana, refuses his feast, rebukes his hatred of the Pandavas, and dines at Vidura's house.
Vidura warns Krishna during the night that Duryodhana is wicked and overconfident and that his counsel will be ignored.
Krishna replies that he will try for peace despite Duryodhana's wickedness, then goes to sleep.
Krishna rides to the Kuru court, is honoured by the assembly, and the Rishis who have come to watch are given seats.
Krishna urges Dhritarashtra to restrain his sons and grant the Pandavas their share, warning of ruin, and the kings silently approve.
Rama tells Duryodhana the parable of a proud king defeated by the sage Nara, then urges peace with the Pandavas.
Kanwa urges Duryodhana to make peace, then tells the story of Matali searching for a husband for his daughter.
Narada and Matali travel to Varuna's realm, where Narada describes its marvels, including a bow linked to Arjuna's Gandiva.
Narada describes the wonders of Patala, and Matali rejects the region as unsuitable for a groom.
Narada shows the Danavas' city of Hiranyapura, and Matali refuses to seek a groom among enemies of the gods.
Narada describes the realm of the birds, the sons of Garuda, and their chiefs, then offers to move on.
Narada describes Rasatala, the home of Surabhi, and the origin of the Milky Ocean.
Narada describes Bhogavati and its Nagas, and Matali picks out the young Naga Sumukha as a groom for his daughter.
Matali's plan wins Sumukha's marriage to Gunakesi, with Indra granting him long life rather than immortality.
Garuda, angry at Indra, is humbled by Vishnu; Kanwa applies the lesson to Duryodhana, who scoffs at it.
Janamejaya asks why no one restrained Duryodhana, and Narada tells the tale of Galava and the sage Viswamitra.
Galava, unable to find the horses, laments and resolves to seek Vishnu, when Garuda appears and offers help.
Garuda describes the eastern quarter as the source of the sun, the Vedas and the gods' prosperity, and offers to take Galava there.
Garuda describes the southern quarter, the realm of the ancestors and of Yama, and asks which way Galava wishes to go.
Garuda describes the western quarter, Varuna's realm, and asks Galava to choose the direction.
Garuda describes the northern quarter, its sacred sites and the sages who guard the source of the Ganges.
Galava asks to be carried east, is terrified by the flight, and despairs; Garuda laughs and suggests a rest on Mount Rishabha.
Garuda loses his wings after resting with Sandili, is forgiven and restored, and Viswamitra demands the fee again.
Garuda explains that wealth must come from a king and proposes King Yayati, who welcomes them and hears Galava's story.
Yayati, unable to meet the full need, gives his daughter Madhavi to Galava, who then goes to King Haryyaswa.
Haryyaswa admires Madhavi, takes her for one son, and then returns her when Galava comes back for the rest of the dower.
Galava brings Madhavi to Divodasa, who agrees to father one son, and Narada lists celebrated couples of the gods and kings.
Galava takes Madhavi to King Usinara, who fathers one son, Sivi, and Galava then returns to Garuda.
Garuda sends Galava to Viswamitra with Madhavi and the steeds, and Madhavi bears Ashtaka.
Madhavi rejects all suitors at Yayati's swayamvara and chooses an ascetic life in the forest, and Yayati later falls from heaven through pride.
Yayati, hurled from heaven, lands among four kings holding a sacrifice in Naimisha, and Madhavi arrives with her sons and Galava to help him back to heaven.
Yayati is recognised and rises to heaven as his grandsons each give him the merit of their deeds.
Yayati is restored to heaven, Brahma explains that his fall came from vanity, and Narada turns the lesson to Duryodhana.
Dhritarashtra asks Krishna to persuade Duryodhana, and Krishna gives a long plea for peace.
Bhishma, Drona, Vidura and Dhritarashtra each plead with Duryodhana to accept Krishna's offer of peace.
Bhishma and Drona list the horrors of war that have not yet begun and urge Duryodhana to make peace.
Duryodhana angrily refuses Krishna's terms, saying he will not yield a needle's point of land while his father lives.
Krishna rebukes Duryodhana, Dussasana threatens to bind him, and Duryodhana storms out of the court, while Krishna urges that he be bound.
Gandhari pleads with Duryodhana to restrain his greed and wrath and make peace with the Pandavas, and Duryodhana is brought back to the court.
Duryodhana plots to seize Krishna, Satyaki warns the court, and Dhritarashtra and Vidura rebuke the prince, recalling Krishna's feats.
Krishna answers Duryodhana's plot with a display of his universal form, then takes leave of the elders and rides to Kunti.
Krishna reports to Kunti, who sends Yudhishthira a message urging him to fight as a Kshatriya.
Kunti tells the tale of Vidula, who scolds her defeated son and urges him to fight bravely.
Vidula continues to scold her son, telling him a Kshatriya who avoids battle is a thief, and urging him to fight for his kingdom.
Vidula scolds her son for his despair, and he asks what he can do with no wealth or allies.
Vidula urges her son to act, gain allies and treat his followers well.
Vidula tells her son that friends and hidden treasure remain to him, and his despair lifts; Kunti recommends the tale to others.
Kunti gives Krishna messages for her sons and Draupadi, and Krishna departs for Upaplavya after speaking with Karna.
Bhishma and Drona warn Duryodhana of the Pandavas' strength and the omens of ruin, and beg him to make peace.
Duryodhana stays silent, and Bhishma and Drona each lament that they must fight the Pandavas, urging peace.
Dhritarashtra asks what Krishna told Karna, and Sanjaya reports Krishna's offer to make Karna king among the Pandavas.
Karna declines Krishna's offer, describes the war as a sacrifice, and asks Krishna to bring Arjuna to him in single combat.
Krishna tells Karna that victory will be the Pandavas', citing omens, and sets the battle for the new moon.
Karna lists omens of the Kauravas' defeat and a vision of Pandava triumph, then embraces Krishna and returns in gloom.
Vidura tells Kunti that war is near, and Kunti goes to the Ganga to find Karna.
Karna asks Kunti's purpose, and Kunti reveals he is her son by Surya and urges him to join his brothers.
Surya's voice supports Kunti, but Karna refuses to desert Duryodhana and promises to spare four of Kunti's sons.
Krishna reports his failed mission to the Pandavas, and Yudhishthira asks him to recall the full speeches of the Kuru assembly, starting with Bhishma's.
Drona, Vidura, and Suvala's daughter each speak against Duryodhana's claim, urging that the Pandavas receive half the kingdom.
Dhritarashtra tells Duryodhana the family history of passed-over heirs, argues that Yudhishthira is the rightful king, and asks him to give up half the kingdom.
Krishna tells the Pandavas that Duryodhana rejected every offer, has gathered an army at Kurukshetra, and that the war cannot now be avoided.
Yudhishthira asks his brothers to choose a commander, and each proposes a candidate, from Virata to Sikhandin.
Yudhishthira hands the decision to Krishna, who names Dhrishtadyumna as the army's leader.
The Pandava army marches to Kurukshetra in formation, leaves Draupadi behind at Upaplavya, and blows its conches on arrival.
The Pandavas set up camp on the plain of Kurukshetra by the Hiranwati, with a moat, tents, supplies, and skilled workers, and allied kings arrive to join them.
Janamejaya asks what Duryodhana planned, and the narrator describes Duryodhana ordering the army's preparations and the kings arming for battle.
Krishna tells Yudhishthira that peace is impossible, Yudhishthira reluctantly orders the army to battle, and Arjuna insists they must fight, so the brothers prepare for war.
Duryodhana arranges and equips his eleven akshauhinis, the narrator explains the military units, and Duryodhana places senior warriors over the divisions.
Duryodhana asks Bhishma to lead the army, Bhishma sets his conditions, Karna vows not to fight while Bhishma lives, and the army marches to Kurukshetra amid omens.
Yudhishthira names seven leaders for his army, and Balarama arrives, predicts the slaughter, and explains his wish to stay out of the fight.
Balarama takes leave of the Pandavas and sets out for the sacred waters.
Rukmi offers to fight for Arjuna, Arjuna declines, and Duryodhana rejects Rukmi too, so he leaves the battle.
Janamejaya asks what the Kauravas did next, and Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya for the news, who answers with a view on fate and human agency.
Duryodhana briefs Uluka and sends him to Yudhishthira, with a message that includes a cat-and-mice parable and then taunts to Krishna, Bhima, and Nakula.
The message continues with challenges to Sahadeva, Virata, Drupada, Dhrishtadyumna, and Sikhandin, and ends with a long boast to Arjuna listing the Kaurava army.
Uluka presents himself to the Pandavas and repeats Duryodhana's taunts to Yudhishthira and then to Arjuna.
The Pandavas answer Uluka in turn, with Bhima, Sahadeva, Arjuna, and Yudhishthira each swearing to fight Duryodhana.
Krishna adds his own reply, saying he will act only as Arjuna's charioteer and warning that Duryodhana cannot hide from Arjuna's car.
Arjuna answers Uluka with a vow to kill Bhishma, and Bhima, Nakula, Sahadeva, Virata, and Drupada send their replies.
Sikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna, and Yudhishthira send their final replies, and Uluka reports back to Duryodhana, who orders the army arrayed before dawn.
Dhrishtadyumna arranges the Pandava army and assigns a Pandava warrior to face each leading Kaurava champion.
Dhritarashtra asks about the Kaurava response to Arjuna's vow, Bhishma takes command, and Bhishma begins ranking the Kaurava warriors at Duryodhana's request.
Bhishma continues the ranking of Kaurava warriors, naming kings and princes and describing how each will fight.
Bhishma keeps ranking the Kaurava warriors, praising Ashvatthama and Drona, and naming more princes and kings, ending with Bhagadatta.
Bhishma and Drona belittle Karna, Karna swears he will not fight while Bhishma lives, Bhishma answers him, and Duryodhana asks for a report on the enemy.
Bhishma ranks the Pandava brothers and says Arjuna is unmatched, and the narrator notes the Kaurava kings losing heart.
Bhishma ranks Draupadi's sons, Uttara, Abhimanyu, Satyaki, and other allies, and says that Virata and Drupada will fight with great determination.
Bhishma gives his ratings for Sikhandin, Dhrishtadyumna, Dhrishtaketu, and a long list of Panchala and allied kings.
Bhishma rates more Pandava allies, declares whom he will fight, and explains why he will not harm Sikhandin.
Duryodhana asks Bhishma why he will spare Sikhandin, and Bhishma recounts how he won the princesses of Kasi for his brother.
Bhishma reports the abduction to Satyavati, who rejoices, and Amba asks Bhishma to release her so that she can marry Salwa.
Bhishma sends Amba to Salwa, who rejects her, and Amba protests and pleads to be accepted, but Salwa refuses.
Amba laments her fate, vows vengeance on Bhishma, and goes to a hermitage, where the sage Saikhavatya comforts her.
The ascetics debate Amba's future, Amba refuses to go back to Kasi, and her grandfather Hotravahana sends her to Rama for help.
Akritavrana questions Amba about her wishes, Rama arrives, Hotravahana introduces Amba, and Amba begs Rama to slay Bhishma.
Rama declines to fight except on the command of Brahmanas, Amba urges him to slay Bhishma, and Akritavrana reminds him of his vow.
Rama agrees to confront Bhishma with Amba, and the party travels to Kurukshetra and camps by the Saraswati.
Rama orders Bhishma to marry Amba, Bhishma refuses, Rama challenges him to fight, and Ganga pleads with Bhishma in vain.
Bhishma dismounts to honor Rama, Rama answers with a shower of arrows, and Bhishma wounds Rama in return.
The duel resumes at dawn, Rama wounds Bhishma into a swoon, Bhishma revives and wounds Rama, and the battle ends at dusk with arrows filling the sky.
The duel escalates with celestial weapons, Bhishma defeats Rama's lance and darts, Rama breaks Bhishma's chariot, and the fight stops at sunset.
The duel resumes, Rama kills Bhishma's charioteer and wounds him, Bhishma is raised by eight Brahmanas and his mother Ganga helps, and Bhishma wounds Rama into unconsciousness.
Bhishma prays for a sign, and in a dream eight Brahmanas reveal the Praswapa and Samvodhana weapons and promise his victory.
Bhishma resumes the fight after his dream, both wound each other, and both invoke the Brahma weapon, and Bhishma resolves to use the Praswapa.
Narada and the gods stop Bhishma from using the Praswapa, Rama's ancestors urge him to stop fighting, and Rama and Bhishma agree to end the combat.
Rama admits defeat, Amba vows to kill Bhishma, and she performs penance for many years until Ganga tells her she will become a river.
Amba refuses the ascetics' advice, the trident-bearing god promises her vengeance and a male rebirth, and Amba burns herself on a pyre by the Yamuna.
Duryodhana asks how Sikhandin became a man, and Bhishma explains Drupada's prayer, the god's promise, and the secret raising of the child as a son.
Sikhandin is raised and trained, married to the Dasarnaka princess, and the discovery of the deception leads to Hiranyavarman's threat against Drupada.
Hiranyavarman prepares his army and plots to depose Drupada, and Drupada, now fearful, asks his queen about the truth.
The queen admits the truth, Drupada prepares his defences and prays, and Sikhandini, ashamed, goes to a Yaksha in the forest and asks him to change her into a man.
Sikhandini and Sthuna swap sexes, Sikhandin is cleared of the deception, Kubera curses Sthuna, and Bhishma explains to the Kauravas why he will not fight Sikhandin.
Duryodhana asks the commanders how long each would need to destroy the Pandava army, and each gives his estimate.
Yudhishthira calls his brothers, relays the Kaurava boasts, and asks Arjuna how long he will need, and Arjuna answers with confidence and names the allies.
The Kaurava army marches out in divisions, takes position at Kurukshetra, and Duryodhana sets up a grand camp with provisions for all.
Yudhishthira orders his divisions out in battle array, and the chapter closes the Udyoga Parva before the footnotes begin.
Footnotes 2 to 6 explain divination by stars, the sage's answers on action and liberation, and the link between the soul and the Supreme Soul.
Footnotes 7 to 11 explain the kinds of troops, a name for a fire, an allusion to Vishnu, and the literal sense of an epithet.
Footnotes 12 to 16 explain the story of Vishwamitra, sacrificial offerings, the sacred syllable, a unit of time, and the bodily marks thought auspicious.
Footnotes 17 to 19 cover a river, the classification of weapons, and the story of Kartaviryarjuna, followed by running heads.
A heading names Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa as the author.
The two armies assemble at Kurukshetra, the Pandavas make camp and organise their forces, and both sides agree on rules of combat before the fighting begins.
Vyasa speaks privately with Dhritarashtra, gives Sanjaya the power to report the battle, and describes the omens of disaster he sees around the field.
Vyasa lists portents of a coming slaughter and urges Dhritarashtra to restrain his sons, and Dhritarashtra replies that he is powerless over them.
Dhritarashtra asks about the signs of victory, and Vyasa describes them, warning about panic in an army and the uncertainty of war.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to describe the lands from which the armies came, and Sanjaya explains the kinds of living things and why the earth is worth fighting over.
Dhritarashtra asks for a survey of the earth, and Sanjaya explains the five elements and then describes the island Sudarsana.
Sanjaya lays out the mountains, lands and sacred places of the world, starting with the mountains that divide it and ending with the hare-shaped region.
Sanjaya describes the Northern Kurus, the eastern land of Bhadraswa with its great trees, and the mountain Malyavat with its fire and its ascetics.
Sanjaya lists the remaining Varshas and their mountains and peoples, and Dhritarashtra reflects on Time and on the power of Vishnu.
Dhritarashtra asks about Bharatavarsha, Sanjaya blames Duryodhana for the greed over it, and he gives long lists of its mountains, rivers and peoples before explaining why kings fight over earth.
Dhritarashtra asks about the people of the neighbouring lands, and Sanjaya explains the four ages and how the people of each age differ.
The Bhumi Parva opens with Dhritarashtra's request for the size of Jamvudwipa and its neighbouring islands, and Sanjaya describes Sakadwipa.
Sanjaya names the seven mountains of Sakadwipa, their Varshas and rivers, the Saka tree and the four peaceful provinces, and Dhritarashtra asks why the people there are dark.
Sanjaya describes the outer islands and their oceans, mountains and peoples, then the heavenly bodies, and closes with advice to Dhritarashtra and the merit of hearing the Bhumi Parva.
Sanjaya enters the court and announces that Bhishma has fallen, recalling his greatness and blaming Dhritarashtra's evil counsel.
Dhritarashtra, overwhelmed with grief, asks a long series of questions about how Bhishma fell, who protected him, and what his sons and allies did, and he begs Sanjaya to tell him everything.
Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra not to blame Duryodhana, describes his divine sight, and recounts Duryodhana's orders to protect Bhishma from Sikhandin.
At dawn both armies take their positions, Sanjaya lists the Kaurava commanders and Bhishma at the front, and he compares the two armies to great oceans.
On the first day, Bhishma urges the kings to fight, Karna lays down his arms, the Kaurava divisions advance under their leaders, and their battle formation is set out.
The armies clash in uproar and display, and Sanjaya lists the warriors and peoples who guard Bhishma and the size of the Kaurava force.
Yudhishthira asks Arjuna for a formation, Arjuna sets out the Vajra array, and omens of wind, dust and thunder appear at dawn.
Dhritarashtra asks which side was eager and which had the omens, and Sanjaya describes both armies, the omens and the Kaurava commanders.
Yudhishthira is dismayed by Bhishma's array, and Arjuna answers that victory lies with righteousness and with Krishna.
Yudhishthira arranges the Pandava army and urges it to fight fairly, Sanjaya describes the commanders and Arjuna's car, and Krishna points out Bhishma and urges Arjuna to attack him.
Krishna urges Arjuna to pray to Durga, and Arjuna recites a long hymn to the goddess before the battle.
Durga appears and promises Arjuna victory, Krishna and Arjuna blow their conches, and Sanjaya explains the benefits of the hymn and the reason for victory.
Dhritarashtra asks who began the fight in high spirits, and Sanjaya says that both armies were equally eager and the clash was fierce.
The Gita opens as Dhritarashtra asks about the armies, Duryodhana names the leaders on both sides, the conches sound, and Arjuna asks to see the warriors before battle.
Krishna places Arjuna's car between the armies, Arjuna sees his kinsmen, and he is overcome with grief, lays down his bow and sits down in his car.
Arjuna, overcome with grief, refuses to fight, and Krishna rebukes him for his weakness.
Krishna teaches that the soul is eternal, that a warrior must fight his just battle without attachment to results, and describes the steady-minded sage.
Arjuna asks why he must act, Krishna teaches action without attachment as sacrifice, and then names desire as the enemy that must be overcome.
Krishna explains how this teaching was passed down, answers Arjuna's question about his births, and teaches action, sacrifice and knowledge before urging Arjuna to cast off doubt.
Arjuna asks which is better, renunciation or action, and Krishna explains that acting with devotion is superior and describes the sage who is at peace.
Krishna describes the true renouncer and the practice of meditation, and he and Arjuna discuss how hard it is to still the restless mind.
Krishna says the devotee who falls away is not lost, and that the one who worships him with faith is the most devout.
Krishna explains his lower and higher natures, his presence in all things, the illusion that hides him, the classes of worshippers, and who truly reaches him.
Arjuna asks about Brahman, the self and the hour of death, and Krishna explains remembering him at death, the cycles of time and the two paths.
Krishna reveals the royal mystery of his presence in all things, the cycles of creation, and the open door of devotion to all who turn to him.
Krishna declares that he is the source of gods and sages, Arjuna praises him and asks for his powers, and Krishna lists his many manifestations.
Arjuna asks to see Krishna's true form, and Krishna grants him divine sight to behold the universal form.
Krishna reveals himself as Time and the destroyer, Arjuna praises and fears him, and Krishna returns to his gentle form.
Arjuna regains his composure, and Krishna explains that only devotion can reveal him.
Arjuna asks which devotees are best, and Krishna explains the path of personal devotion, the harder path of the unmanifest, and the qualities of those he loves.
Krishna explains the field and its knower, the virtues that make up true knowledge, the supreme Brahman, and the difference between nature and spirit.
Krishna teaches how the three qualities bind the soul and how to transcend them, and he describes the person who has risen above them when Arjuna asks.
Krishna describes the eternal fig tree of the world, the soul as his part, his presence in the light of the world, and his supreme nature beyond the perishable and imperishable.
Krishna sets the divine and demonic qualities side by side, describes the demonic people and their fall, and names the three gates of hell.
Arjuna asks about faith outside scripture, and Krishna explains the three kinds of faith, food, sacrifice, penance and gifts, ending with the sacred words OM, TAT and SAT.
Arjuna asks about renunciation, Krishna explains the three qualities of action, knowledge and duty, urges surrender to him, and Arjuna accepts; Sanjaya then closes the dialogue.
A closing marker that ends the Bhagavad Gita.
Yudhishthira walks unarmed toward the Kaurava elders, and his brothers question him as he goes.
Yudhishthira salutes Bhishma, who grants him leave to fight and says he is bound to the Kauravas by their wealth.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma how he can be defeated, and Bhishma says no one can beat him while his time has not come.
Yudhishthira asks Drona for leave and blessing, and Drona grants them, confessing that he too is bound to the Kauravas by wealth.
Drona tells Yudhishthira that he can be killed only when he lays down his arms, and Yudhishthira goes on to Kripa.
Yudhishthira seeks leave from Kripa and Salya, who both grant it while saying they must fight for the Kauravas.
Yudhishthira asks Salya to weaken Karna, Salya agrees, and Krishna goes to Karna to urge him to switch sides.
Karna refuses to desert Duryodhana, Yuyutsu joins the Pandavas, and both armies prepare for battle.
Dhritarashtra asks who struck first, and Sanjaya describes the first clash of the two armies, led by Bhishma and Bhima.
The battle opens with a huge uproar and a series of single combats between the leading warriors of both sides, until the fighting becomes a confused melee.
Sanjaya describes the slaughter among foot soldiers, elephants, horses and chariots, where kin kill one another, and the Pandava divisions begin to waver before Bhishma.
Bhishma's guards press forward, Abhimanyu fells Bhishma's standard, and Sweta's charge against Salya is halted and Salya rescued.
Dhritarashtra asks what happened when Sweta charged Salya, and Sanjaya describes the duel between Bhishma and Sweta, Sweta's death and the nightfall withdrawal.
Dhritarashtra questions Sanjaya about the Pandava response and his own guilt, and Sanjaya describes the fighting of the day, with Bhishma routing the Pandava forces until nightfall.
Yudhishthira laments Bhishma's power before Krishna, is comforted, appoints Dhrishtadyumna commander, and the Pandava army is drawn up in the Krauncharuma array for the next day.
Duryodhana arranges his own army against the Pandava array, and both sides sound their conches before advancing.
Dhritarashtra asks how the battle began, Duryodhana orders the attack, and Bhishma and Arjuna fight a long duel that the gods regard as unmatched.
Dhritarashtra asks about the duel between Drona and Dhrishtadyumna, and Sanjaya describes Drona's victories, Dhrishtadyumna's defiance, and Bhima's rescue.
Dhritarashtra asks how the Kalinga king fought Bhima, and Sanjaya describes Bhima's rampage through the Kalinga forces and the rescue by Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki.
Dhrishtadyumna, Abhimanyu and Arjuna fight the Kaurava leaders, Arjuna scatters the army, and Bhishma withdraws the Kaurava forces at sunset.
Bhishma forms the Garuda array, Arjuna answers with a half-moon array, and the armies clash at dawn.
Arjuna cuts down Kaurava car leaders, the armies fight in a general melee, and both sides push and break each other's ranks.
Kings attack Arjuna, Bhima wounds Duryodhana and routs his army, and Duryodhana rebukes Bhishma, who vows to fight alone.
Bhishma storms the Pandava army, Krishna and Arjuna face him in a duel, Arjuna holds back Krishna's attack on Bhishma, and Arjuna's Indra weapon brings carnage until nightfall.
The third day opens with Bhishma leading the Kaurava army against Arjuna, the armies clash, and Bhishma and Arjuna duel while Abhimanyu attacks the Kaurava ranks.
Abhimanyu battles the Kaurava princes, Dhrishtadyumna rescues him, Samyamani's son is killed, and Samyamani and Salya attack Dhrishtadyumna.
Dhritarashtra asks about the battle, and Sanjaya describes the clashes of Dhrishtadyumna, Abhimanyu and Salya, followed by Bhima's rampage against the Magadha elephants.
Duryodhana sends his army against Bhima, who holds them off with his mace, and Satyaki then advances toward Bhishma until Bhurisravas steps in to fight him.
The duels of Satyaki and Bhurisravas and of Bhima and Duryodhana unfold, with Bhagadatta and Ghatotkacha joining, until Bhishma orders a withdrawal at nightfall and Duryodhana mourns.

Dhritarashtra questions Sanjaya, Sanjaya blames the sons' wickedness and Duryodhana's refusal to listen, Duryodhana asks Bhishma for the cause of Pandava victory, and Bhishma tells the story of Brahma's praise of Vishnu.
Brahma's account of the god's agreement to be born among men and Bhishma's warning against despising Vasudeva, followed by Bhishma's explanation of why the Kauravas are wrong to oppose him.
Duryodhana asks about Vasudeva, and Bhishma describes his creation of the world, his slaying of Madhu, and his role as protector, and says Yudhishthira has taken refuge in him.
Bhishma recites a hymn in which various seers praise Vasudeva, and Sanjaya reports Duryodhana's change of heart, Bhishma's renewed plea for peace, and Duryodhana's return to his tent.
The armies form their battle arrays, Bhima and Arjuna attack Bhishma, Duryodhana asks Drona to break the Pandava line, and Drona and Sikhandin clash with their opponents.
Bhishma fights to protect the Kauravas from Bhima, Sanjaya describes the carnage across the field, and both armies press against Bhishma.
Arjuna drives at Bhishma, the Kaurava army falls back behind him, allied kings arrive, opposing warriors are matched in pairs, and the field is strewn with dead elephants, horses and chariots.
Duels spread across the field, Bhishma defeats Bhima's attack and wrecks Satyaki's chariot, and the Pandava forces attack again.

Virata and Bhishma exchange arrows, Arjuna and Aswatthaman fight and Arjuna holds back, Bhima and Duryodhana trade hits, Abhimanyu fights Chitrasena and Lakshmana until Kripa carries Lakshmana away, and Bhishma's attacks leave the field strewn with bodies.

Satyaki duels Bhurisravas, Satyaki's sons die fighting him, Satyaki and Bhurisravas continue on foot until they are pulled away, and Arjuna's destruction of the Kaurava chariots ends the day as the armies withdraw at twilight.
The two armies form their arrays, Yudhishthira's Makara meets Bhishma's crane, and the fighting is broken into many clashes until Drona and Bhishma drive the Pandavas back.
Dhritarashtra describes the strength and loyalty of his army, its leaders, and its vast size, then wonders why such an army is being slaughtered and blames fate and his son's refusal to heed Vidura.

Sanjaya blames the king for the war, Bhima fights through the Kaurava host and is rescued by Dhrishtadyumna, Duryodhana's forces turn on the rescuers, Drona neutralises the Pramohana weapon, and Drona drives the Pandava army into retreat.
Duryodhana regains consciousness and fights Bhima, the brothers of Duryodhana attack Bhima, and Yudhishthira sends reinforcements led by Abhimanyu so that the sons withdraw.
Abhimanyu and Bhima attack the Kauravas in the afternoon, Abhimanyu defeats Vikarna and others, Bhishma and Arjuna carry out slaughter, and the field is described as a sea of blood.

Bhima confronts Duryodhana with a long speech of accusation and wounds him, Kripa and Jayadratha rescue Duryodhana, Abhimanyu and the sons of Dhritarashtra clash in many duels, and Bhishma routs the Pandavas at sunset.
After resting, Duryodhana asks Bhishma how to win, Bhishma promises to fight hard, and Duryodhana's army advances in full array.

Bhishma names the Kaurava allies and heals Duryodhana, sets up the Mandala array and the Pandava Vajra array, the armies pair off, and Arjuna and Krishna face the kings with the Aindra weapon until Bhishma rescues the fleeing warriors.

Duryodhana sends the kings to shield Bhishma as he meets Arjuna, and a series of single combats follows, including Drona against Virata, Aswatthaman against Sikhandin, Satyaki against Alamvusha, Dhrishtadyumna against Duryodhana, and Bhima against Kritavarman.
Dhritarashtra asks why his side always loses, Sanjaya blames the king's misconduct, and the battles of Iravat, Ghatotkacha, Bhagadatta and the twins against Salya are reported in turn.
Yudhishthira defeats Srutayush, Kripa fights Chekitana, Dhrishtaketu and Bhurisravas clash, Abhimanyu faces several Kaurava warriors, and Arjuna moves against Susarman and his followers.

Arjuna clears the way toward Bhishma, Yudhishthira rebukes Sikhandin for failing to keep his oath, Sikhandin resumes his attack, Bhishma defeats Yudhishthira, and Bhima and Chitrasena fight until Chitrasena's chariot is smashed.
Bhishma routs Yudhishthira and the twins, the Pandavas gather their allies against him, Dhrishtadyumna and Satyaki fight the Kauravas, and at dusk both armies withdraw to their tents.
Both armies march out, the Kauravas form a line led by Bhishma, Yudhishthira answers with the Sringataka array, and a fierce general battle begins with Bhishma charging the Pandavas.

Bhishma cuts down the Pandava forces until Bhima takes on Bhishma's charioteer and then kills Duryodhana's brothers one after another, Duryodhana accuses Bhishma, and Bhishma answers that the Kauravas cannot win.

Dhritarashtra asks about the losses, Sanjaya blames the king for ignoring Vidura, and the midday battle is described with the Pandavas attacking in three groups, Drona slaughtering the Srinjayas, and Bhima and the twins destroying elephants and horses.

Sakuni and Kritavarma attack the Pandavas, Iravat leads his cavalry against the Kauravas, fights off the sons of Suvala, and is killed by Alamvusha after a long illusion-filled battle. The field is then filled with slaughter, Arjuna unknowingly kills Bhishma's guards, and Bhishma and Drona terrify the Pandavas.

Dhritarashtra asks what the Pandavas did after Iravat's death, Sanjaya describes Ghatotkacha's roar and his assault on the Kaurava elephants, Duryodhana fights the Rakshasas, and Ghatotkacha accuses Duryodhana of his crimes.
Duryodhana endures Ghatotkacha's arrows, Ghatotkacha kills Bhagadatta's elephant with a dart, Bhishma sends a rescue force, and Ghatotkacha wounds or disables the rescuers one after another.
Ghatotkacha rises into the sky, Yudhishthira sends Bhima and his allies to save Ghatotkacha, and the two sides fight in a chaotic, bloody battle that drives the Kaurava forces back.

Duryodhana wounds Bhima, the Kaurava and Pandava warriors clash around them, Nila and Aswatthaman fight, Ghatotkacha uses an illusion that routs the Kauravas, and Sanjaya and Bhishma try in vain to hold the army together.

Duryodhana reports his defeat to Bhishma, Bhishma sends Bhagadatta to face Ghatotkacha, Bhagadatta's elephant battles the Pandava warriors and wounds Bhima, Arjuna joins the fight, and Bhima reports Iravat's death.

Arjuna laments the war, Bhima fights Drona and kills several of Dhritarashtra's sons, Bhishma and his allies go after Arjuna, Abhimanyu unseats Amvashta, the close fighting spreads, and both armies withdraw at night.

Duryodhana and his counsellors plan the next day's fighting, Karna urges that Bhishma withdraw, and Duryodhana goes to Bhishma's tent in a grand procession and presses him to act, but Bhishma stays silent.

Bhishma answers Duryodhana's taunts with the story of the Pandavas' victories, pledges to spare Sikhandin, Duryodhana orders his army to protect Bhishma, and Arjuna places Sikhandin before Bhishma in the battle.
Bhishma and Yudhishthira both form their arrays and command their forces, the two armies advance with loud noise, and omens of disaster appear in the sky and on the earth.

Abhimanyu routs the Kaurava ranks, Duryodhana sends Alamvusha against him, Alamvusha defeats the five sons of Draupadi, and the chapter ends with Alamvusha and Abhimanyu clashing in a duel watched by both armies.
Dhritarashtra asks for a full account, Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu's duel with Alamvusha in which the illusions are overcome, and the battle then spreads to Bhishma, Arjuna, Kripa, Satyaki and Drona.

Dhritarashtra asks how the two heroes came to fight, Sanjaya explains the duty of Kshatriyas, Arjuna defeats the Trigartas with the Vayavya weapon while Drona counters, and Bhima fights the Kaurava elephants with his mace.

The midday battle between Bhishma and the Somakas becomes general, with Bhishma sparing Sikhandin, the fighting spreading across the field, the river of blood described, and Duryodhana urging his men on.

Arjuna routs Susarman's men, Duryodhana leads a counterattack on Arjuna, the Pandavas gather around Bhishma and fight a series of duels including Satyaki's clash with Bhishma, and the battle resumes at full strength.
Duryodhana orders his brother to shield Bhishma, Sakuni's horsemen are destroyed by the Pandavas, Salya fights Yudhishthira, and Bhima hurries to his brother's aid as the sun sets.

Bhishma routs the Pandava army, Krishna urges Arjuna to fight him, Arjuna and Bhishma duel, Krishna jumps down and rushes at Bhishma, Arjuna halts him, and Bhishma's shafts drive the Pandavas back until sunset.

The armies withdraw at dusk, Yudhishthira despairs at night and Krishna offers to fight, the Pandavas visit Bhishma's tent and ask how he can be beaten, and Bhishma explains the conditions under which he can be defeated.
Arjuna refuses to fight his grandfather, Krishna urges him to fight as a Kshatriya must, and Arjuna proposes to place Sikhandin before Bhishma.

Dhritarashtra asks about Sikhandin and Bhishma, Sanjaya describes the battle arrays, Bhishma defeats the Pandava warriors on the tenth day, refuses to fight Sikhandin, Sikhandin taunts and wounds him, and Arjuna urges Sikhandin on.
Dhritarashtra asks about the tenth day, Sanjaya describes Arjuna's arrival and Duryodhana's plea, and Bhishma answers with a vow and a massive slaughter of Pandava troops.
Arjuna urges Sikhandin on, the Pandava and Kaurava warriors pair off across the field, Dussasana blocks Arjuna, and Arjuna wounds Dussasana and Duryodhana before Duryodhana retreats.
Satyaki battles Alamvusha and Bhagadatta, Duryodhana orders the Kauravas to surround Satyaki, and a series of duels spreads across the field among Bhishma's guards and the Pandava warriors.

Drona describes the bad omens he sees, warns that Arjuna will attack Bhishma and that Sikhandin is an ill omen, and sends his son Aswatthaman against Sikhandin and Bhima while he goes against Yudhishthira.
Ten Kaurava warriors attack Bhima, who wounds them all and defeats their projectiles, Arjuna arrives to help, and Duryodhana sends Susarman against both Pandava brothers.
Arjuna and Bhima battle Susarman's Trigartas and the Kaurava kings, Drona and the Magadha king attack Bhima, Bhishma and Duryodhana advance, and Sikhandin and the Pandavas charge Bhishma.

Dhritarashtra asks about Bhishma's fighting on the tenth day, Sanjaya describes Bhishma's resolve to be slain, Yudhishthira accepts and plans the attack, and both armies clash in a huge general battle.

Abhimanyu, Aswatthaman, Paurava and Dhrishtaketu, Chitrasena and Susarman, and Drona and Dhrishtadyumna all clash in duels across the field, while Bhima destroys the elephant division and Yudhishthira and Salya exchange blows.
Arjuna pushes toward Bhishma, scattering the Kaurava warriors, while Bhishma fights back with his weapons and drives the Pandava army back.

Sikhandin attacks Bhishma, Bhishma refuses to strike him, Arjuna urges Sikhandin on, Dussasana and Arjuna fight, and Duryodhana rallies his allies to face Arjuna. Arjuna scatters the Kaurava forces, and Bhishma confronts Arjuna until the armies are thrown into confusion.

The armies fight without order, Salya and the Kaurava warriors push back the Pandavas, Bhishma destroys thousands of their warriors, Dhrishtadyumna orders an attack on Bhishma, and Arjuna and Sikhandin move against him.
The Pandavas surround Bhishma, Arjuna and Sikhandin cut down his bows, Bhishma resolves to die, and when he falls at sunset he waits on his bed of arrows until the sun turns north.

Dhritarashtra mourns Bhishma's fall and asks what happened, Sanjaya describes the Kaurava grief, the halt in the fighting, the gathering of kings, and Bhishma's request for a pillow fit for a warrior.

Arjuna props up Bhishma's head with arrows, Bhishma praises him, Bhishma refuses the physicians, the armies gather around him and then go to rest, and Krishna and Yudhishthira speak together about the victory.
The kings gather around Bhishma in the morning, Bhishma asks for water and then for Arjuna, Arjuna makes a spring rise, Bhishma praises him and urges Duryodhana to make peace, and Duryodhana refuses.
Karna comes to the dying Bhishma, who embraces him, reveals that Karna is Kunti's son, and urges peace with the Pandavas before giving him leave to fight.
