Janamejaya asks about Dhritarashtra's grief after Bhishma's fall, and Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to report what the Kauravas did next.
Sanjaya describes the Kauravas and Pandavas after Bhishma's fall and the call for Karna, and Dhritarashtra replies with doubt about whether Karna can hold the army together.
Karna goes to the field after Bhishma's fall, speaks to the soldiers, consoles the Kauravas, prepares his arms and car, and rides out to battle.
Sanjaya describes Bhishma lying on the arrow-bed, and Karna dismounting in grief to greet him and vow to fight the Pandavas.
Bhishma blesses Karna and orders him to lead the army, and Karna goes to the Kaurava warriors, who welcome him with shouts and noise.
Duryodhana asks Karna whom to appoint as commander after Bhishma, and Karna names Drona as the best choice.
Duryodhana makes his request to Drona with long praise, and the Kaurava kings cheer, and Drona prepares to answer.
Drona agrees to lead and is installed as commander, the two armies take their formations, and the battle opens with omens and Drona's assault on the Pandava ranks.
Yudhishthira orders the Pandavas to surround Drona, Drona's rampage through their ranks, and Sanjaya's report that Dhrishtadyumna killed him.
Dhritarashtra mourns Drona, wonders how the master could be slain, and asks Sanjaya a string of questions about the battle, then pauses his questioning.
Dhritarashtra faints, is revived by his attendants, and asks Sanjaya a long series of questions about which Kaurava warriors opposed each Pandava hero as they attacked Drona.
Dhritarashtra praises Krishna's exploits, predicts Kaurava defeat if Krishna joins the Pandavas, blames his own acts for the ruin, and asks for a full account of the battle.
Drona offers a boon, Duryodhana asks for Yudhishthira to be seized alive, Drona agrees on conditions, and Duryodhana publicizes the pledge.
Yudhishthira hears of Drona's pledge and asks Arjuna to protect him, Arjuna vows to do so, and the armies clash while Drona attacks Dhrishtadyumna's division.
Drona's rampage is described as a river of carnage, the Pandava champions attack him, and a series of single combats ends with the Kauravas closing in on Abhimanyu.
Dhritarashtra asks about Salya's combat with Abhimanyu, Sanjaya describes Salya and Bhima's mace duel, and the Kaurava army breaks and flees.
Vrishasena fights off the Pandava warriors, Drona charges Yudhishthira and kills his defenders, Arjuna arrives, and the two sides break off at sunset.
Drona asks Duryodhana to lure Arjuna away, the Trigartas swear an oath to do so, Arjuna takes up the challenge with Yudhishthira's leave, and the armies clash.
The Samsaptakas meet Arjuna in battle, he stuns them with his conch and kills Sudhanwan, and their king rallies the fleeing warriors to return to the fight.
Arjuna and Krishna fight the Samsaptakas, using illusory weapons and a wind weapon to win, while Drona presses his assault on Yudhishthira.

Drona arrays the Kaurava army as a Garuda, Yudhishthira prepares a counter-array and asks Dhrishtadyumna for protection, and the battle degenerates into a bloody melee that carries Drona toward Yudhishthira.
Drona kills Satyajit and Satanika, Yudhishthira flees, and a rush of Pandava warriors fails to stop Drona as he routs their armies.
Dhritarashtra asks who stood against Drona, Duryodhana boasts to Karna of the enemy's defeat, Karna warns of the Pandava return, and both sides move back toward Drona.
Dhritarashtra asks for the warriors who attacked Drona, Sanjaya lists them by their horses, standards and bows, and then describes the many duels that broke out across the field.
Dhritarashtra asks about Arjuna, Sanjaya describes Bhima's fight with Duryodhana's elephants and Bhagadatta's elephant, and Bhagadatta's elephant rampages through the Pandava host.
Arjuna sets out for Bhagadatta, is challenged by the Samsaptakas, chooses to destroy them first with the Brahma weapon, earns Krishna's praise, and turns to Bhagadatta.
Arjuna defeats Susharman and his brothers, scatters the Kaurava host, and sets up a clash with Bhagadatta's elephant, where he refuses to strike from behind.
Dhritarashtra asks how the duel ended, Sanjaya describes the fight between Arjuna and Bhagadatta, and Krishna explains the Vaishnava weapon before Arjuna kills Bhagadatta.
Arjuna kills Vrishaka and Achala, Sakuni conjures illusions that Arjuna dispels, Sakuni flees, and Arjuna's arrows cut down the Kaurava host.
Dhritarashtra asks about the Kaurava mood after the rout, Sanjaya describes the fierce struggle over Drona, and Ashvatthama kills Nila while the Pandavas lose heart.
Bhima, Drona and the Pandava host clash in a furious melee, Arjuna arrives and fights Karna, Karna is rescued from Satyaki, and both armies withdraw at sunset.
The Kauravas retire after defeat, Duryodhana blames Drona, Drona sets up his array while the Samsaptakas draw Arjuna away, Abhimanyu breaks in and falls, and Dhritarashtra laments.
Sanjaya agrees to describe the slaying of Abhimanyu in detail.
Sanjaya praises the Pandavas and Abhimanyu, Dhritarashtra asks for an account of his death, and Sanjaya describes the Kaurava circular array before the battle begins.
The Pandavas fail to break Drona's array, Yudhishthira asks Abhimanyu to do it, and Abhimanyu and the Pandava leaders agree.
Yudhishthira blesses Abhimanyu, and Abhimanyu orders his charioteer to drive toward Drona's army.
Sumitra warns Abhimanyu against recklessness, Abhimanyu drives into Drona's array, and he cuts down warriors and beasts until the Kauravas flee in terror.
Duryodhana attacks Abhimanyu, Drona orders the king rescued, the Kaurava warriors surround Abhimanyu, and he kills and wounds his way through them until the army flees.
Dhritarashtra asks who opposed Abhimanyu, Sanjaya describes Salya's brother's death, and Abhimanyu routs the followers who come after him.
Dhritarashtra asks for the story again, Sanjaya describes Abhimanyu's rampage and Drona's praise, Duryodhana orders the attack, and Duhsasana fights Abhimanyu in a car duel.
Abhimanyu taunts and wounds Duhsasana, who is carried off, Karna challenges Abhimanyu and is stripped of his umbrella, steeds and bow, and the Pandavas rejoice.
Karna's brother is killed, Karna flees, Abhimanyu routs the Kaurava army, and the field is strewn with the dead as Abhimanyu blazes through the enemy.
Dhritarashtra asks about the Pandava pursuit, Sanjaya says Jayadratha rallied the Kauravas, and Sanjaya explains Jayadratha's austerities and the boon he received from Mahadeva.
Jayadratha, on his magnificent chariot, fights off the Pandava leaders one after another and closes the path Abhimanyu had opened.
Abhimanyu drives Vrishasena from the field, kills Vasatiya, and slaughters the warriors who surround him until the battlefield is strewn with dead.
Abhimanyu seizes Satyasravas, slays Rukmaratha and a band of princes with the Gandharva weapon, and drives Duryodhana back.
The Kaurava army flees, Drona and others attack Abhimanyu, Lakshmana is slain, and Abhimanyu breaks through the elephant division and kills Kratha's son.
Dhritarashtra asks who surrounded Abhimanyu, Sanjaya describes the six great warriors' attacks, and Abhimanyu's killings and wounds scatter the Kaurava kings.
Abhimanyu duels Karna and kills many warriors, Drona advises disarming him, the Kauravas strip him of his bow, steeds and charioteers, and he is left to charge Drona with a wheel.
Abhimanyu is disarmed, fights on with a mace, and is killed by Duhsasana's son, and Yudhishthira then rallies his routed troops.
The Kauravas leave the field at dusk, and Sanjaya describes the battlefield of corpses, the scavengers, the river of blood, and Abhimanyu's body.
The Pandava warriors sit mourning, Yudhishthira blames himself for Abhimanyu's death, and predicts Arjuna's vengeance on the Kauravas.
Yudhishthira laments Abhimanyu's death, Vyasa tries to console him, and Yudhishthira asks what Death is.
Vyasa tells the story of King Akampana, whose son was slain, and of Narada's account of the origin of Death.
Shiva pleads with Brahma to stop his fire, Brahma explains his anger, Shiva asks for mercy, and Brahma names Death and sets her to her task.
Narada tells how Death pleads with Brahma, is told to kill anyway, performs austerities, is ordered again, and finally accepts, and how Narada comforts Akampana.
Vyasa tells Yudhishthira to cast off grief, recalls Abhimanyu's heavenly reward, and urges him to set out for battle.
Yudhishthira asks for more examples, and Vyasa tells the story of Srinjaya's gold-producing son, his death at the hands of robbers, and Narada's consolation using King Marutta.
Narada recounts Suhotra's wealth, sacrifices and death, and tells Srinjaya not to grieve for a son who gave no sacrifices.
Narada recounts King Paurava's vast gifts at his sacrifices and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve for his son.
Narada recounts King Sivi's enormous gifts, Rudra's boon, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve for his son.
Narada recounts Rama's exile, his slaying of Ravana, his golden reign and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve for his son.
Narada recounts Bhagiratha's gifts, the river Ganga choosing him as her father, and his ascent to heaven, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Dilipa's hundreds of sacrifices, his gift of the earth and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Mandhatri's unusual birth, his conquests, his vast sacrifices and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Yayati's sacrifices, his lesson that desire is never satisfied, his retreat to the forest, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Amvarisha's single-handed victories, his hundred sacrifices and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Sasavindu's many sons, his vast gifts at the Horse-sacrifice, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Gaya's long devotion, Agni's boons, his splendid sacrifices and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Rantideva's feeding of Brahmins, his gifts of gold, the river named after his sacrificial hides, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada recounts Bharata's childhood mastery over wild beasts, his many Horse-sacrifices and gifts, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Narada describes Prithu's golden reign, his milking of the Earth by all classes of beings, his great gifts, and his death, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.

Narada recounts Rama's campaign against the Kshatriyas, his gift of the earth to Kasyapa, his retreat to Mount Mahendra, and the fact that all such great men die, and again tells Srinjaya not to grieve.
Srinjaya's grief is lifted, Narada restores his son, Vyasa draws the lesson of Abhimanyu's death, and Yudhishthira, consoled, worries about facing Arjuna.
Arjuna and Krishna return to camp at sunset, Arjuna finds the camp joyless and his brothers grieving, Arjuna laments Abhimanyu's death, and Krishna consoles him.
Yudhishthira recounts Abhimanyu's death, Arjuna swoons and rises in rage, swears two oaths to kill Jayadratha, and sounds his conch.
Jayadratha, frightened by Arjuna's vow, asks to leave, Duryodhana reassures him, and that night Drona answers his question about Arjuna's skill and promises protection.
Krishna rebukes Arjuna's rash oath, spies report the Kaurava dismay, Jayadratha pleads for protection, and Drona sets up a cart-and-lotus array with six champions guarding Jayadratha.
Arjuna's boast and oath against Jayadratha, followed by his request that Krishna ready the chariot for dawn.
A night of frightening omens, and Krishna's visit to comfort the grieving women and promise Jayadratha's death.
Subhadra's lament for Abhimanyu, the arrival of Draupadi and Uttara, and Krishna's comfort to the grieving women.
The night before the battle: the rites in Arjuna's tent, the camp's worry, and Krishna's midnight orders to Daruka.
Krishna's dream counsel to Arjuna, the spirit journey to Shiva's mountain, and the hymn of praise that wins the Pasupata weapon.
Shiva grants Arjuna the Pasupata weapon through the bow and arrow taken from the lake, and the pair return to camp.
Yudhishthira's morning routine of music, bathing, worship and gifts, followed by his reception of Krishna.
The assembly of warriors, Yudhishthira's plea to Krishna for help, and Krishna's promise that Arjuna will kill Jayadratha that day.
Arjuna reports his meeting with Shiva to Yudhishthira, the three heroes set out for battle, and Arjuna assigns Satyaki to protect the king.
Dhritarashtra's grief over the silent camps, his regret over ignoring peace counsel, and his demand to hear what Duryodhana did next.
Sanjaya rebukes Dhritarashtra for his late regret and blames him for failing to restrain his sons.
Drona arrays the troops and places Jayadratha behind a strong guard, and Duryodhana sees the formation and rejoices.
The start of the battle with omens and conch blasts, Durmarshana's challenge, and Arjuna's rout of the Kaurava army.
Dhritarashtra's question about who resisted Arjuna, and Duhsasana's failed elephant charge and flight to Drona.
Arjuna's request for Drona's blessing, their duel at the entrance of the array, and Arjuna's push forward past Drona toward Jayadratha.
Arjuna's duels with Drona, Kritavarman, Srutayudha and Sudakshina, and the death of these allies of the Kauravas.
Arjuna's slaughter of the Kaurava allies, his temporary collapse under a spear and Krishna's comfort, and the end of the battle at the blood river.
Duryodhana's appeal to Drona, Drona's refusal to chase Arjuna, and Drona's blessings and story of the armour as it is tied on Duryodhana.
Drona's account of how the armour passed from Shiva to Drona, and the armoured Duryodhana setting out against Arjuna.
The main battle at the gate of Drona's array, the Kaurava host splitting under Dhrishtadyumna's attack, and Jayadratha's rear guard.
A series of single combats across the battlefield, ending with Sakuni fleeing and the Pandava fury described as unstoppable.
The general carnage of the battle, Dhrishtadyumna's daring leap onto Drona's chariot, and Satyaki's rescue of him.
Dhritarashtra's question, the duel between Drona and Satyaki, the cancelled celestial weapons, and the rush to rescue each champion at sunset.
Arjuna and Krishna's advance toward Jayadratha at sunset, the slaying of Vinda and Anuvinda, and Arjuna's stand on foot against the Kaurava army.
Arjuna's stand on foot, Krishna's care for the horses, and the renewed charge toward Jayadratha with Duryodhana joining the defence.
Arjuna and Krishna cross the divisions of Drona and the Bhojas, plan Jayadratha's death, and Duryodhana charges to block them.
Krishna's speech urging Arjuna to face Duryodhana, Arjuna's agreement, and Duryodhana's challenge to Arjuna.
Duryodhana's armour blocks Arjuna's arrows, Aswatthaman blocks the arrows Arjuna prepares, Duryodhana is left carless, and the Kaurava forces rush to protect him.
The Kaurava champions surround Arjuna, the blasts of the conches, and Arjuna's counterattack against the eight champions.
Dhritarashtra's request, Sanjaya's list of the standards on both sides, and his blame of the king's policy for the slaughter.
The afternoon fighting between the Panchalas and Drona's division, and Drona's defeat of Yudhishthira, which leaves the king fleeing.
A run of single combats, each won by a Pandava side or ally, ending with Drona turning on Satyaki.
Somadatta's son is killed by the five sons of Draupadi, and Bhima's duel with the Rakshasa Alamvusha, ending with Alamvusha's retreat.
Ghatotkacha's duel with Alamvusha, the Pandava attack on Alamvusha, and Ghatotkacha's killing of him.
Dhritarashtra asks about the Drona and Satyaki duel, the Pandava rush to save Satyaki, and Yudhishthira's appeal to Satyaki to go aid Arjuna.
Satyaki's pledge to aid Arjuna, his worry about leaving Yudhishthira unguarded, and Yudhishthira's decision to send him onward.
Satyaki's decision to obey Yudhishthira and follow Arjuna, his list of enemy forces, and his departure after the rites and farewell to Bhima.
Satyaki's rout of the Kaurava troops, his clash with Drona, his escape toward Karna's host, and his duel with Kritavarman.
Dhritarashtra's lament over his army's defeat and Sanjaya's reply blaming the king, followed by Kritavarman's one-man stand against the Pandavas.
Satyaki's duel with Kritavarman, his rout of the Trigarta elephants, his killing of Jalasandha, and Drona's approach.
Satyaki's clash with Drona, Duhsasana and other sons of Dhritarashtra, his wounding of Duryodhana, and his defeat of Kritavarman.
The duel between Drona and Satyaki, Satyaki's self-driving, and Drona's withdrawal to protect his array.
Satyaki's scornful remark, his killing of King Sudarsana, and his advance along Arjuna's track.
Satyaki's advance toward the foreign troops before Jayadratha, his charioteer's reassurance, his vow, and his slaughter of the Yavanas, Kambojas and Sakas.
Satyaki's advance through the Kaurava army, his duel with Duryodhana and the princes, and the rout of the Kaurava forces.
Dhritarashtra's despair, Sanjaya's blame of the king, Satyaki's slaughter of the Samsaptakas and mountain tribesmen, and Drona's decision to pursue him.
Drona's rebuke of Duhsasana, Drona's slaughter of Panchala princes, his duel with Dhrishtadyumna, and his return to his own array.
Duhsasana's failed attack on Satyaki, the Trigarta assault and its defeat, Satyaki's sparing of Duhsasana, and his advance toward Arjuna.
Dhritarashtra's questions, Sanjaya's account of the Pandava call to arms, Duryodhana's assault on the Pandava host, and Drona's rescue of Duryodhana.
Drona's duels with Vrihatkshatra, Dhrishtaketu and his son, Jarasandha's son, Kshatradharman and Chekitana, and Drupada's counterattack.
Yudhishthira's anxiety about Arjuna and Satyaki, and his decision to send Bhima after them.
Bhima's departure with Yudhishthira's blessing, his confrontation with Drona, and his killing of many of Dhritarashtra's sons.
Bhima's mace attack, his duel with Drona and his advance through the Bhojas and Kambojas, and Yudhishthira's relief and anxious reflections.
Dhritarashtra's fearful question about who could stand against Bhima, and Karna's duel with Bhima, which Bhima wins.
Duryodhana's appeal to Drona, Drona's plan to protect Jayadratha, and Duryodhana's fight with the two Panchala princes.
Sanjaya introduces Karna's attack on Bhima, Dhritarashtra's questions about their fight, and the duel that leaves Karna wounded and chariot-less.
Dhritarashtra's questions about Karna's retreat, and the renewed duel in which Bhima recalls the Kaurava wrongs and fights on until the field is strewn with dead.
Dhritarashtra's dismay at Karna's defeats, and Sanjaya's account of the duel in which Bhima kills Durjaya and surrounds Karna with arrows.
Karna's second chariot is wrecked, Durmukha is sent to his aid and killed by Bhima, and Karna retreats wounded while Bhima stays in the field.
Dhritarashtra laments Karna's defeat and blames fate; Sanjaya rebukes him and reports the deaths of five more sons at Bhima's hands.
The duel between Karna and Bhima continues: Bhima breaks Karna's bow and mace attack, kills six of Duryodhana's brothers, and the two heroes keep trading heavy wounds.
Karna's renewed charge, Bhima killing seven more brothers and roaring in triumph, Yudhishthira's advance on Drona, and Sanjaya's blame of Dhritarashtra.
Dhritarashtra asks how the battle is going, and Sanjaya describes the carnage caused by Karna and Bhima and the rout of the Kaurava troops.
The long duel between Karna and Bhima: both sides break bows and cars, Karna taunts the carless Bhima but spares him, and Arjuna arrives to drive Karna away and rout the Kauravas.
Dhritarashtra laments the setbacks and asks about Satyaki; Sanjaya reports Satyaki's fight with Alamvusha, the death of Alamvusha, and his attack on Duhsasana's steeds.
Satyaki cuts through the Trigarta, Surasena and Kalinga divisions to reach Arjuna, Krishna praises him, and Arjuna frets over Yudhishthira's safety and the danger to Satyaki from Bhurisravas.

Bhurisravas and Satyaki fight with arrows, swords and wrestling until Bhurisravas grabs Satyaki by the hair, and Krishna urges Arjuna to intervene, which Arjuna does with an arrow that cuts off Bhurisravas's arm.
Arjuna's arrow takes Bhurisravas's arm; Bhurisravas accuses Arjuna of foul play, Arjuna answers him, Bhurisravas fasts unto death, and Satyaki beheads him against the protests of others.
Satyaki defends the killing, citing the death of Abhimanyu, and the chapter closes with the silent respect shown to Bhurisravas.
Dhritarashtra asks why Satyaki was defeated, and Sanjaya gives the family history of Sini and Somadatta and the boon that explains the defeat.

After Bhurisravas's death, Arjuna pushes toward Jayadratha, Duryodhana and Karna try to block him, Arjuna overwhelms their divisions and disables Karna, and Ashwatthaman protects the Sindhu king as the sun sinks.
Arjuna's rampage through the Kaurava army, Krishna's illusion of sunset, Jayadratha's beheading and the curse-driven death of his father, and the night battle that follows.

Kripa and Ashwatthaman attack Arjuna, Arjuna grieves over his wounded teacher, and Krishna tells him Satyaki can handle Karna; Dhritarashtra asks how the Satyaki-Karna duel went, and Sanjaya explains Krishna's foresight and Satyaki's new chariot.
Sanjaya describes the new chariots brought to Satyaki and Karna and tallies the sons of Dhritarashtra lost so far.
Bhima asks Arjuna to keep their vow, Arjuna answers Karna and vows to kill Vrishasena, Krishna praises Arjuna and shows him the battlefield, and Krishna tells Yudhishthira that Jayadratha is dead.
Yudhishthira hears of Jayadratha's death and praises Krishna, Krishna and Arjuna predict the Kauravas' ruin, and Arjuna welcomes back the wounded Bhima and Satyaki.
Duryodhana grieves over Jayadratha's death and the slaughter of his army, goes to Drona, and vows to fight on to the end or die to join his fallen allies.
Dhritarashtra asks about Duryodhana's grief, and Sanjaya reports Drona's bitter reply, his refusal to lay down arms, and his instructions to Ashwatthaman before he goes into battle.
Duryodhana blames Drona and Karna's defence follows, then the Pandava divisions advance and the battle resumes, with Sanjaya blaming Dhritarashtra's policy.
Duryodhana breaks into the Pandava host, Yudhishthira wounds him, a rumor says the king is slain, and Drona comes to Duryodhana's rescue as the battle deepens.
Dhritarashtra asks about Drona's protectors, and Sanjaya describes the Pandava divisions converging on Drona in the night and the chaotic battle that follows.
Dhritarashtra asks about the night battle, and Sanjaya reports Drona's kills, Bhima's fist-fights with the Kalinga prince and others, and the flight of the Kaurava kings.

Somadatta and Satyaki duel, Drona drives into the Pandava host and is met by Arjuna and Bhima, and Ghatotkacha and Ashwatthaman clash, with Ashwatthaman killing Anjanaparvan and the two trading threats.
Duryodhana sends Sakuni against the Pandavas, Ashwatthaman destroys the Rakshasa army and kills several Pandava princes, and Ghatotkacha is struck down and carried off.

The night fight continues: Bhima kills Valhika and many Kaurava warriors, Yudhishthira routs Kaurava divisions, and Drona and Yudhishthira duel with celestial weapons before the Kaurava host is scattered by Arjuna and Bhima.
Duryodhana appeals to Karna, Karna boasts, Kripa mocks him and lists the Pandava allies, and Karna answers with fresh threats and insists that the outcome depends on Fate.
Ashwatthaman charges Karna over his insults to Kripa, and Duryodhana and Kripa restrain him, while Karna is forgiven.
Karna fights the Pandavas with great skill until Arjuna disables him, Duryodhana tries to rally his forces, and Ashwatthaman and Kripa move to stop Arjuna.
Duryodhana reproaches Ashwatthaman for holding back and urges him to slay the Panchalas and Somakas.
Ashwatthaman vows to fight recklessly for Duryodhana, Dhrishtadyumna duels with him, Ashwatthaman destroys his chariot and kills many Panchalas, and the Kauravas applaud his triumph.
Yudhishthira and Bhima surround Ashwatthaman, Duryodhana joins the fight with Drona, Arjuna and Bhima hit Drona from both flanks, and the Kaurava host breaks in the dark.
Satyaki duels Somadatta until he kills him, Yudhishthira is worn down by Drona, and Krishna urges Yudhishthira to turn to Bhima instead.
The night battle is confused and deadly, Dhritarashtra asks how the armies could see again, and Sanjaya describes the lamps lit by both sides and the renewed battle under the glow.
The lit battlefield sees fresh combat, Arjuna breaks into the Kaurava ranks, Dhritarashtra asks about Drona's guard, and Duryodhana orders his men to protect Drona.
Yudhishthira orders an attack on Drona, the Kaurava warriors pair off against the Pandava leaders, and Kritavarman defeats Yudhishthira, who withdraws from the field.
Satyaki kills Bhuri, Ashwatthaman and Ghatotkacha duel until Ghatotkacha is carried off, and Duryodhana fights Bhima until Bhima's mace forces him to flee, leading the Pandavas to believe he is dead.
Karna defeats Sahadeva, mocks him and spares his life for Kunti's sake, and Sahadeva withdraws from the fight.
Salya defeats Virata and Satanika, the Pandava troops flee, Alamvusha challenges Arjuna, and Arjuna overcomes him and drives on toward Drona.
Satanika strips Chitrasena of his armour and weapons, Vrishasena defeats Drupada and drives the Panchalas off, and Duhsasana fights Prativindhya until a general melee breaks out.
Nakula defeats Sakuni, Kripa drives back Sikhandin, and the night battle grows so confused that warriors slay their own kin.

Dhrishtadyumna charges Drona and fights Karna and the Kaurava champions, Satyaki duels Karna and Vrishasena, Karna hears Arjuna's bowstring and urges Duryodhana to target Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna, and Sakuni sets out against Arjuna.
Satyaki routs Duryodhana and his allies, Sakuni and Uluka attack Arjuna and are beaten back, and Dhrishtadyumna fights Drona, while the Pandavas celebrate.
Duryodhana shames Drona and Karna into renewed battle, Drona routs the Pandava host, Krishna and Arjuna and Bhima advance on Drona and Karna, and the night battle grows fierce in the dark.
Karna defeats Dhrishtadyumna and routs the Panchalas, Yudhishthira urges Arjuna to face Karna, Krishna sends Ghatotkacha to fight Karna, and Ghatotkacha rushes into battle against him.
Duryodhana sends Duhsasana to guard Karna, Alamvusha is sent against Ghatotkacha, Ghatotkacha kills him and throws his head before Duryodhana, and he then advances on Karna.

Dhritarashtra asks for a description of Ghatotkacha and his duel with Karna, and Sanjaya gives the portrait and recounts the long duel, in which Karna defeats the Rakshasa's illusions and weapons, and Ghatotkacha retreats with a threat.
Alayudha arrives to avenge his kin, asks Duryodhana for leave to fight Bhima, and sets out on a car like Ghatotkacha's to meet the Pandava kings.
The Kauravas welcome Alayudha, Duryodhana sends him against Ghatotkacha, Krishna directs the Pandava warriors to their tasks, and Bhima fights Alayudha with maces and then fists.
Krishna sends Ghatotkacha against Alayudha, the two Rakshasas duel with illusions and weapons, Ghatotkacha kills Alayudha and throws his head before Duryodhana, and Duryodhana is dismayed.

Ghatotkacha returns to fight Karna and kills his steeds and driver, the Kaurava army is routed by his illusions, Karna uses Indra's dart to kill Ghatotkacha, and Ghatotkacha's fall crushes many Kaurava troops.
The Pandavas mourn Ghatotkacha, Krishna rejoices and explains that Karna's dart and natural armour are gone, and he reminds Arjuna of the earlier enemies slain by means of stratagem.

Arjuna asks how the enemies were slain, and Krishna gives a long account of the deaths of Jarasandha, Ekalavya, the ruler of the Chedis and the Rakshasas, and says Karna's dart is now useless and Drona is pressing hard.
Dhritarashtra asks why Karna did not use his dart on Arjuna, Sanjaya explains the Kaurava debate about the dart and Krishna's power, and Satyaki asks Krishna about Karna's choice.
Krishna explains that the Kauravas always wanted the dart used on Arjuna and that he himself had distracted Karna, and Sanjaya notes Krishna's devotion to Arjuna.
Dhritarashtra questions Sanjaya about Karna's unused dart, Sanjaya explains the failure, and Vyasa halts Yudhishthira's rush toward Karna.
Yudhishthira orders a general attack on Drona, both armies tire and sleep, Arjuna calls a truce, and the battle restarts when the moon rises.
Duryodhana rebukes Drona for going easy on the Pandavas, Drona praises Arjuna and mocks Karna and the others, and the fighting resumes.
At dawn the armies reform and fight, Arjuna breaks into the Kaurava front, Drona kills several Pandava allies, and Dhrishtadyumna and Bhima take on Drona as the sun comes up.
After sunrise the battle grows into a vast slaughter under dust, and the main warriors pair off, with Duryodhana fighting Nakula.
Sahadeva beheads Duhsasana's driver, Karna wrecks Bhima's car after a mace duel, and Drona and Arjuna fight a long duel that ends in a general melee.
Duhsasana is pushed back by Dhrishtadyumna, Duryodhana and Satyaki duel while recalling their friendship, Karna and Bhima fight, and the Pandavas press on to break Drona's guard.
Drona kills huge numbers of Panchalas, the sages urge him to lay down arms, and he asks Yudhishthira whether his son is dead.
Dhrishtadyumna and Drona duel back and forth, Drona disarms and wounds him, Dhrishtadyumna keeps fighting with a sword, and Satyaki saves him from Drona's arrow.
Yudhishthira sends his men against Drona, Bhima rebukes Drona, Drona lays down his arms and dies in meditation, and the army breaks up after Dhrishtadyumna kills him.
The Kauravas flee in panic after Drona's death, Kripa explains how Drona was deceived and killed, and Aswatthama's anger flares.
Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya how Aswatthama responded to Drona's death, praising the young man's skill and calling him a second Drona.
Aswatthama vows vengeance on Dhrishtadyumna and the Pandavas, recounts how he inherited the Narayana weapon, and prepares to use it as the Kuru army rallies.
The Narayana weapon brings omens, Dhritarashtra asks about the Pandava plan, Yudhishthira questions Arjuna about the rally, and Arjuna names Aswatthama and expresses his remorse over Drona.
Bhima rebukes Arjuna for his remorse and vows to fight Aswatthama alone, Dhrishtadyumna defends his killing of Drona, and Arjuna is urged to fight.
Dhritarashtra asks how the Pandavas reacted, Satyaki and Dhrishtadyumna trade insults, Satyaki charges, and Bhima, Sahadeva and Krishna calm the quarrel.
Aswatthama unleashes the Narayana weapon, Yudhishthira despairs, Krishna orders the troops to disarm, and Bhima alone takes on the weapon and is overwhelmed.
Arjuna and Krishna calm the Narayana weapon by making Bhima lay down his arms, and Aswatthama, unable to use the weapon again, renews the fight and wounds several Pandava warriors.
Aswatthama unleashes the Agneya weapon, Arjuna counters with the Brahma weapon, and Aswatthama asks Vyasa why his weapon failed, which leads Vyasa to explain Narayana and Rudra.
Aswatthama bows to Vyasa and withdraws his army, and the chapter closes by recalling Drona's death after five days of battle.
Dhritarashtra asks what came next, Arjuna describes the radiant figure that fought before him, and Vyasa identifies it as Siva, praises him at length, and sends Arjuna back to battle.
The end of the Drona Parva, with Sanjaya's closing benediction and the start of the footnotes.
Footnotes 3 to 7 explain a fabulous animal, the sense of a verse on grief and duty, and several variant readings.
Footnotes 8 to 12 cover a warrior's knowledge of the body, a phrase about walking behind Drona, and some textual differences.
Footnotes 13 to 17 discuss a ready instrument, Arjuna as Drona's pupil, a grammatical construction, Ajatasatru, and Ghatotkacha.
Footnotes 18 to 22 explain Hayaraja and other names, a corrupted translation, Jarasandha, and the Parijata tree.
Footnotes 23 to 27 discuss why the gods do not destroy the host, several corrupt readings, and the wordiness of comparisons.
Footnotes 28 to 32 cover the word for heroic, blows, the nishka coin, a variant reading, and the soldiers sworn to conquer or die.
Footnotes 33 to 37 deal with variant readings, possibly missing verses, and the meaning of ekacharas.
Footnotes 38 to 42 explain the half-moon shape, a cruel attack on a Brahmana, weapons, and some misprints in the Bengal texts.
Footnotes 43 to 47 note corrupt verses, a repeated verse, the sense of not abandoning comrades, and the custom of naming oneself before a fight.
Footnotes 48 to 52 cover the spelling of Draupadeyas, several verse differences, and a note on Suparva and Bhagadatta.
Footnotes 53 to 57 discuss a corrupted word, free renderings, a Bengal reading of a line, and the meaning of the summer and rainy months.
Footnotes 58 to 62 weigh textual readings, the rivalry between Nila and Aswatthaman, and the meaning of dhumaketu.

Skanda kills Taraka and other Daitya chiefs and pierces Mount Krauncha to slay Vana and the Daityas who fled there.
Vaishampayana closes the account of Skanda's installation and tells how Balarama bathes at Taijasa, where Varuna was installed.
Janamejaya asks about Varuna's installation, Vaishampayana describes the gods' decision and Agni's hiding, and Balarama visits several holy places.
Sruvavati's penance, her test by Indra in disguise, Indra's boon and the sanctity of Vadarapachana, the story of Sruvavati's birth, and Balarama's move on to Sakta.
Balarama bathes at Indra's tirtha, Rama's tirtha, the Yamuna and the Aditya tirtha, giving gifts at each, and names the sages who dwell at the last.
Devala's householder life and his guest Jaigishavya, Devala's flight through the heavens, the Siddhas' report, Devala's choice to follow the path of liberation, and Balarama's departure.
Balarama visits Sarasvata's tirtha, and Vaishampayana tells how Dadhichi's seed, held by the river Sarasvati, became her son Sarasvata.
Indra needs Dadhichi's bones for a weapon, the sages are starving in the drought, and Sarasvata feeds and teaches them until they honour him as their teacher.
Janamejaya asks about the maiden, Vaishampayana describes her penance, Narada's words, and her offer of half her merit to a husband.
The marriage of one night, the maiden's departure to heaven, Sringavat's death, and Balarama's news of the war.
The sages tell Rama how Kuru ploughed the field and how Indra promised heaven to those who died there, and they describe its sanctity.
Balarama visits hermitages and tirthas, meets Narada, hears of the war and Duryodhana's challenge, and sets out for the field.
Dhritarashtra asks how the mace duel went, and Sanjaya describes Balarama's arrival, the honours shown to him, the preparations, and the two heroes facing each other while the crowd gathers to watch.
Dhritarashtra grieves over his son's humbling, Sanjaya describes the omens, and the two champions trade boasts and insults before they fight.
The mace duel between Duryodhana and Bhima rages, with each knocking the other down in turn, until Bhima gets up with his armour broken.
Arjuna asks Krishna to judge the two fighters, Krishna advises a trick, Arjuna gives Bhima the signal, and the duel ends with Duryodhana's thighs broken and portents filling the sky.
Bhima taunts the fallen Duryodhana and places his foot on his head, Yudhishthira rebukes him, and Yudhishthira grieves for Duryodhana and the Kurus.
Dhritarashtra asks about Balarama's reaction, Balarama's rage and departure, and Krishna and Yudhishthira's exchange over Bhima's conduct.
Bhima is praised by Krishna, claims the earth for Yudhishthira, and Yudhishthira declares the war is over.
Dhritarashtra asks how the Pandavas reacted, the victors rejoice, Krishna rebukes them, Duryodhana and Krishna trade accusations, and Duryodhana declares his fortune.
Flowers fall from heaven, and Krishna defends his deceptions as the only way to defeat warriors who could not be beaten fairly.
The Pandavas enter the emptied Kaurava camp, and Arjuna's chariot burns to ashes when Krishna gets down from it.
Krishna embraces Yudhishthira and praises the victory, and the Pandavas claim the Kaurava treasure.
The Pandavas camp by the Oghavati, and Krishna sets out to comfort Gandhari in Hastinapura.
Janamejaya asks about Krishna's mission, and Vaishampayana describes Yudhishthira's fear, Krishna's visit to Dhritarashtra and Gandhari, and his hurried departure to warn the Pandavas.
Dhritarashtra asks about Duryodhana's last words, and Sanjaya reports Duryodhana's speech of pride, grief and farewell, including his message to the warriors.
Ashvatthama, Kripa and Kritavarma reach the dying Duryodhana, Ashvatthama vows vengeance, Duryodhana makes him commander, and the Shalya Parva ends.
The three survivors flee to a forest at dusk, and Dhritarashtra laments his sons' defeat and asks what the three did next.
Ashvatthama cannot sleep, watches an owl kill the sleeping crows in the banyan, and resolves to attack the sleeping enemy by stealth.
Ashvatthama tells his companions that Duryodhana is dead and that the Panchalas are celebrating, and asks them for counsel.
Kripa argues that success needs both destiny and effort, that action is never wasted, and that Duryodhana brought disaster on himself by ignoring good advice.
Kripa proposes that the three go and ask the elders what to do, since advice from wise friends is the sound course.
Ashvatthama says each man trusts his own judgment, explains the division of duties among the castes, and declares he will act as a warrior to avenge his father.
Ashvatthama describes how he will attack the Panchalas while they sleep in their camp, after their victory celebration.
Kripa and Kritavarma urge rest and promise support in the morning; Ashvatthama refuses, citing his grief and rage, and vows to strike while the enemy sleeps.
Kripa warns against attacking sleeping and unarmed men, and Ashvatthama answers by citing past unfair killings and vows to strike the Panchalas in their sleep.
Ashvatthama drives toward the Panchala camp with Kripa and Kritavarma, and they stop at the gate.
Dhritarashtra asks what happened at the gate, and Sanjaya describes the guardian, Ashvatthama's failed attack, and his decision to seek Shiva's protection.
Ashvatthama gets down from his chariot and hymns Shiva under many names, then the sacred fire and a host of strange beings appear.
Ashvatthama offers himself as a sacrifice, Shiva appears and enters his body, and he sets out for the Panchala camp with the god's followers.
Ashvatthama enters the camp, kills Dhrishtadyumna in his bed, then kills Uttamauja and Yudhamanyu and the guards who come against him.
Ashvatthama moves through the camp with his sword, killing sleeping and unarmed warriors, Draupadi's sons, Shikhandi and many others, while the terrified men fall into confusion.
In the chaos, animals break loose, men kill their own comrades, and Kripa and Kritavarma slay the fugitives and set fire to the camp, and Ashvatthama finishes the slaughter.
Rakshasas and flesh-eating beings feast on the dead, and at dawn Ashvatthama leaves the camp, meets his companions, and Dhritarashtra asks why he did not act earlier.
Sanjaya explains that Ashvatthama had acted only because the Pandava protectors were absent and the men were asleep, and the three rejoice and head to report to the king.
The three find Duryodhana dying on the field, surrounded by beasts of prey, and they lament his fall and blame Bhima and the Pandavas for the unfair blow.
Ashvatthama tells the dying king of the night's killings, Duryodhana dies pleased, and Sanjaya reports the news to Dhritarashtra.
The charioteer of Dhrishtadyumna reports the night massacre, and Yudhishthira collapses and laments that the victory has turned to defeat through heedlessness.
Yudhishthira grieves for Draupadi, sends Nakula to fetch her, and goes to the battlefield, where he sees his slain sons and friends and falls senseless.
Yudhishthira is overwhelmed by grief, Nakula brings Draupadi, who collapses, and she vows to fast to death unless Ashvatthama is punished and his jewel is brought to her.
Draupadi asks Bhima to avenge her by slaying Ashvatthama, and Bhima sets out from the camp in pursuit of Ashvatthama's chariot.
Krishna warns Yudhishthira that Bhima is in danger, explains that Drona taught Ashvatthama the brahmashira reluctantly, and recalls Ashvatthama's first request for the discus at Dvaraka.

Krishna reports the rest of the meeting: relatives never asked such a thing, Ashvatthama admits he meant to fight Krishna with the discus, and he then leaves Dvaraka, and Bhima must be protected from him.
Krishna's chariot is described, and Krishna drives Arjuna and Yudhishthira after Bhima, and Ashvatthama prepares the brahmashira against the Pandavas.
Krishna urges Arjuna to counter the weapon, Arjuna releases his own brahmashira, and the sages Narada and Vyasa step between the two blazing weapons.
Arjuna asks the sages for help and withdraws his weapon, Vyasa explains why it matters, and Ashvatthama admits he cannot recall his own weapon and offers his gem.
Vyasa tells Ashvatthama to turn the weapon away from the Pandavas, and he directs it at the wombs of the Pandava women.
Krishna foretells that Parikshit will be born and survive, Ashvatthama defies him, Krishna curses him to wander, and Vyasa and Ashvatthama accept the sentence.
Ashvatthama hands over his gem and goes into the forest, and the Pandavas take the gem back to Draupadi, where Bhima recalls her bitter words to Krishna.
Draupadi returns the gem to Yudhishthira, who places it on his head, and she gives up her vow.
Yudhishthira asks how Ashvatthama could do such damage, and the answer tells how Brahma made beings and how Rudra withdrew to the water and then to the mountains in anger.

The gods leave Rudra out of their sacrifice, Rudra attacks it, and after they beg for mercy he restores them, and the answer ends by telling Yudhishthira that Ashvatthama's deeds came from Shiva's grace.
The closing colophon marks the end of the Sauptika Parva and credits the Mahabharata to Vyasa.
Janamejaya asks what Dhritarashtra and the survivors did after the war, and Vaishampayana describes the king collapsing in grief while Sanjaya urges him to stop mourning.
Dhritarashtra laments his losses and blames his own past faults, then Sanjaya scolds him for indulging his son and urges him to bear his grief, and Vidura speaks again.
Vidura speaks to Dhritarashtra at length, urging him to rise, accept death as the common end of all beings, and stop indulging in sorrow over the warriors slain in battle.
Dhritarashtra thanks Vidura and asks how the wise escape sorrow, and Vidura replies with a long account of impermanence, the body as a temporary dwelling, and the role of past deeds.

Dhritarashtra asks for an explanation of the world's wilderness, and Vidura traces the stages of life from the womb through the sufferings and delusions of the living to the final death, urging virtue as the way out.

Dhritarashtra asks for a detailed teaching, and Vidura begins a parable about a Brahmana lost in a terrifying forest, caught in a pit, dangling from creepers, and surrounded by dangers, yet still hoping to live.

Dhritarashtra asks how the man in the parable might be rescued, and Vidura reveals that each element of the story stands for an aspect of human life, from the body and time to desire and the passing seasons.

Dhritarashtra praises the parable and asks for more, and Vidura gives a long discourse on life as a journey, the body as a chariot, the senses as horses, and self-restraint and compassion as the way to freedom.

Dhritarashtra faints, is revived, and wishes to die, then Vyasa explains that the war was destiny, recounts the divine origin of Duryodhana, and urges the king to live, after which Dhritarashtra accepts this and Vyasa departs.
Janamejaya asks what happened after Vyasa left, and Sanjaya returns and reports the deaths, prompting Dhritarashtra to collapse and Vidura to offer comfort once more.
Dhritarashtra orders the royal women to be brought out, and they come together in wailing, then Vidura escorts them from the city while the whole population of Hastinapura joins in mourning.
Kripa, Ashvatthama and Kritavarma report Duryodhana's death and their night massacre of the Pandava camp, then Kripa consoles Gandhari and the king, after which the three warriors part ways.

Yudhishthira meets the lamenting women and then his uncle, who embraces him reluctantly, then seeks to crush Bhima, but Krishna has put an iron image in Bhima's place and the king breaks it, falls, and is soothed and rebuked by Krishna.
Krishna reproaches Dhritarashtra for following Duryodhana and ignoring advice, then the king admits his wrong, sets aside his anger, and embraces the Pandava brothers.

The Pandavas go to see Gandhari, Vyasa arrives to head off her curse, and he reminds her of her own words of righteousness, and Gandhari responds that her grief is real but she is angered by Bhima's foul blow to Duryodhana.

Bhima defends his deeds to Gandhari, who rebukes him and then grieves, while Yudhishthira offers himself to her curse, she comforts the Pandavas, and the women lament together before the closing line of the section.

The lamentation of the women begins with Gandhari's spiritual vision of the battlefield, the royal party's journey to Kurukshetra, the women's horror at the corpses, and Gandhari's speech to Krishna, which ends as she sees Duryodhana.
Gandhari collapses over her son's body, recalls their last exchange before the battle, mourns the fall of a once-powerful king and his grieving wife, and declares that her son has won heroes' heaven.
Gandhari recounts the deaths of her sons, the suffering of the daughters-in-law, and the fall of Duhshasana, reminding Krishna of the insult to Draupadi and of her own failed warnings to Duryodhana.
Gandhari mourns her sons Vikarna, Durmukha, Citrasena, Vivingsati and Duhsaha in turn, describing each body and the grief of the women who remain with them.

Gandhari mourns Abhimanyu and describes his widow Uttara weeping over him and addressing him, then the Matsya women drag Uttara from the body of her father Virata, and Gandhari names other young men slain in the battle.
Gandhari mourns Karna's death at Arjuna's hands, describes his wives lamenting and his mother-in-law faint at the sight, and notes the animals that have already started feeding on his corpse.
Gandhari points out the bodies of the lord of Avanti, Bahlika and Jayadratha, speaks of Jayadratha's widows and her daughter Duhshala, and remembers how Jayadratha once tried to dishonour Draupadi.
Gandhari mourns in turn Shalya, Bhagadatta, Bhishma on his bed of arrows, and Drona, whose funeral pyre is lit and attended by his wife Kripi and disciples as they head for the Ganga.

Gandhari describes Somadatta mourning his son Bhurishrava, whose widows hold his severed arm and rebuke Arjuna and Satyaki, and then she turns to the death of Shakuni at Sahadeva's hand and her fear that he will stir up trouble in the next world.

Gandhari mourns a long list of fallen kings and their women, then faints, blames Krishna for not preventing the war, and curses him; Krishna replies that the Yadavas will perish by their own hands, and the Pandavas despair.
The holy one rebukes Gandhari, Dhritarashtra asks Yudhishthira for the tally of the fallen and their fates, and Yudhishthira describes the regions where the warriors went according to how they died.

Dhritarashtra asks how Yudhishthira has such knowledge, and Yudhishthira explains that he got spiritual sight from Lomasa, then Dhritarashtra asks about the rites, and Yudhishthira has the dead of both sides cremated before going to the Ganga.

At the Ganga the women make water offerings, Kunti tells her sons that Karna was their brother, Yudhishthira laments and makes the offering for Karna, and then the Stri Parva closes with its colophon.
The Pandavas mourn after the war, sages console Yudhishthira, and he confesses that Karna, killed by Arjuna, was his secret elder brother.
Narada explains how Karna trained under Drona and Rama, and how he came to be cursed for killing a sacred cow.
Rama teaches Karna the Brahma weapon, a worm attacks Karna, and Rama curses him for deceiving him about his birth.
Duryodhana carries off a princess at a bride-choosing in Rajapura, and Karna defeats the kings who pursue them.
Karna defeats Jarasandha and is given Malini, and Narada lists the causes of Karna's death and urges Yudhishthira not to grieve.
Narada falls silent, Kunti explains her failed attempts to reconcile Karna, and Yudhishthira blames her and despairs.
Yudhishthira mourns the dead, blames Duryodhana and Dhritarashtra, and resolves to give up the kingdom for the forest.
Arjuna argues that wealth and kingly duty require Yudhishthira to rule and perform sacrifices rather than renounce.
Yudhishthira rejects Arjuna's advice and describes at length the forest renunciation he intends to undertake.
Bhimasena rebukes Yudhishthira's plan to renounce, arguing that Kshatriyas must act and cannot earn heaven through forest life alone.
Indra as a golden bird rebukes young ascetics who abandoned home, and teaches the value of sacrifice and the householder's duties.
The ascetics give up renunciation for household life, and Arjuna urges Yudhishthira to rule.
Nakula argues that householder life, sacrifice and duty are superior to renunciation, and urges Yudhishthira to govern and give gifts.
Sahadeva argues that inner detachment matters more than outward renunciation, that the soul is eternal, and that a king should enjoy the earth he holds.
Draupadi rebukes Yudhishthira, reminds him of his vow to fight Duryodhana, lists his conquests, and urges him to rule and sacrifice.
Arjuna argues that punishment and force sustain dharma and order, that killing is part of life, and that Yudhishthira must rule.
Bhima accuses Yudhishthira of being clouded by grief, recalls the family's past humiliations, and urges him to rule and hold the horse-sacrifice.
Yudhishthira replies to Bhima that desire is endless, praises renunciation and detachment, and says understanding is what matters most.
Arjuna tells the story of Janaka and his queen, whose rebuke favours householders over empty renunciation, and then concludes that householders can reach bliss.
Yudhishthira rebukes Arjuna's view of wealth and argues that renunciation and knowledge of Brahma lead to the highest good.
Devasthana argues that wealth belongs to sacrifice and that a king who has won the earth should not abandon it.
Devasthana quotes Vrihaspati's teaching that contentment and non-injury are the highest religion, and that a righteous king who retires to the forest is rewarded.
Arjuna urges Yudhishthira to act as a Kshatriya, perform sacrifices, and accept that the dead have gained the highest end.
Vyasa backs Arjuna, praises householder life and the rod of punishment, and tells the tale of Likhita and Sankha.
Vyasa concludes that ruling and punishing are a king's duty, and that shaving the head is not.
Vyasa urges Yudhishthira to rule, sacrifice and protect his subjects, and tells the story of King Hayagriva.
Yudhishthira laments his grief, and Vyasa answers that Time governs all, grief should be borne calmly, and a king's sacrifice is battle and governance.
Yudhishthira argues that sages gain heaven without wealth, that wealth brings sin, and that it should be spent on sacrifice and worthy gifts.
Yudhishthira laments the deaths of his kin and teachers and resolves to fast to death; Vyasa counsels that all is destiny and that one must act.
Vyasa tells the tale of Asma's answer to Janaka on grief and impermanence, and urges Yudhishthira to cast off his grief and rule.
Krishna tells Yudhishthira not to grieve for the heroes who died in battle, and Narada tells Srinjaya that great kings died too, so he should not grieve for his son.
Srinjaya is freed from grief, and Narada promises to return his dead son, Suvarnashthivin, to life.
Krishna recounts how Narada and Parvata quarrelled over Narada's love for Sukumari, cursed each other, and later lifted the curses.
Narada explains that the boy was killed by a tiger sent by Indra, that he restored him to life, and that the prince later ruled a long reign.
Vyasa tells Yudhishthira that kings must punish wrongdoers and that action brings its fruits, and urges him not to give up his life.
Yudhishthira laments his role in the slaughter, and Vyasa answers that Time caused the deaths and urges the Horse-sacrifice and good rule.
Vyasa lists the lapses that require expiation and the acts that carry no sin, answering Yudhishthira's question.
Vyasa describes the expiations for killing a Brahmin and other sins, and urges Yudhishthira to atone and not give up his life.
Vyasa passes on Manu's teaching on clean and forbidden food and on whom it is proper to give to.
Vyasa directs Yudhishthira to Bhishma for counsel; Yudhishthira objects, and Krishna urges him to accept his duty.
Yudhishthira is persuaded and enters the city in a grand procession, welcomed by the citizens.
Yudhishthira is welcomed into the city, but the disguised Rakshasa Charvaka accuses him and is slain by the Brahmins' power.
Krishna explains that Charvaka was doomed by his own boon and urges Yudhishthira to rule well and honour Brahmins.
Yudhishthira is anointed as king with sacred water, receives blessings and gifts from people and Brahmins, and is installed on the throne.
Yudhishthira tells his people to honour Dhritarashtra, and appoints his brothers and ministers to government posts.
Yudhishthira performs funeral rites and gifts for the fallen, cares for their families, and honours the elders.
Yudhishthira praises Krishna with a long hymn of thanks, and Krishna is pleased.
Yudhishthira rests his brothers and assigns them the palaces of the Kaurava princes.
Janamejaya asks what happened next, and Vaisampayana describes Yudhishthira's generosity and his visit to Krishna, who sits in meditation.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna about his stillness, and Krishna explains that Bhishma's wisdom must be learned before he dies; the chariot is then readied.
Bhishma prepares to die at the northern turn of the sun, hymns Krishna at length, and receives heavenly knowledge; Krishna and the others then depart.
The party crosses the battlefield of Kurukshetra, Krishna recalls Rama's destruction of the Kshatriyas, and Yudhishthira asks how the order was revived.
Krishna begins Rama's story with the lineage of Kusika and Gadhi and the swap of sacred food that gave Satyavati a fierce son, and her argument with her husband Richika.
Krishna tells how Rama destroyed the Kshatriyas, how Kasyapa took the earth, and how the hidden Kshatriya survivors were installed as kings.
Krishna and Yudhishthira visit Bhishma, Krishna praises him and asks him to comfort Yudhishthira, Bhishma hymns Krishna, and Krishna reveals his form and sets the time of Bhishma's death.
Bhishma asks Krishna to speak for him, Krishna grants him a boon of clear mind and freedom from pain, and the company leaves at sunset.
Krishna prepares for the visit, sends Satyaki to Yudhishthira, and they drive out without an army to see Bhishma.
Narada urges the Pandavas to question Bhishma, Krishna asks about his health, and Krishna urges Bhishma to teach Yudhishthira.
Bhishma agrees to speak, defends the Kshatriya duty to fight, even against kin in unjust battle, and invites Yudhishthira to ask.
Yudhishthira asks Bhishma about kingly duties, and Bhishma teaches exertion, truth, moderation and care of subjects, with warnings about over-familiarity.
Bhishma urges a king to act with vigour and justice, gives examples of severe discipline, and describes the qualities of a good king.
Bhishma stresses protecting subjects and exertion, lists the methods of protection, and says he has taught only part of kingly duty.
Bhishma recounts the origin of kingship: a decline into disorder, Brahma's treatise on punishment, the tyrant Vena, and the first true king Prithu.
Bhishma gives the general and specific duties of the four orders, ending with the claim that sacrifice belongs to all.
Bhishma names the four stages of life and outlines the duties of each, from student to forest hermit and mendicant.
Bhishma says the four modes of life belong to Brahmins, that a Brahmin straying into other callings is disgraced, and that all acts are shaped by Time.
Bhishma says what is improper for a Brahmin, and that the Kshatriya's duties underlie all the other duties.
Bhishma tells how Mandhatri met Narayana in the form of Indra, who explained that kingly duties are the foremost of all duties.
Indra explains that kings must uphold their duties, sets out duties for robber tribes, and warns of decline when kingly rule fails.
Bhishma closes by telling Yudhishthira to follow the path set by the ancients.
Yudhishthira asks about the four modes of life, and Bhishma explains that a king who practises the duties of each mode gains its merit, while protecting subjects is the king's chief task.

Bhishma explains why a king must be crowned, then tells the story of Manu, who was reluctant until the people offered him a share of their produce and merit, and gives advice on how a king should conduct himself.
A heading marks the start of the next section, LXVIII.

Yudhishthira asks about the king's divine status, and Bhishma tells the story of Vrihaspati instructing King Vasumanas on the king's role, the disorder that follows without him, the forms he takes, and the loyalty owed to him.
Bhishma gives detailed advice on self-control, spies, war and peace, justice and defence, and then argues that the king's rule decides which age of the world comes.
Bhishma lists the virtues a good king should practise, and Yudhishthira, taking the teaching to heart, begins to rule by it.
Bhishma briefly sums up the king's eternal duties, including respect for Brahmanas, fair taxation, self-control, and protecting subjects as the highest duty.

Bhishma recommends appointing a priest, then recounts how Pururavas asks the wind god about the origin of the four orders, the Brahmana's precedence and the claim to the earth, and the wind god answers at length.
Bhishma urges a king to appoint a learned priest, and Aila and Kasyapa discuss how quarrels between Brahmanas and Kshatriyas bring ruin and how Rudra is tied to the sins of men.
Aila asks why destruction falls on the innocent as well as the guilty, and Kasyapa answers that the sinless should avoid mixing with the sinful.
Kasyapa says the next world differs sharply for the righteous and the sinful, and concludes that a king should install a priest and honour Brahmanas.
Bhishma recounts how King Muchukunda and Vaisravana clash over sovereignty, with the Rakshasa army and the priest Vasishtha in the middle, and Muchukunda's firm answer to the Lord of Alaka.

Bhishma describes the king's conduct, including protection, generosity and sharing in his subjects' merit and sin, and then Yudhishthira wishes to retire to the forest, which Bhishma rejects in favour of duty.
Bhishma says the one who relieves fear is most worthy of heaven and urges Yudhishthira to rule cheerfully, protect the good and punish the wicked.
Bhishma sorts Brahmanas by conduct and tells the king how to treat each group, including the unworthy and the thief.
Bhishma explains the king's duty to support Brahmanas, then tells how the Kaikeya king escapes a Rakshasa by reciting his righteous rule, and closes with advice to protect Brahmanas.
Bhishma permits a distressed Brahmana to farm or keep cattle, lists the goods he must not sell, explains lawful exchange, and Yudhishthira asks how a king can stay protector if the orders revolt.

Bhishma says the orders should strengthen a weakened king, that fighting for Brahmanas brings heaven, that others may take up arms when Kshatriyas fail, and that whoever protects the helpless deserves to rule.
Bhishma describes the qualities of a good sacrificial priest, and then answers Yudhishthira's questions about dakshina, sacrificial character and penance.
Bhishma explains how to classify friends, when to trust or mistrust them, how to choose ministers, and how a king should deal with his kinsmen.
Vasudeva describes his troubles with his kinsmen to Narada, who answers that the trouble is of his own making and that gentle speech and generosity are the right remedy.
Bhishma tells how the sage Kalakavrikshiya exposes the king's corrupt officers, how the king is warned about his servants, and how the king takes the sage as his priest and rules successfully.
Bhishma explains how a king should choose and test his legislators, war ministers, courtiers, counsellors and generals, and how he should consult with them in secret.
Bhishma recounts Vrihaspati's teaching to Sakra on the value of agreeable speech, and urges Yudhishthira to practise it.
Bhishma explains the composition of the king's council, the rules of justice and punishment, and the duties of envoys, aid-de-camps, ministers and commanders, closing with advice on trust.
Bhishma describes the six kinds of citadel, the features of a good capital, the stores and people a king should keep, and his duties toward ascetics and friends.
Bhishma describes the tiered village administration, the principles of fair taxation, and the care the king should show toward the Vaisya traders and farmers.
Bhishma advises gradual, mild taxation, checking vice and idleness, honouring the wealthy, and ruling with truth and restraint.

Bhishma gives advice on protecting trees, Brahmanas, spies and the king's own reputation, and then, answering Yudhishthira, explains how the strong rule the weak and why traders and farmers must be spared.
Bhishma introduces Utathya's teaching to Mandhatri, which sets out the king's duty to uphold righteousness, the dangers of pride, and the disasters that follow neglect.
Utathya's long teaching sets out how the king shapes the age, the duties of kingship, and the dangers of weakness and pride, and Bhishma says Mandhatri followed it.
Vamadeva advises King Vasumanas to rule by righteousness, to avoid force, wicked ministers and caprice, and to be generous, honest and willing to take counsel.
Vamadeva gives a long list of advice on personal conduct, choosing officers, dealing with neighbours and rivals, and guarding against false friends.
Vamadeva explains how a king's power is confirmed and why he should win by wisdom rather than battle, and Bhishma closes by applying the teaching to Yudhishthira.
Bhishma explains how a king should approach a conquest, and then gives the rules of fair combat between Kshatriyas and why righteous victory matters.
Bhishma lays down the rules a victorious king should follow with the defeated, the captured and the conquered people, and gives examples of righteous kings.
Bhishma explains how a king is purified by righteous conduct, and describes the merit of bravery in battle and the shame of cowardice and an ignoble death.
Bhishma recounts how Amvarisha, in heaven, sees his former general Sudeva raised above him, and how he questions Indra about it.
Indra describes the battle-sacrifice in full detail, with its priests, offerings and fees, and says heroes who die bravely win the highest regions while cowards sink to hell.
Janaka rallies his troops with pictures of heaven and hell, sets their battle order, and warns against pursuing a routed enemy too far.
Bhishma sets out the king's military preparations, the rules for who may not be attacked, the rewards for courage, and the battle formations and deceptions used to win.
Bhishma describes the fighting styles of different peoples and the physical and temperamental signs of courageous soldiers.
Bhishma lists the omens of an army's success, explains why battle should be avoided where possible, and advises a mixture of forgiveness and severity toward the enemy.
Vrihaspati advises Indra on dealing with foes: concealment, patience, sweet words while planning, timed strikes, and dividing and corrupting the enemy's forces.
Vrihaspati lists the signs of a wicked person, and Indra acts on the teaching to subdue his enemies.
Kshemadarsin, ruined and distressed, asks the sage what to do, and the sage teaches detachment from wealth, the impermanence of things, and the advantage of a simple life.
The sage offers a plan for recovering the kingdom by serving Janaka and then weakening enemies through division, luxury, depleted treasuries and deceit.
Kshemadarsin rejects deceit, the sage introduces him to Janaka, and the two kings make peace and exchange honours.
Bhishma explains how enmity grows between the king and the nobility, and how the king should consult their leaders and keep the nobles united.
Bhishma names the honour owed to parents and teachers as the highest duty, ranks the teacher above the parents, and describes the sins of neglecting them.
Bhishma explains when truth and falsehood are proper, what righteousness is, and how to deal with the honest and the deceitful.
Bhishma lists the kinds of people who overcome difficulties and identifies Krishna with Narayana, whose refuge protects those who seek it.
Bhishma tells how the reborn jackal becomes the tiger's minister, is framed by envious courtiers, and leaves the court after being cleared and insulted.
The jackal retires to the forest and ends his life by fasting, rejecting the tiger's pleas, and goes to heaven.
Bhishma tells of the idle camel that was killed after gaining a long neck by boon, and draws the lesson that a king should act with intelligence, avoid idleness and seek wise counsel.
The Ocean and the rivers discuss why canes survive floods, and Bhishma draws the lesson that a wise man should yield to a stronger foe.
Bhishma explains why patience under abuse is wise, how the abuser's merit and sins pass between them, and why slanderers should be avoided.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should gratify his people and choose his servants, and Bhishma explains the qualities of the servants, ministers and officials a king needs.
A forest sage, served by its animals, protects a devoted dog from a threatening leopard by transforming it, and then protects it again from a tiger.

The sage keeps transforming the dog into a larger beast whenever a stronger creature threatens it, until the animal turns ungrateful and plans to kill him, and the sage then recounts the transformations and returns it to dog form.
Bhishma draws the lesson of the dog story for kings, describing how to choose ministers and servants, the virtues of a good king, and the value of a loyal army.
Bhishma applies the dog story to the appointment of servants, counsels the king on ministers, treasury and kinsmen, and asks what more Yudhishthira wants to hear.
Bhishma gives a long, detailed summary of the king's duties, comparing the wise king to a peacock and setting out how to govern, tax, watch enemies and choose officers.
Yudhishthira asks what Chastisement is, and Bhishma explains its nature, names and forms, its roots in the Vedas and royal authority, and the king's duty to apply it to all alike.

Mandhatri asks Vasuhoma about the origin of Chastisement, Vasuhoma recounts how it arose and passed through the gods and sages to Manu, and Bhishma says the teaching brings its reward to those who follow it.
Bhishma explains how the three aims relate and how their flaws are purged, and then recounts Kamandaka's advice to King Angaristha on undoing sin.
Bhishma introduces the exchange between Duryodhana and Dhritarashtra, in which Duryodhana laments Yudhishthira's wealth and his father urges him toward good conduct.
Duryodhana asks how such conduct is acquired, and Dhritarashtra tells the tale of Prahlada, who lost his sovereignty to Indra when his conduct and other virtues departed from him.
The goddess Prosperity explains that Indra took Prahlada's sovereignty by taking his conduct, and Dhritarashtra then explains how conduct is built and urges Duryodhana to follow it.
Yudhishthira asks about the nature of Hope, and Bhishma introduces the tale of King Sumitra, who chases a wounded deer deep into the forest.
Sumitra introduces himself to the ascetics at the hermitage, explains his loss and his disappointed hope, and asks which is vaster, hope or the sky.

Rishabha recounts his meeting with Tanu, who was approached by King Viradyumna searching for his lost son, and Tanu's first answer about a sage's disappointment, after which the sages question the king.
Viradyumna explains his search for his lost son, and Tanu, long slighted by the king, answers that hope is the most slender thing.
Tanu lists the hopes that are slenderer than his own body, the king accepts his teaching, Tanu restores the prince and reveals himself, and Bhishma applies the lesson to Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira asks for more, and Bhishma tells of Gotama's meeting with Yama, in which Yama explains how to honour one's parents and win heaven.

Yudhishthira poses a dilemma about a besieged, weak king, and Bhishma answers that in great distress a king may gather wealth from others, but that righteous means are better and that the treasury, army and people sustain one another.
Yudhishthira asks about a king in ruin, and Bhishma answers with advice on peace, retreat and courageous fighting.
Yudhishthira's question about a Brahmana's livelihood in a time of disorder, and Bhishma's long answer on conduct in distress.
Bhishma's advice on filling the treasury, keeping a firm hand on the kingdom, and handling robbers.
Bhishma on a Kshatriya's duties, the primacy of power over abstract righteousness, and the penance for one who has sinned.
The story of the robber Kayavya, his election as leader, the rules he sets, and the lesson Bhishma draws from it.
Bhishma quotes Brahman's verses on which wealth a king may take, and closes with a comparison about moral questions.
Bhishma's fable of the three fish and the lesson on acting in time.
Yudhishthira's question about a besieged king, and the fable of the mouse Palita and the cat Lomasa, which ends with the mouse rejecting the cat's offer of friendship.
The cat, shamed, pleads for renewed friendship, and the mouse answers with advice to keep a steady distrust of everyone.
Yudhishthira's doubt about mistrust, and the story of the prince who kills Pujani's chick and her revenge on him, which ends with an argument over whether the score is settled.
The two argue over whether a wronged party can ever trust the one who wronged them, and whether living together softens hostility.
Brahmadatta blames Time for all acts, Pujani answers with a long case for exertion and good rule, and she takes her leave.
Yudhishthira asks about kingship in an age of decline, and Bhishma gives Bharadwaja's advice to King Satrunjaya on statecraft in hard times.
Yudhishthira's question, the account of the famine that drives Viswamitra to the Chandala's hut, and the sage's first theft attempt and plea.
The Chandala says only certain animals are clean food, and Viswamitra cites Agastya's precedent to justify eating the dog's meat.
Viswamitra argues that a sage cannot sin and that his body must be kept alive, and the Chandala answers that hunger must be conquered.
The Chandala tries to restrain the sage as a friend, and Viswamitra asks to be saved by giving up the meat, which the Chandala refuses.
Viswamitra argues that saving life outweighs the sin of unclean food, and the Chandala says he is ignoring the Veda and the code of the Aryas.
The Chandala gives a final warning, and Viswamitra takes the meat, offers it to the gods and ancestors, and eats it.
Yudhishthira's dismay at Bhishma's teaching on severity, Bhishma's answer on how duty is found, and his final advice to honour Brahmanas.
The question about protecting suppliants, and the story of the cruel fowler, caught in a storm, who comes to the tree at night.
The pigeon's lament for his missing wife and his praise of a wife's value.
The captured she-pigeon hears her husband's words and advises him to show hospitality to the fowler.
The pigeon's hospitality, his sacrifice of himself in the fire, and the fowler's grief.
The fowler's remorse, his vow to live by righteousness, and his release of the she-pigeon.
The she-pigeon's lament, her death in the fire, and the reunion of the pigeon couple in heaven.
The fowler's resolve to imitate the pigeon, his death in a forest fire, his ascent to heaven, and Bhishma's closing praise of protecting suppliants.
Yudhishthira's question about cleansing ignorant sin, and the story of Janamejaya's wanderings and the rebuke from Indrota.
Janamejaya's plea and repentance, and Saunaka's demand that the king honour Brahmanas, ending with the king's oath.
Saunaka's long teaching on penance, sacred places and graded purification, with the gods' question to Vrihaspati and his answer, and the king's final purification.
A dead child is taken to the cremation ground, where a vulture tells the kin to leave and a jackal persuades them to turn back and reconsider.
The kin return to the child, the vulture rejects any hope of revival and warns of night dangers, and the jackal keeps urging them to wait.
The jackal insists the kin wait while the sun shines, and Sankara comes in answer to their prayer and restores the child.
Yudhishthira's question about a weak man who has provoked a powerful foe, and the opening of the tale of the Salmali tree and the wind god.
Narada's remark to the Salmali tree about the wind's protection, the tree's boast of strength, and Narada's rebuke.
Narada reports the tree to the wind-god, the wind's threat, and the tree's private reckoning that leads it to protect itself.
The Salmali strips itself, the wind's mocking verdict, the tree's shame, and Bhishma's moral on provoking the powerful.
Yudhishthira's question about the source of sin, Bhishma's account of covetousness as its root, and his portrait of good people who are free of it.
Yudhishthira asks about ignorance, Bhishma defines it and links it to covetousness, and he urges the king to avoid greed.
Yudhishthira asks about the highest merit, Bhishma's praise of self-restraint and the path of the ascetic, and the king's renewed delight.
Bhishma's teaching that penance is the root of all success and that abstaining from food is its highest form.
Yudhishthira's question about truth, and Bhishma's account of its thirteen forms and its supreme worth.
Yudhishthira's question about the vices, and Bhishma's account of their sources and the means of overcoming them.
Yudhishthira's question about malevolent people, and Bhishma's portrait of them set against the generous man.
Bhishma's long code on gifts, sacrifices and the king's duties to Brahmanas, with the penances for many kinds of wrongdoing.
Nakula's question about weapons, and Bhishma's long account of the creation of the sword and its passage down the royal line.
Yudhishthira's question about the three aims of life, and the views of Vidura and Arjuna.
The views of Nakula, Sahadeva and Bhima, Yudhishthira's own conclusion on liberation, and the praise that follows.
Yudhishthira's question about friendship, Bhishma's lists of those to avoid and those to befriend, and the opening of the tale of Gautama.
Gautama's journey after the elephant attack, his rest beneath the banyan, and his meeting with the crane who welcomes him.
Rajadharman's hospitality, his promise to help the poor Brahmana, and his message sending Gautama to the Rakshasa king.
Virupaksha's questions and Gautama's answers, the king's feast and gifts of gold, and Gautama's ungrateful plot against the crane.
Gautama's murder of the crane, the king's search and his order to kill the traitor, and the refusal of the Rakshasas and robbers to eat him.
The crane's revival, Indra's explanation, Gautama's restoration and curse, and Bhishma's moral on gratitude to friends.
The heading of the Mokshadharma Parva, Yudhishthira's questions on duty and grief, and the Brahmana's first words to King Senajit.
Senajit asks what wisdom ends grief; the Brahmana answers with a long teaching on impermanence and detachment, and tells the story of Pingala.
Yudhishthira's question, and the son's first question to his father about how to live when life is short, with the father's reply on the four stages of life.
The son's warning that death is near and his call to truth and renunciation, with Bhishma's closing advice to Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira's question, and the verses of Sampaka praising poverty and renunciation over wealth.
Yudhishthira's question about desire for wealth, and the story of Manki, who renounces desire after losing his bulls to a camel.
Janaka's saying, Yayati's son's question to the sage Vodhya, and Vodhya's six teachers of tranquillity.
Yudhishthira's question, and Prahlada's conversation with the wandering sage who lives by the Ajagara vow of contentment.
Yudhishthira's question on refuge, Bhishma's praise of wisdom, and the story of Indra's disguised rebuke to Kasyapa.
Yudhishthira's question, and Bhishma's teaching on the fruits of action and on the way to cleansing past sins.
Yudhishthira's questions on creation, and Bhrigu's account of the primeval being Manasa and the origin of the elements and Brahman.
Bhrigu's account of the boundless sky and the layers of water and fire, and his explanation of the lotus that Brahman sprang from.
Bharadwaja's question about creation, Bhrigu's account of water as the first creation, and the celestial voice describing how the elements arose.
Bharadwaja's question about the five elements, Bhrigu's answer on how they make up all things, and the argument over whether trees contain them.
Bharadwaja's question on bodily heat and wind, and Bhrigu's account of the breaths and the path of the yogins.
Bharadwaja's sceptical objections about life, death and the usefulness of gifts after death.
The debate on whether the living creature survives death, with Bhrigu's fire analogy, Bharadwaja's objections and Bhrigu's teaching on the inner Soul.
Bhrigu's account of Brahman's first creations and the colours of the four classes, Bharadwaja's objection, and Bhrigu's explanation of how the classes arose from conduct.
Bharadwaja's question on the marks of each class, and Bhrigu's description of the Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaisya and Sudra and the path to Brahma.
Bhrigu's teaching that truth leads to light and happiness, Bharadwaja's doubt, and Bhrigu's reply on the miseries of the untruthful.
Bharadwaja's questions on the rewards of gift, conduct and penance, the duties of each person, and the four modes of life.
Bhrigu describes the student's discipline, the householder's life and duties, and the forest life.
Bhrigu's descriptions of forest hermits and wandering renouncers, Bharadwaja's question about the northern region, Bhrigu's account of it, and Bhishma's closing.
Yudhishthira requests a discourse on the ordinances of conduct, and Bhishma gives a long list of daily rules and the reasons for them.
Bhishma teaches the Adhyatma doctrine: the elements, the senses and mind, the understanding, the three qualities, and the soul as a witness, with a call to self-knowledge and detachment.
Bhishma explains how a yogin restrains the senses and mind, why the mind keeps slipping away, and how steady practice brings a felicity and final liberation.
