Yudhishthira asks about the rewards and path of silent reciters, and Bhishma answers by linking recitation to the Sankhya and yoga paths and describing the renunciate reciter's way to the Soul.
Bhishma names the faults that send reciters to hell, and Yudhishthira asks why even those who reach Brahma return to embodied life.
Bhishma contrasts the heavens of the gods, which he calls a kind of hell, with the supreme region of the Soul that is free from time and the qualities.
The Brahmana's long recitation earns a boon from Savitri, and Dharma offers him heaven, which he refuses.
The Brahmana repeatedly refuses to leave his body, even for heaven, because he loves his recitation.
Dharma brings Yama, Time and Mrityu to the Brahmana, and each of them announces that the time has come for him to go.
King Ikshvaku arrives, honours the Brahmana, and offers him wealth; the Brahmana explains that he has given up accepting gifts, and the king replies that a Kshatriya speaks of battle, not giving.
The Brahmana and the king trade sharp words about their duties, and the king asks for the fruit of the recitations.
The Brahmana offers half or all of his recitation fruit, and the king refuses it because he does not know what it is.
The Brahmana insists on the power of truth and gives the fruit away, Ikshvaku pleads his Kshatriya duty, and Dharma and Heaven settle the dispute.
The king sends the Brahmana toward heaven and offers his own rewards; the Brahmana declines and says he will keep his vow of abstention.
The king offers to share rewards, and two oddly dressed strangers arrive, each claiming the other owes him a debt.
Virupa explains the chain of cow gifts that links him to Vikrita, and Vikrita refuses repayment.
Both men and the Brahmana press the king, and he accepts the gift while complaining that the duties of kings and Brahmanas have trapped him.
The king accepts the Brahmana's gift, Virupa reveals that the two strangers are Desire and Wrath, and Bhishma explains where reciters go.
Yudhishthira asks what became of them, and Bhishma describes the gods gathering, the Brahmana and king being absorbed into Brahma.
Brahman says that those who study the scriptures or practise yoga will join him, and then departs with the gods.
Yudhishthira asks his question, and Bhishma introduces Vrihaspati's questions to Manu and Manu's first reply about desire and action.
Vrihaspati states that human aims are gained through acts, and Manu explains how liberation from acts leads to Brahma, how acts are shaped by the qualities, and describes the supreme being.
Manu describes how bodies dissolve into the elements, how knowledge and the Self relate to the senses, and how the Soul passes from one body to the next carrying its acts.
Manu argues that the Soul is the witness of the mind and senses, is known only through wisdom, and is not lost when it leaves the body, using images of the moon, Rahu and the sun.
Manu compares sleep and death to dreams, explains that a calm mind lets the Soul be seen, and says restraint and knowledge lead the Soul back to the Supreme.
Manu gives advice on dealing with sorrow, explains how the understanding must be drawn into the mind and contemplation to reach Brahma, and ends with the rules of rebirth and liberation.
Manu describes how the soul moves between bodies by its acts, how the chain of knowledge, desire and action is broken, and how Vishnu, beyond Time, is the Supreme Brahma.

Yudhishthira requests a full account of Vishnu, and Bhishma recounts Vishnu's acts of creation, his killing of Madhu, the families of sages and gods, the four orders of men, the ages of the world and the sinful peoples, and declares Krishna to be supreme.
Bhishma lists the Prajapatis and the gods, and assigns the great Rishis to the four quarters of the world.
Bhishma recounts how the Danavas oppressed the gods and the earth, how Vishnu became a boar to destroy them, and how the gods learn that the boar is the Supreme God.
Yudhishthira asks about emancipation, and the preceptor answers his disciple by describing Vasudeva as the cause, the structure of primordial matter, and the Soul's passage through bodies.
Bhishma completes the preceptor's answer, describing the Soul as untouched by the wheel of existence and saying that knowledge frees it from rebirth.
Bhishma advises against attachment to the senses and sets out the states produced by the three qualities, then Yudhishthira asks which faults to abandon and Bhishma explains how to remove them.
Bhishma describes the chain from passion and darkness through desire and acts to rebirth in the womb, and says release comes when the senses are weakened.
Bhishma explains Brahmacharya and the restraint of passion, the body's channels through which desire acts, and the way a disciplined person escapes rebirth.
Bhishma advises seekers on giving up attachment, practising virtue and restraint, and gradually controlling the mind and senses until Brahma is reached.
Bhishma explains why dreams occur, how deep sleep returns the mind to the Soul, and how crossing darkness lets the yogin reach the Supreme Brahma.

Bhishma explains the two paths of activity and renunciation, the distinction between Prakriti and Purusha, the yogic discipline and the worship of Brahma, and then concludes that desire weaves the universe and that knowledge frees one from it.
Bhishma tells how the sage Panchasikha teaches King Janadeva of Mithila the Sankhya doctrine, refuting those who deny that the Soul survives the body.
Janadeva questions the point of knowledge and ritual if nothing survives death, and Panchasikha answers by describing the body and senses and urging renunciation.
Yudhishthira asks what brings happiness and freedom from fear, and Bhishma praises self-restraint and describes the self-restrained man.
Bhishma explains that eating sacrificial remnants with forbidden food is a fall, and that fasting is not true penance, while renunciation and humility are.
Bhishma describes how a Brahmana is regarded as always fasting, celibate, vegetarian and hospitable.
Indra questions the fallen Prahlada, who says that acts and beings flow from Nature, that the person is not the true doer, and that he feels no grief or desire.
Prahlada names the means to wisdom and tranquillity, and Indra praises him and returns home.
Indra asks Brahma where Vali is, and Brahma tells him that Vali has been reborn as a beast and should be spared, and that Indra should learn morality from him.
Indra finds Vali as an ass, recalls his past splendour and asks whether he grieves; Vali replies that the wise are not moved by fortune.
Indra taunts Vali, and Vali replies that fortune and misfortune are ordained, that Time rules all beings, and that Indra too will pass away.
Indra sees the goddess Sree come out of Vali, and she refuses to name herself to him beyond her many names.
Indra asks why Sree is leaving Vali, and she explains that Vali has lost truth, gifts and devotion to the Brahmanas and has begun to boast.
Sree says no being can bear her forever, and Indra asks how she may stay, and she tells him to divide her into four parts.
Sree gives a quarter each to the earth, the waters and fire, and Indra assigns the places.
Sree gives the last quarter to the good among men, and Vali predicts a later battle, but Indra, bound by Brahma's command, lets him go, and explains the sun's yearly course.
Vali goes south and Indra goes north, and Indra ascends to the sky.
Indra asks the fallen Namuchi whether he grieves, and Namuchi explains that sorrow is useless and that all events are ordained, so the wise remain calm.
Bhishma tells how Indra questions the calm Vali, who explains that Time rules all rise and fall and that grief helps nothing, and how Indra then makes peace and returns to heaven.
A heading marks the start of Section CCXXVIII.
Bhishma introduces the meeting of Narada and Indra with Sree, and she explains who she is and why she is turning away from the Asuras.
Sree recalls the virtues the Danavas once had and the decline that drove her away, and Narada and Indra welcome her, and prosperity returns to the world.
Devala asks Jaigishavya the source of his wisdom, and Jaigishavya describes the even-minded wise who attain Brahma beyond primordial nature.
Bhishma recites Kesava's answer to Ugrasena, praising Narada for his learning, self-control, equal regard and freedom from envy and pride, which make him loved and honoured everywhere.
Yudhishthira asks about creation and time, and Bhishma recounts Vyasa's teaching to Suka on the units of time, the four yugas and Brahman's day and night.
Vyasa describes how Brahma creates the elements, the body and the living world, how the Vedas and penance shape creation, and how Time governs all.
Vyasa describes the dissolution of the universe at the end of Brahman's day, with the elements, Mind and Time withdrawn into the unmanifest supreme Brahma.
Vyasa lists the duties of a Brahmana, from study and householder life to giving and sacrifice, and names the kings and sages who gained heaven through their gifts.
Vyasa tells the Brahmana to study the Vedas and live with restraint, and compares Time to a river that only the wise can cross on the raft of knowledge.
Vyasa describes knowledge as the raft over life's stream, the requirements and stages of yoga, the powers gained over the elements, and the agreement of the Sankhya and yoga paths.
Vyasa tells Suka to hold to knowledge, Suka asks what knowledge is, and Vyasa explains the limits of belief in nature alone and the rank of the wise Brahmana.
Vyasa discusses whether Brahmana duties are obligatory, reviews rival causes of action, and describes how the Vedas and duties decline through the ages under Time.
Suka asks how Brahma is attained, Vyasa answers that knowledge, penance and renunciation lead there, and describes the Soul as present in all beings and reached by inner light.
Vyasa lays out the yoga method, including overcoming the five impediments, restraining the senses and mind, avoiding distractions and powers, and reaching Brahma after six months of practice.
Suka asks whether knowledge or action leads to the better end, and Vyasa describes the path of action, which brings rebirth, and the path of knowledge, which leads to eternal Brahma.
Suka asks which path is right, Vyasa recommends the forest path of detachment, and then explains the four stages of life as a ladder to Brahma, describing the student's service to his preceptor.
Vyasa lays out the householder's graded ways of storing food, his duties of hospitality and self-restraint, the merit of his relatives, and the rising order of the stages of life.
Bhishma announces the forest stage, and Vyasa describes the life of the forest recluse, the sages who attained heaven through it, and the final renunciation.
Suka asks how to practise yoga in the last stage of life, and Vyasa describes the renouncer's way of life, the marks of a true Brahmana, and the supreme duty of harmlessness.
Vyasa describes the hierarchy of reality, the yogic withdrawal into the Soul, and the limits on who may receive this teaching.
Suka asks about Adhyatma, Vyasa describes the five elements and their unequal distribution, and explains which element gives rise to each sense and each quality.
Vyasa explains how the understanding becomes mind and the senses, how the Soul witnesses the qualities without mingling with them, and how it is perceived once darkness is removed.
Vyasa explains that the Soul presides over the objects the understanding creates, advises cutting the knot of the heart through knowledge, and says that acts done without desire do not bind.
Suka asks which duty is foremost, and Vyasa gives a long teaching on restraint, knowledge of the Soul, and freedom from rebirth.
Vyasa describes the marks of a true Brahmana, the danger of desire, and the freedom of the yogin who has transcended Prakriti.
Vyasa explains how the five elements and the senses in the body are linked, how the mind, understanding and Soul fit in, and what this knowledge frees a person from.
Vyasa explains how yogins perceive the subtle Soul, why ordinary people cannot, which duties Sandilya taught, and how one reaches high Brahma.
Vyasa describes the tree of desire, the way yoga can cut it down, and how the mind and understanding in the body can be corrupted by rajas.

Bhishma repeats the list of properties of the elements, mind and understanding, Yudhishthira asks for an explanation, and Bhishma explains that the entities are created, not eternal, and that tranquillity comes from knowing Brahma.
Yudhishthira asks about death, Bhishma introduces King Anukampaka and the sage Narada, and Narada begins his tale of overpopulation and the Grandsire's wrath.
Shiva asks for mercy, the Grandsire explains his reasons, Shiva pleads for living beings, and the Grandsire creates Death and orders her to slay creatures.

Death pleads that she cannot slay innocent creatures, and then accepts the task only after the Grandsire's order and her long austerities, with the tears becoming diseases and wind described as the life of all beings.
Yudhishthira asks about the nature and sources of righteousness, and Bhishma explains the sources, gives examples of right conduct, and gives a closing warning.
Yudhishthira questions Bhishma's account of righteousness, arguing that scripture cannot settle duty, that the age and circumstances change it, and that the rule of following the good is circular.
Bhishma introduces Jajali and his penances, tells how the birds nested on his head and left, and describes Jajali's pride, the voice, his journey, and his meeting with Tuladhara.
Jajali asks how Tuladhara knows so much, and Tuladhara explains his idea of morality as harmlessness, his even-minded life as a merchant, and his criticisms of cruelty and of the Nahusha episode.

Jajali objects to Tuladhara's teaching, Tuladhara explains that sacrifice should be done with faith and without animal slaughter, and Jajali asks for more, which Tuladhara gives before Bhishma closes the passage.
Tuladhara asks Jajali to summon the birds, the birds speak about faith and harmless acts, and Bhishma reports that Tuladhara and Jajali both went to heaven.
Bhishma recounts King Vichakhy's protest at a sacrifice of slaughter, and Yudhishthira asks how a man who avoids harm can keep his body, with Bhishma's short reply.
Yudhishthira asks how to judge hard acts, and Bhishma tells the story of Chirakarin, whose long deliberation saved his mother, ending with Gautama's praise of reflection.
Yudhishthira asks how a king can protect subjects without harm, and Bhishma recounts the debate between Dyumatsena and Satyavat about capital punishment, mercy, and the ages.
Yudhishthira asks which path is higher, Bhishma tells of Kapila and the cow, and the cow's voice, speaking for Syumarasmi, defends sacrifice and the authority of the Vedas.
Kapila praises renunciation and Syumarasmi defends the householder life, with Kapila describing self-control of the four doors and Syumarasmi asking how the Vedas can both urge and forbid acts.
Syumarasmi introduces himself and asks what visible fruit the yogis gain, Kapila explains that knowledge and self-control lead to liberation, and Syumarasmi asks to be taught about Emancipation.

Kapila praises the purity and self-discipline of men of old and describes renunciation as the highest end, and Syumarasmi and Kapila then debate whether householders or renouncers reach the higher place.
Bhishma tells how a poor Brahmana sought wealth from the cloud Kundadhara, how the gods granted him virtue instead, and how he rose to spiritual power and was shown kings in hell.
Kundadhara rebukes the Brahmana for his greed and points out the vices that enchain men, and the Brahmana repents and is forgiven, with the lesson that virtue outweighs wealth.
Yudhishthira asks which sacrifice is for virtue alone, and Bhishma passes on Narada's story of Satya, the deer, and Dharma, which ends with the teaching that harmlessness is the highest religion.
Yudhishthira asks how sin, virtue, renunciation and liberation come about, and Bhishma traces the path of the sinful man and the righteous man, ending with an exhortation to adhere to virtue.
Yudhishthira asks for the means to liberation, and Bhishma gives the single path, with its remedies for anger, desire, fear, greed and ignorance, and the control of the soul by the soul.

Narada asks about creation and destruction, and Asita-Devala answers with the five essences, the organs of knowledge and action, the states of sleep and dream, and the migration of the Jiva to Brahma.
Yudhishthira laments the killing and asks how to end greed, and Bhishma tells of the king of Videha's teaching to the sage Mandavya, who turns to liberation.
Yudhishthira asks what good to seek, and Bhishma tells how the learned son Medhavin asks his father what to do, and the father gives the conventional four-stage advice.
The son answers that Death and decrepitude are always near, urges truth, sacrifice of the self, and renunciation, and the father follows him.
Yudhishthira asks which conduct leads to Brahma, and Bhishma describes the life of the renouncer and the path that the sage Harita taught.

Yudhishthira laments his sorrow and asks when he will renounce, Bhishma says nothing is permanent and explains ignorance, and Vritra speaks to his preceptor Usanas about rebirth and asks how to reach Brahma.
Usanas and Vritra hear Sanatkumara's long teaching on Vishnu's greatness, the cycles of creation and the stages of the soul, and Vritra's peaceful death in yoga.
Yudhishthira asks whether Krishna is the Lord Sanatkumara described, Bhishma identifies Kesava as a portion of the Supreme, and he reassures the Pandavas about their future.
Yudhishthira asks how Vritra was defeated, Bhishma describes the battle, Vasishtha revives Indra, and Mahadeva and Vishnu give their help to Indra.
Indra vows to slay Vritra, the Asuras are confused by Mahadeva's fever, and Indra's form on his car is so awe-inspiring that no one can look at it.
Vritra's fever and death at Indra's thunderbolt, the sin of Brahmanicide seizing Indra, and Brahma's search for a way to free him.
Brahma gives Agni, the trees and herbs, and the Apsaras each a portion of the sin, with a condition for each.
Brahma gives the Waters a portion of the sin, with a condition on how it passes to men.
Indra is cleansed by a horse sacrifice, the origin of the unclean cocks is explained, and Bhishma says the tale brings freedom from sin.
Yudhishthira asks where Fever came from, and Bhishma describes Mahadeva's court on Mount Meru, Daksha's sacrifice, and Uma's question about why Mahadeva does not attend.

Mahadeva explains that he has no share of the sacrifices, Uma grieves, Mahadeva's followers destroy the sacrifice, Brahma makes peace, and Fever is spread among creatures, with Bhishma's closing words.
Janamejaya asks about the destruction of Daksha's sacrifice, and Vaisampayana describes the gathering on Himavat, Dadhichi's warning, and Daksha's refusal to honour Shiva.
Uma asks Shiva how he may win a share, Shiva answers with pride and creates a fierce being, and Virabhadra and the spirits wreck the sacrifice.
Virabhadra says he came to destroy the sacrifice, Daksha praises Shiva, and Shiva grants Daksha's request that the wrecked offerings be made useful to him.
Yudhishthira asks for Daksha's names of the god, Bhishma gives the long hymn, a heading marks the next section, and Shiva accepts Daksha's praise and promises him the fruit of many sacrifices.
Shiva consoles Daksha, teaches him the Pasupata religion, and disappears, and Bhishma explains the power of the hymn to protect and to bring success.
Yudhishthira asks about Adhyatma, and Bhishma explains the five essences, the senses, the understanding, the three qualities, and the difference between the understanding and the Soul.

Yudhishthira asks how to escape sorrow and death, and Bhishma tells of the sage Samanga, whose calm Narada admires, and whose explanation of past acts and freedom from desire shows why grief cannot touch him.

Yudhishthira asks what benefits a doubting man, and Bhishma tells of Galava's question to Narada about the good among differing scriptural paths, with Narada's long reply on virtue, places to live, and the rule of kings.
Yudhishthira asks how a king should live, Bhishma introduces Arishtanemi's teaching to Sagara, Sagara asks for the good, and Arishtanemi describes the way to freedom from attachment.
Yudhishthira asks about Usanas's alliance with the Asuras and his name, and Bhishma tells how Usanas robbed Kubera, was swallowed by Shiva, and got out through the urethra, with Uma saving him.
Shiva lets Usanas go, and Bhishma ends the story of the Bhargava.

Yudhishthira asks what good acts to do, Bhishma tells of Janaka's question to Parasara, and Parasara explains righteousness, the duties of the classes, the fruits of acts, and the rule against doing what one would condemn in others.

Parasara explains how to steer the body and senses with knowledge, the difference between knowing and unknowing wrongdoing, the value of judgment in acts, and the duties of kings and of those who retire to the forest.
Parasara discusses self-interest, fair wealth, the debts a man owes, and the honour due to parents, the sacred fire, and teachers.
Parasara sets out the duties of each class, the value of keeping to one's own duty, and the best way to make gifts.

Parasara explains the lawful means of livelihood for each class, traces the rise of pride and desire among men, the defeat of the Asuras by Shiva, and the rule that followed, and urges avoiding injury and seeking knowledge of the Soul.
Parasara describes how attachment to household life leads to despair, study and penance, warns against penance done for reward, and tells householders to do their duties with honest effort.
Janaka asks why the classes differ, and Parasara explains the four classes, the mixed castes, the sages born of mixed wombs, and the Gotras, then Janaka asks for the duties.
Parasara sets out the special and common duties of the classes, and answers Janaka that acts stain a man more than birth, and that the way of acts free from harm leads to Yoga and liberation.

Parasara discusses devotion to elders, rules of battle, the dissolution of the body, rebirth, the good death, the four stages of life, and the duties to the dead, and Bhishma closes by naming the king of Videha as the listener.
Bhishma introduces Janaka's question, Janaka asks about the best path, Parasara answers at length on detachment, knowledge, harmlessness and past acts, and Janaka is pleased.
Janaka hears the sage's words and is made very happy.
Yudhishthira asks about the virtues, Bhishma introduces the golden swan and the Sadhyas, and the swan answers the first question with a long teaching on restraint, forgiveness and truth.
The Sadhyas ask the swan about what covers the world, who is truly happy among Brahmanas, and what makes a Brahmana divine or impure, and the swan answers each question.
Bhishma ends the discourse by saying that the body is the seat of acts and the Jiva is truth.
Yudhishthira asks about the two systems, Bhishma compares the schools and their reasons, explains the strength a Yogin needs, and describes the meditation that brings liberation.
Bhishma lists the diets and restraints that build a Yogin's power, describes the hard path of Yoga and its highest fruit, and closes the section.

Yudhishthira asks Bhishma to explain the Sankhya principles, and Bhishma describes the doctrine's view of the world, the body's faults and the way of liberation. Yudhishthira then raises the question of whether consciousness survives liberation.

Bhishma answers that the senses serve the soul, that a freed soul merges into Brahma, and that Sankhya knowledge is the source of other learning. He ends by describing Narayana as the one who creates and withdraws the universe.
Vasishtha teaches king Karala about the Destructible and the Indestructible, covering the cosmic cycles, the twenty-four principles and the twenty-fifth beyond them.
Vasishtha describes the endless births and sufferings of the forgetful soul, the bodies and practices it takes on, and the cycle of acts driven by Prakriti.
Vasishtha compares the soul to the moon's sixteen portions, explains how ignorance keeps Jiva in repeated births, and defines emancipation as freedom from Prakriti.

Janaka asks how Emancipation can exist given the constant union of Purusha and Prakriti, and Vasishtha answers that texts must be understood, then explains the Supreme Soul and the difference between unity and multiplicity.
Janaka asks for a fuller account of unity and multiplicity; Vasishtha explains the Yoga practice of contemplation, then the Sankhya principles and how the Soul is known as the true knower.

Vasishtha defines knowledge and ignorance through the Sankhya principles, gives the Jiva's lament at its bondage to Prakriti and its resolve to turn to the Supreme Soul, and notes that Sankhya and Yoga agree.

Vasishtha contrasts the Supreme Soul with the Jiva, explains how the Jiva is freed, and says who may receive the teaching. Bhishma then closes the discourse with its line of transmission and an assurance to the king.
King Vasuman asks a Bhrigu-line Rishi how to gain lasting good, and the Rishi advises righteousness, gifts, firmness and the company of the virtuous. The king takes this advice to heart.

Yudhishthira asks for teaching on the eternal and indestructible, and Bhishma introduces a dialogue in which Janaka questions Yajnavalkya, who begins by listing the principles and the stages of creation.
Yajnavalkya describes Brahma's day and night, his emergence from a golden egg, the creation of the elements and senses, and the mind's rule over them.
Yajnavalkya describes the dissolution of creation at the end of Brahma's day, from Maharudra's fire to the absorption of all into Sambhu, and introduces the three frames of teaching.
Yajnavalkya pairs each sense and faculty with its inner, outer and divine aspects, explains how Prakriti multiplies the three qualities, and lists the qualities that belong to each.

Yajnavalkya explains how the three qualities mix to decide rebirth, and how Prakriti creates only under the presence of Purusha. Janaka then asks how the two differ and asks for fuller teaching on Emancipation.
Yajnavalkya explains how Purusha seems bound to attributes while in truth being distinct from Prakriti, illustrates this with several images, and then announces the teaching of Yoga.
Yajnavalkya presents Yoga as one with Sankhya, describes breath and sense control, the eight powers and the two kinds of practice, and portrays the calm of one absorbed in Samadhi.
Yajnavalkya describes where the soul goes depending on the exit point from the body, then lists the signs that foretell death and advises the wise to unite with the Supreme Soul.
Yajnavalkya recounts receiving the Yajush texts and compiling the Satapatha Brahmana, then answers the Gandharva Viswavasu's questions on Prakriti, Purusha and the Supreme Soul.
Yajnavalkya says liberation comes through knowledge open to all orders, and Bhishma describes how king Daivarati handed his kingdom to his son and took up the life of a renunciant.
Yudhishthira asks how death can be avoided, and Bhishma tells the old dialogue in which Janaka questions the sage Panchasikha, who says that only renunciation leads beyond birth and death.
Bhishma tells how the mendicant Sulabha tests king Janaka's freedom by entering his mind through Yoga, and the two debate at length on renunciation, kingship and the purity of the soul.
Bhishma notes that Janaka, having heard Sulabha's reasoning, has no answer.
Vyasa urges his son Suka at length to master the senses, live righteously and prepare for death, and Suka then leaves to seek a teacher of liberation.
Bhishma explains that sinful acts bring hardship and righteous acts bring joy, since every deed ripens in its own time and follows the doer into the next life.
Bhishma explains that Suka's greatness comes from restraint, and recounts how Vyasa's long penance before Mahadeva on Mount Meru won him the promise of a son.
Vyasa's desire for Ghritachi leads to Suka's birth from the fire-sticks, the gods celebrate, and Suka studies the Vedas under Vrihaspati and turns toward liberation.
Vyasa sends Suka to Janaka, Suka walks to Mithila, is kept waiting and tested by palace women, and remains calm, spending the night absorbed in Yoga.
Janaka receives Suka with honour, and the two discuss the four stages of life. Janaka explains that knowledge is the means to liberation and tells Suka that he already has it.
Suka returns to the Himalayas and reports to his father Vyasa, and the disciples then ask a boon that Vyasa answers with rules for teaching the Vedas.
Vyasa's disciples leave to spread the Vedas, Narada reproaches Vyasa for the silence of recitation, and Vyasa answers with a long account of the winds and the two paths after death.
Narada visits Suka and passes on Sanatkumara's teaching on detachment, the crossing of the river of life, and the knowledge of the Supreme Soul.
Narada advises Suka that wisdom, not grief, is the cure for sorrow, and that contentment and self-control bring happiness, since all worldly things are transitory.
Narada describes how fortune, suffering and rebirth lie beyond human control, and Suka resolves to attain an eternal state through Yoga, then takes leave of his father and goes to Kailasa.
Suka enters Yoga on a mountain, rises into the sky to the wonder of the heavenly beings, and asks the world to answer his father's calls when he has gone.
Suka passes into Brahma with cosmic omens, and Vyasa grieves until Mahadeva consoles him with the promise of his son's fame and a shadow of him.
Yudhishthira asks about the highest deity and the path to Emancipation, and Bhishma relates Narada's visit to Narayana, who teaches that the inner soul is the highest object of worship.
Narada visits the White Island, Yudhishthira asks about its inhabitants, and Bhishma tells the story of King Uparichara and the treatise composed by the seven seers.
Vrihaspati presides over Uparichara's sacrifice, Hari takes his share unseen, and the Sadasyas calm Vrihaspati with the account of the White Island and Vasu's fall and rise.
The gods and Rishis dispute whether sacrifices should use goats or grain, and Vasu is asked to judge between them.
Vasu sides with the gods and is cursed to fall, and the gods and Narayana then provide for him and lift him back to heaven. Bhishma then turns to Narada's journey to the White Island.
Narada reaches the White Island, takes up silent Yoga there, and offers Narayana a long hymn of praise.
Narada's hymn brings Narayana before him in universal form, and the god explains his nature, his fourfold manifestation and his descents, then sends Narada back to repeat the teaching.

Yudhishthira asks why Brahman did not know Narayana's greatness, Bhishma traces how the narrative was handed down and commends it to devotees, and the frame closes with Vaisampayana's words and Suta's account of the sacrifice at Naimisha.
Sauti introduces Vaisampayana's answer to Janamejaya, which recalls Vyasa's account of creation through Aniruddha and the eight Prakritis, and the gods' appeal to Brahman.
Narayana grants the gods shares in sacrifice and foretells the decline of righteousness through the four ages, and Brahman sees him in a horse-headed form.
Narayana charges Brahman with creation and vanishes, and Vaisampayana closes by describing the blessings that come to those who hear and recite the narrative.
Janamejaya asks for the meanings of Hari's names, and Vaisampayana recounts Krishna's explanation to Arjuna of how his names arise from his nature and deeds.
Krishna narrates the origin of Agni and Soma, the stories of Indra and the Brahmanas, many of his own names, and the battle between Rudra and Narayana that ends in peace.
Krishna concludes that Rudra and Narayana are one, and tells Arjuna to bow to Rudra, whom he calls his own wrath-born form.
Saunaka's praise and question, Sauti's framing of Janamejaya's request, and Vaisampayana's account of Narada's journey to Vadari and his welcome by Nara and Narayana.
Narada describes what he saw on White Island and says he has come back under the Lord's orders to live with Nara and Narayana.
Nara and Narayana teach Narada about the Supreme Soul, the elements, and the path of the liberated, and Narada then settles into devotion and long residence at Vadari.
Nara questions Narada about his rites, Narada explains his worship, and the two sages tell the origin of the Pitris and the Pinda offering.
Narada's departure, Vaisampayana's advice to the king to continue the horse sacrifice, and Sauti's account of the king's rites and a praise of Narayana.
Janamejaya's question, Sauti's framing, and Vaisampayana's account of the dissolution and creation, the theft of the Vedas, and Brahma's lament.
Brahma's hymn to Narayana, the horse-headed form and recovery of the Vedas, the battle with the demons, and Vaisampayana's closing praise of this form.
Janamejaya's questions about devotion, Vaisampayana's account of how the teaching was handed down, and his explanation of the three dispositions and who receives grace.
Vaisampayana's closing summary: the path of renunciation of action, the unity of the teachings, and the warning that this doctrine is hard to practise.
Janamejaya's question about the systems, Vaisampayana's praise of Vyasa, and Vyasa's account of his birth from Narayana as told to his disciples.
Vaisampayana's survey of the main cults, all centred on Narayana, and Janamejaya's question about one Purusha or many.
Brahma and Mahadeva meet on Mount Vaijayanta, and Brahma explains which Purusha he meditates on.
Brahma's full answer to Mahadeva about the one Purusha, his nature, his manifestation as Narayana, and the origin of everything from him.
Sauti's introduction, Yudhishthira's question to Bhishma about the foremost duties of each stage of life, and Bhishma's answer that he will recount Narada's talk with Indra.
Bhishma introduces a householder's doubts about duty, his conversation with a guest about renunciation, and the guest's reply that many paths lead to heaven.
The guest's instruction, naming the Naga Padmanabha in Naimisha and describing his character.
The host's gratitude, the night spent in talk about renunciation, and the host's departure the next morning.
The Brahmin's arrival at the Naga's house, his request to see the Naga, the wife's reply about her husband's absence, and his decision to wait by the Gomati.
The Naga's relatives plead with the fasting Brahmin, and he refuses, sending them home.
The Naga's return, his questions to his wife about his household duties, and her reply on the duties of each class and her appeal that he meet the waiting Brahmin.
The Naga questions whether the guest is human, his wife urges him to attend to the guest, and the Naga agrees to meet him after a reflection on the harm of wrath.
The Naga meets the Brahmin on the Gomati, the Brahmin introduces himself and his purpose, and the Naga offers his service.
The Brahmin's request for a marvel, the Naga's account of the Sun's wonders, and his description of the radiant being who joined the Sun.
Surya's explanation of the radiant being as a Brahmin who attained heaven through the Unccha vow, with the Naga's concluding remarks.
The Brahmin's farewell to the Naga, his resolve to live by the Unccha vow, his initiation by Chyavana, and the chain of teachers through whom the story reached Bhishma.

Matanga asks for other boons, Sakra grants him fame, Matanga dies, and Bhishma draws the moral.
Yudhishthira's question, the wars between the Haihayas and the kings of Kasi, Pratarddana's victory, Vitahavya's elevation by Bhrigu, and the genealogy.
Yudhishthira's question, Krishna's question to Narada, Narada's list of revered Brahmanas, and Bhishma's advice to Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira's question, the pigeon's plea to King Vrishadarbha, the hawk's objection, and the king's first offer of other meat.
The hawk's demand for the king's own flesh, the king's sacrifice, his reward in heaven, and the moral for Yudhishthira.
Yudhishthira's question and Bhishma's long answer on the king's duty to honour and protect the Brahmanas.
Bhishma's case for honouring Brahmanas, the Earth's teaching to Vasudeva on serving them, and Bhishma's closing advice to Yudhishthira.
Bhishma's praise of the Brahmanas, Brahma's verses on their duties, and the closing notes of the section.
Sakra's disguised visit to Samvara, Samvara's account of his devotion to Brahmanas and Soma's teaching, and Sakra's rise after taking up the same course.
Yudhishthira's question on the choice of recipients, Bhishma's answer on worthiness, and the householder's duties to others.
Yudhishthira's request, Narada's meeting with Panchachuda, and her agreement to answer.
Panchachuda's account of the faults she ascribes to women.
Yudhishthira's series of questions on why men are drawn to women, whether women can be restrained, and whether anyone has managed it.
The account of how women were created, and Devasarman's instruction to Vipula to protect his wife Ruchi from Indra.
Devasarman's description of Indra's disguises and Vipula's decision to enter Ruchi's body to guard her.
Indra's visit to the hermitage, Vipula's rebuke of Indra, and Devasarman's reward to his disciple.
Vipula's pride after his penance, the errand for flowers, the oaths overheard on the road, and his realisation of his own fault.
Devasarman's welcome of Vipula, his explanation of the witnesses to Vipula's fault, and the closing lesson Bhishma draws about women.
Yudhishthira's question on choosing a bridegroom, Bhishma's account of marriage forms and rules, and Yudhishthira's question about dower and promises.
Yudhishthira's question about a rejected dowry suitor, and Bhishma's answer on dower, sale, and the rites that make a marriage.
Yudhishthira's question on a jilted dowry-giver, Bhishma's rules on maintenance and inheritance by daughters and their sons, and his condemnation of sale in marriage.
Bhishma's verses on dowry and sale, his teaching on respect for wives, and the verse on women's duty and protection.
Yudhishthira's question on inheritance among a Brahmana's sons, Bhishma's shares for the Brahmana's sons, Yudhishthira's objection, and Bhishma's reasons for ranking the wives.
Yudhishthira asks about other classes, and Bhishma gives the Kshatriya and Vaisya rules and the rule of the eldest son.
Yudhishthira's question on mixed-class duties, Bhishma's list of mixed-class offspring and their occupations, and Yudhishthira's question on how to recognise mixed birth.
Bhishma on how birth shows in conduct, and his list of the kinds of sons and of the sons of mixed unions.
Yudhishthira's debate on seed versus soil in determining sonship, and Bhishma's ruling on abandoned and made sons.
Bhishma on the foundling who is raised by a rearer, and the purification rites for such children.
Yudhishthira's questions, Chyavana's vow in the river, the fishermen's catch, and Chyavana's refusal to leave the fish.
Nahusha's arrival and his first offer of a thousand coins, which Chyavana refuses.
Nahusha's offers of a hundred thousand coins and then a crore, both refused.
Nahusha's offer of half his kingdom, its refusal, and the cow-born sage's proposal that a cow is the price.
Nahusha accepts the cow as the price, Chyavana praises cows, and the fishermen offer to return the cow, which Chyavana accepts while freeing them.
The fishermen and the fish ascend to heaven, the sages grant Nahusha boons, and Nahusha returns to his city, and Bhishma ends by listing the topics he has covered.
Yudhishthira's questions on Rama and the Kusika line, Chyavana's plan, Kusika's welcome, and the king's service to the sage until the sage vanishes.
Yudhishthira's question, Kusika's repeated service to Chyavana, the burnt food, the goading in the battle-car, Chyavana's gifts and healing, and the transformed riverbank.
Kusika's visit to the golden palace and its disappearance, Chyavana's praise of the king, and Kusika's reply.
Chyavana's offer, Kusika's list of questions, Chyavana's explanation of his trials, and Kusika's request for details of the Brahmana descent.
Chyavana's prophecy of the Bhargava-Kshatriya conflict and the marriage and exchange of sons that link the two families, and Bhishma's closing confirmation.
Yudhishthira's grief over the war, Bhishma's long account of the rewards of penance and gifts, and the brothers' acceptance of the grandsire's words.
Yudhishthira's question, and Bhishma's account of the merit of tanks and of tree planting.
Yudhishthira's question on the best gift, and Bhishma's long answer on giving, the merit of Brahmanas, and the duty of kings to them.
Yudhishthira's question on gifts to a begging versus a non-begging Brahmana, and Bhishma's answer on contentment and the worth of gifts to the unasking.
Yudhishthira's questions on gifts and sacrifices, Bhishma's advice on royal giving, and his warnings about the king's duty to protect his people.
Yudhishthira's question, Bhishma's praise of the gift of earth, the exchange between Indra and Vrihaspati, and the closing advice on reciting the verses.
Yudhishthira's question, Bhishma's recollection of Narada's teaching on food-gifts, and Narada's account of the heavenly rewards, with a closing heading.
Yudhishthira's question, Narada's list of gifts for each lunar constellation as told to Devaki, and Bhishma's note on how the teaching was passed on.
Bhishma's survey of the gifts praised by Atri, Harischandra, Manu and Sandilya, including wells, ghee, firewood, umbrellas and cars.
Yudhishthira's question on sandals and his request for more on sesame, land, cows and food, followed by Bhishma's praise of sesame and the story of the gods' request for earth.
Brahma's grant of earth, the gods' sacrifice, and Bhishma's teaching on gifts of land, shelter, cows and food.
Yudhishthira's question on drink, and Bhishma's account of why water is the highest gift.
Yudhishthira's question, and Yama's instructions to a Brahmana through the story of a mistaken summons.
The Brahmana's return to the world and his practice of the gifts, and Bhishma's closing teaching on lamps, gems, robes and offspring.
Yudhishthira's question on which gifts all classes may make, Bhishma's account of kine, earth and knowledge as gifts of equal merit, and his rules on fit recipients.
The story of king Nriga, the lizard in the well, Nriga's account of his sin, Yama's judgement, and Krishna's rescue and moral.
Yudhishthira's request, the story of Uddalaki and Nachiketa, Nachiketa's visit to Yama and Yama's rules for gifts of cows, and Yama's teaching on substitute cows.
Yudhishthira's question about the regions of cow-givers, and Indra's questions to Brahma about those regions and the merit of many versus few cows.
Brahma's description of the cow-givers' regions, the virtues and sins that decide who reaches them, the merit of cow-gifts by class and source, and the rules for recipients and the gift itself.
Indra's question about cow thieves and sellers, Brahma's answer on the punishments and on gold as Dakshina, and Bhishma's account of how the teaching was handed down.
Yudhishthira's list of questions on the rewards of virtue, and Bhishma's answers on self-restraint, study, heroes, truth, celibacy and service to elders.
Yudhishthira's request for the ritual, Bhishma's account of the rite taught to Mandhatri, and Yudhishthira's obedience to it.
Yudhishthira's second request, Bhishma's rules on the choice of cows, and Yudhishthira's question about the Kapila cow.
Bhishma's history of Surabhi and the Kapila cows, the story of Mahadeva and Daksha, and Yudhishthira's gifts to the Brahmanas.
Saudasa's question to Vasishtha, Vasishtha's praise of cows, and his rules for honouring them.
Vasishtha's account of the cows' penance and boon, and his list of heavenly rewards for giving cows of each colour and to each deity.
Vasishtha's mantra in praise of cows and his account of their rewards, followed by Bhishma's note that Saudasa gave many cows and won heavenly regions.
Yudhishthira's question, Bhishma's account of cows' sanctity and the cow-givers' rewards, Suka's question to Vyasa and Vyasa's answer on cows, and Bhishma's closing note on Suka.
Yudhishthira's question, Sree's arrival among the cows, and the cows' first refusal.
Sree's plea for a place among the cows, the cows' final offer of urine and dung, and Sree's acceptance.
Sree's thanks, her disappearance, and Bhishma's introduction of his next topic.
Bhishma's opening on the sanctity of cows and ghee, Brahma's answer to Indra about the realm of cows, and Surabhi's reward; and Bhishma's closing on the rewards of devotion to cows.
Yudhishthira asks about gold. Bhishma answers with his own dream of the ancestors, the legend of Parashurama and the sages' teaching, and the myth of Rudra's seed and the threat of Taraka.
The gods appeal to Brahma against Taraka, and Brahma sends them to find Agni, who hides from them while his curses fall on the frogs, elephants and parrots.

The gods find Agni in a Sami tree and ask him to father a son. The golden child is born from the seed in Ganga and grows into Kartikeya, and Vasishtha then recounts the sacrifice of Rudra and the birth of the sages.

Rudra, Agni and Brahma each claim the offspring of that sacrifice, and Brahma settles the matter. The chapter then ends with the merit of gold gifts at different times of day and Kartikeya's victory over Taraka.
Yudhishthira asks how Taraka was destroyed. Bhishma describes the birth and upbringing of Kartikeya by the Krittikas, the gifts the gods bring him, and his killing of Taraka.
Yudhishthira asks for the Sraddha rules. Bhishma stresses honoring the Pitris first, then lists the benefits of each lunar day and the preferred times for the rite.
Bhishma lists the offerings that keep the Pitris satisfied for set periods, names those that never run out, and quotes verses on the Magha constellation and the merit of Gaya.
Bhishma lists the constellations under which optional Sraddhas are performed and what each brings, and says that Sasavindu followed them to rule the earth.
Bhishma explains how to examine Brahmanas for Sraddhas, lists those who pollute the line and those who sanctify it, and warns against inviting friends or unworthy people in their place.
Yudhishthira asks about the origin of Sraddha. Bhishma tells how Nimi began the rite, how Atri confirmed it, and which deities, foods and people are to be included or excluded.

The Pitris and gods, overloaded with offerings, are sent from Soma to Brahma and then to Agni, who agrees to share the food. Bhishma then sets out the order of cakes, water offerings and the Pitris, and closes the teaching.
Yudhishthira asks whether vowed Brahmanas may eat Sraddha offerings and whether fasting counts as penance. Bhishma says renunciation is the best penance and lists the observances of a Brahmana.
Bhishma defines the fasts, celibacy, truthfulness and leftover-food rules, and then the giver and receiver of gifts. He begins the tale of the starving sages and King Saivya's offer of cattle.
Vasishtha, Kasyapa, Bharadwaja, Gautama and Viswamitra each speak on the danger of accepting gifts and the endless nature of desire.
Jamadagni and Arundhati speak on penance and righteousness, Ganda and Pasusakha on fear and the value of righteousness, and the sages wish the king joy of his gifts.
The sages leave the figs behind, and the angry king creates the Rakshasi Yatudhani and sends her to kill them. In the forest, Arundhati admires a well-fed mendicant with a dog.
The sages compare the mendicant's well-fed state with their own hunger, lapsed duties and worries, each giving a reason.
The sages reach a lotus lake guarded by Yatudhani, who refuses to say who she is and says she guards the lake.
Yatudhani lets the sages take lotus-stalks if they give their names, and Atri explains his name before she sends him into the lake.
Vasishtha, Kasyapa and Bharadwaja each explain their names, and Yatudhani calls each explanation incomprehensible.
Gotama and Viswamitra explain their names, and Yatudhani rejects both explanations.
Jamadagni and Arundhati explain their names, and Yatudhani again finds them incomprehensible.
Ganda and Pasusakha explain their names, and Sunahsakha gives his name without explanation.
Sunahsakha strikes Yatudhani with his triple stick and reduces her to ashes. The sages return to find their lotus-stalks gone and suspect one another of theft.
Atri, Vasishtha, Kasyapa, Bharadwaja and Jamadagni each swear innocence and call down a list of penalties on the thief.
Gotama, Viswamitra, Arundhati, Ganda and Pasusakha each swear to their innocence and call down penalties on the thief.

Sunahsakha confesses that he took the stalks to test them, reveals that he is Indra, and the sages ascend to heaven with him. Bhishma closes with a lesson against greed and the merit of reciting this tale.

The sages, touring the holy waters, find Agastya's lotus-stalks gone. Agastya laments the decline of righteousness, and the first sages, Bhrigu, Vasishtha, Kasyapa and Gautama, swear their oaths of innocence.
Angiras, Dhundhumara, Dilipa, Puru and Sukra each swear oaths of innocence and call down penalties on the thief.
Jamadagni, Sivi, Yayati, Nahusha and Amvarisha each swear oaths and call down penalties on the thief.
Narada, Nabhaga, Kavi, Viswamitra and Parvata each swear oaths and call down penalties on the thief.
Bharadwaja, Ashtaka, Galava, Arundhati and the Valakhilyas each swear oaths and call down penalties on the thief.
Sunahsakha and Surabhi swear the last oaths. Indra, pleased, blesses the thief instead of cursing him, and Agastya accuses Indra of taking the stalks.

Indra says he took the stalks to hear the sages' talk of duty and asks forgiveness. Agastya takes back his stalks, and the sages go on to other holy waters, and Bhishma closes with the merit of the tale.
Yudhishthira asks the origin of giving umbrellas and sandals, and Bhishma tells how Jamadagni, angry at the sun's heat, vowed to shoot it, and Surya came to plead with him.
Jamadagni keeps his anger, and Surya, as a Brahmana, begs for protection. Jamadagni agrees to shield him and asks for a remedy for the heat.
Surya gives Jamadagni an umbrella and sandals and establishes the gift as a custom. Bhishma urges Yudhishthira to give them to Brahmanas and lists the rewards.
Bhishma tells how Vasudeva asked the goddess Earth about the householder's duties, and she lists the rites of worship, offerings, hospitality and feeding others, which lead to fame and heaven.
Manu tells Suvarna of Sukra's teaching to Vali on flowers, incense, lamps and Vali offerings, and the teaching passes down to Narada and to Bhishma.
Bhishma tells how the proud Nahusha stopped his rites and made the Rishis carry him, and how Bhrigu and Agastya discuss how to stop him, since Brahma's boon protects him.
Bhishma tells how Nahusha was yoked and kicked, how Bhrigu cursed him, and how Brahma restored Indra, and closes with the merit of lamps at evening.
Yudhishthira asks where Brahmana-property thieves go, and Bhishma introduces a Chandala and a Kshatriya, who sees the Chandala washing milk spots from his body.

The Chandala explains how stolen kine's milk fell on Soma and sent the thieves and drinkers to hell, admits his own pride and sins, and asks how to be freed. The Kshatriya tells him to die in battle to protect a Brahmana's wealth, which he does, and Bhishma concludes that Brahmana property must be protected.
Bhishma tells how Gautama's raised elephant is seized by King Dhritarashtra, who offers wealth in its place, and Gautama refuses.
Gautama vows to follow the king to Yama's realm. The king says only the faithless go there, and Gautama promises to follow him to Mandakini, the region of Kuvera.
The king names the regions of the hospitable and the learned Brahmanas, and Gautama answers each with a place he will pursue him to, such as Meru's woods and Narada's woods.
The king describes the regions of those who love music, are free from desire and avoid meat, and Gautama answers with the Uttara-Kuru land and Sakra's realm.
Gautama and the king exchange regions for givers, Vedic students and the faithful, ranging from Soma's abode to the Sun and Varuna.
The king names the regions of those who keep the Chaturmasya vow and sacrifice, and Gautama says he will follow to Indra's own abode.
The king names the regions of Sakra, the Prajapatis, kings of the Rajasuya, and kine-givers and pilgrims, and Gautama answers with each.
Gautama names the region of Brahma, and the king says he will not be found there. Gautama recognizes the king as Indra, who admits his identity and bows, and Gautama asks for the elephant.
Indra gives the elephant back to Gautama and praises him for recognizing him. He invites Gautama and the elephant to heaven, and Bhishma closes with the merit of reciting the tale.

Yudhishthira asks which penance is the highest. Bhishma answers with fasting, recounts Bhagiratha's discourse with Brahma on the great gifts that did not win heaven and the fast that did, and urges Yudhishthira to fast and honor Brahmanas.
Yudhishthira asks what makes people live long and prosper. Bhishma answers that conduct is the key, and lists the daily rules of good conduct, ending with the praise of conduct.
Bhishma explains the duties of the eldest brother toward younger brothers, including fair sharing of property, and ranks the teacher, father and mother in order of reverence.
Yudhishthira asks about the merits of fasting, and Bhishma repeats Angiras's rules on how long, how often and with what rewards, ending with the praise of fasting.

Yudhishthira asks how poor people can earn sacrificial merit. Bhishma, citing Angiras, lists fasts of growing length, each matched to a sacrifice and a heavenly reward, and concludes that fasting gives the poor the same fruit.
Yudhishthira asks for the greatest Tirtha. Bhishma names the inner Tirtha of Manasa, explains that inner purity surpasses water-bathing, and says outer and inner purity together are best.
Bhishma recites a twelfth-day fast for each month, paired with a name of Krishna and a sacrifice's merit, and says the vow ends with gifts to Brahmanas and is unsurpassed.
Vaisampayana introduces Yudhishthira's question to Bhishma, and Bhishma describes the Chandravrata vow, its timing by constellation and its fruit.
Vrihaspati is summoned and asked what friend follows the dead, and he answers that only righteousness follows, so one should seek lawful wealth and piety.
Yudhishthira asks how piety can follow a body that becomes unseen. Vrihaspati explains that the elements and mind witness deeds, and how the vital seed forms and causes conception.
Vrihaspati explains how the soul enters the seed, and then lists the animal rebirths that follow particular sins, ending with the call to hold to righteousness.
Vrihaspati says repentance and confession cleanse sin, and that gifts of lawfully earned food to learned Brahmanas, given by each class according to its means, are the highest merit.

Yudhishthira asks which of the six practices brings the most merit. Vrihaspati says compassion and treating others as oneself is the highest, and Vaisampayana reports that Vrihaspati ascended to heaven.
Yudhishthira asks how to cleanse harm done to others. Bhishma explains the four parts of compassion, the three sources of injury, and why eating meat is a sin.
Yudhishthira asks how meat offerings square with non-injury, and Bhishma answers that abstaining from meat and harm is the highest religion, and sets out the limited cases in which meat may be used.
Yudhishthira is dismayed at the craving for meat and asks about its merits and demerits. Bhishma admits its taste and strength, but teaches that abstaining from cruelty is the highest virtue.
Yudhishthira asks about those who die in battle. Bhishma tells how Vyasa met a worm fleeing a cart, and the worm explains its fear of death.
The worm explains why it clings to life, recalls its cruel life as a Sudra usurer, and asks Vyasa what is good for it.
Vyasa says the worm can rise again through merit. The worm is crushed by the cart and reborn a Kshatriya, thanks Vyasa, and Vyasa explains the steps by which a low birth can rise.
The Kshatriya, recalling his past births, undertakes penance, and Vyasa tells him to protect his subjects. He becomes a Brahmana, and Vyasa consoles him about death.
The former worm sets up a thousand sacrificial stakes and reaches Brahma's realm, and Bhishma tells Yudhishthira not to mourn the Kshatriyas who fell at Kurukshetra.
Yudhishthira asks which is superior. Bhishma tells of Vyasa's meeting with Maitreya, and Vyasa explains that gift is the highest sacred act and the three tracks of conduct.
Maitreya praises Vyasa, and argues that gifts bear fruit only when made to learned, pure Brahmanas, and that worthy receivers share the giver's merit.
Vyasa answers that penance surpasses gifts, advises Maitreya on householder duties, and leaves with a blessing that Maitreya returns.
Bhishma tells how Sandili, asked by Sumana how she reached heaven, describes her devotion to her husband and household, and says reading this tale brings heaven.
Yudhishthira asks whether conciliation or gifts is more effective. Bhishma tells how a Brahmana, seized by a Rakshasa, appeased him with flattery and won his release.

Yudhishthira asks how a poor man should act and which gift is best. Bhishma begins the teaching, and a heavenly messenger asks the Pitris about the three rice-balls of the Sraddha and the ban on sex on Sraddha days.

The Pitris explain the fate of each rice-ball, and the sage Vidyutprabha asks Indra how to atone for killing lesser creatures. Indra and Vrihaspati give rites of purification and list the sins against the sun, wind, fire and cows, and the gods ask the Pitris how to repay the debt to ancestors.
The Pitris explain the merit of freeing blue bulls, giving sesame and water on the new moon, and lighting lamps in the rains, and Bhishma closes the teaching.
Indra asks Vishnu what pleases him. Vishnu says honoring Brahmanas and worshipping the Aswattha and the cow please him most, and Baladeva adds a dawn rite of touching cow products and mustard seeds.
The deities, Dharma, Agni and Viswamitra give rules on copper vessels, unfit Sraddha recipients, the sin of kicking a cow, fire or Brahmana, a Bhadrapada rite and a prayer to the cow.
The seven Rishis, led by Vasishtha, ask Brahma how the poor can earn sacrificial merit, and Brahma gives the moonlight rite of Pausha.
A string of teachings from Vibhavasu, Sree, Angiras, Gargya and Dhaumya on offerings, the household items that displease the gods, and the duties that bring merit.
Jamadagni teaches that an impure heart undoes even great sacrifices, while a pure heart is worth as much as them.
Vayu's rainy-season duties, the sins of improper ritual helpers, and the three-day expiation that restores the sinner's standing.
Lomasa's warnings against adultery, barren women and theft from Brahmanas, followed by praise of gifts such as sesame vessels and lamps and the merit they bring.
Arundhati's teaching on the cow-horn rite, the praise of the gods, and the words of Brahman, Yama and Surya on charitable gifts and the five sinners to shun.
The Pramathas explain which conduct makes men vulnerable to them and which household practices keep them away.
Brahman sends Renuka to the elephants, who teach an ant-hill offering that brings merit and supports their work of holding up the earth.
Maheswara teaches that feeding and worshipping cows brings great merit, and explains why he favours them.
Skanda's earth-and-honey rites, Vishnu's praise of hearing and reciting these teachings, and Bhishma's warning about whom to teach.
Yudhishthira's question on eating rules, and Bhishma's answer on whose food each class may accept and whose it must refuse.
Yudhishthira's question about expiations, and Bhishma's list of purification rites for different foods, gifts and settings.
Yudhishthira asks which is better, charity or devotion, and Bhishma lists the royal and sage donors who gained heaven, then defers further answers to morning.
Yudhishthira's questions about kinds of gift, and Bhishma's classification of gifts by motive.
Yudhishthira's request, Bhishma's opening, and Krishna's vow-time episode in which fire from his mouth burns and then restores a mountain, followed by his explanation to the sages.
The ascetics ask Narada to tell the story of the Himavat wonder, and he begins.
Narada describes Shiva's retreat on the Himavat, Uma covering his eyes, the third eye that burns the mountain, and Uma's questions about his form and actions.
Shiva is pleased and agrees to explain the reasons for his forms.
Shiva explains his four faces, his blue throat, the bull that is his mount, and why the crematorium is a sacred place to him.
Uma asks what marks religion, and Shiva names the chief duties of the householder and the five key duties.
Uma asks for the duties of each class and of all classes, and Shiva lays out the duties of Brahmanas, householders, kings, Vaisyas and Sudras, then the paths of Pravritti and Nivritti.
Uma asks about the religion of the Rishis, and Shiva describes ascetic groups such as the Phenapas and Valkhilyas and the practices of the Munis.
Uma asks about forest recluses, and Shiva describes their rites, austerities and virtues, including harmlessness and sincerity.
Shiva lists the rewards that come from different austerities, from heavenly realms to kingship.
Uma asks how castes are lost and gained, and Shiva explains that conduct, not birth alone, decides a man's standing, with lists of faults and of good conduct.
Uma asks about the deeds, words and thoughts that bind or free men, and Shiva lists the conduct and speech that lead to heaven.
Shiva describes the good mental habits that lead to heaven, and then explains how cruelty and compassion shape a person's lifespan and fortune.
Shiva describes the generous giver and the stingy or cruel, with their rewards and punishments, and then answers Uma's questions on wisdom and bodily defects.
Shiva explains that those who seek instruction gain wisdom, and that conduct guided by the Vedas differs from conduct led by folly.
Mahadeva asks Uma about women's duties, she consults the rivers, and then she sets out the ideal wife's conduct.
Mahadeva praises Uma and dismisses the assembly, which departs.
The Rishis ask about Vasudeva, and Shiva praises Hari, traces his future lineage, and urges worship of him.
The Rishis describe what they saw and praise Krishna, Bhishma extols Krishna and urges Yudhishthira not to grieve, and Yudhishthira prepares to ask again.
Yudhishthira asks which god and which hymn bring liberation, and Bhishma answers by reciting the thousand names of Vasudeva and describing the benefits of reciting them.
Yudhishthira asks for the most effective mantra, and Bhishma gives the Savitri mantra with the list of gods and Rishis to be named and the benefits of reciting them.
Yudhishthira asks whom to honour, and Bhishma says Brahmanas deserve reverence whatever their learning or conduct.
Bhishma tells of King Arjuna's boons from Dattatreya, his scorn for Brahmanas, and the wind god's warning, and ends with Arjuna's question.
The wind god lists the feats of Brahmanas as proof of their superiority, and then argues that Brahman was not born from an egg.
The wind god tells the stories of Kasyapa and the earth, and of Utathya's wife, to show Brahmanas surpass Kshatriyas, and then asks Arjuna for a reply.
The wind god tells of Agastya and Vasishtha, each defeating Danavas or Asuras to save the gods, and asks Arjuna whether any Kshatriya surpasses them.
The wind god tells of Atri, who dispelled the darkness caused by Rahu, and of Chyavana, who first asks Indra to let the Aswins drink Soma.
Indra refuses, Chyavana threatens him, creates the monster Mada, and Indra submits; Mada is then given his dwelling places.
The wind god tells how the gods lost heaven and earth, how the Brahmanas destroyed the Kapas, and Arjuna's response.
The wind god urges Arjuna to protect the Brahmanas and warns him of future danger from the race of Bhrigu.
Yudhishthira asks his question, and Bhishma, near death, refers him to Krishna while praising Krishna as creator, protector and the whole universe.
Yudhishthira asks Krishna about Brahmanas, and Krishna tells the story of Durvasa's stay in his house and the lesson he drew from it.
Krishna recites the Sata-rudriya praise of Mahadeva, recounts his deeds, and reveals that Durvasa was Mahadeva.
Krishna names Rudra and explains the meaning of his names, his two forms, and the worship owed to him.
Yudhishthira asks which source of knowledge is authoritative, and Bhishma says reasoning alone cannot settle it and that Righteousness rests on three supports, which Yudhishthira then questions.
Bhishma says Righteousness is one, lists its basic virtues, describes the fates of those who love or hate it, and gives many rules for the good man's conduct.
Yudhishthira asks why wealth and success do not follow effort or learning, and Bhishma answers that austerity, generosity and harmlessness are the way to better fortune in later lives.
Bhishma explains that Time moves creatures, that Righteousness keeps the soul pure and is eternal, and that the unequal lots of men follow their past acts.
