Yudhishthira collapses by the Ganga, the Pandavas gather around him, and Dhritarashtra consoles him while confessing his own failure to heed Vidura.
Krishna advises Yudhishthira to act as a king and perform rites; Yudhishthira asks to retire to the forest; Vyasa rebukes him.
Vyasa argues for sacrifice as a cure for sin; Yudhishthira says he cannot pay for it; Vyasa names Marutta's buried gold as the remedy and Yudhishthira asks for its history.
Yudhishthira requests the story of Marutta, and Vyasa begins a genealogy of the royal line, ending with Marutta's golden sacrifice on Mount Meru.
Yudhishthira asks about Marutta's wealth; Vyasa describes Indra's jealousy and Vrihaspati's refusal to abandon Indra's side for Marutta; Indra is calmed and goes home.
Vyasa introduces the legend; Marutta asks Vrihaspati to be his priest, and Vrihaspati refuses on the grounds that he serves only the Immortals; Narada then finds the troubled king.
Marutta tells Narada of his rebuff and despair; Narada points him to Samvarta, who would perform the sacrifice if pleased.
Narada gives Marutta the method for finding Samvarta; Marutta leaves a corpse at the gate, follows the sage, is smeared with filth, persists, and Samvarta finally rests under a fig tree.
Samvarta asks how Marutta found him and whether Narada sent him; Samvarta, pretending to be mad, refuses and says Marutta must go back to Vrihaspati first.
Marutta explains Vrihaspati's refusal and swears loyalty; Samvarta demands his steadfastness and agrees to officiate.
Samvarta describes Shiva's mountain and tells Marutta to worship Shiva for the gold; Marutta prepares the sacrifice, and Vrihaspati falls ill with envy.
Indra asks Vrihaspati why he is in pain; Vrihaspati says his rival's sacrifice and Samvarta's role trouble him, and Indra dismisses the worry.
Vrihaspati asks Indra to restrain his rival; Indra sends Agni, who sets out and reaches Marutta, who greets him as the fire-god.
Agni delivers Indra's offer to present Vrihaspati; Marutta asks about the gods and refuses, insisting that Samvarta be his priest.
Samvarta threatens to burn Agni with his evil eyes if he returns; Agni reports the failure to Indra, who orders him back with a threat.
Agni refuses to go again, and Indra boasts of his power; Agni recalls how the sage Chyavana overcame Indra and the demon Mada, and says he will not oppose Samvarta.
Indra sends Dhritarashtra, a Gandharva, with a threat; Marutta refuses and the Gandharva warns him that the thunderbolt is coming.
Marutta asks Samvarta for protection; Samvarta promises to calm the storm and offers Marutta a boon.
Marutta asks that Indra come to the sacrifice in person; Samvarta summons him by incantation, and Indra arrives and drinks the Soma.

Indra praises Samvarta and orders the sacrifice's preparations; Marutta distributes gold to the Brahmanas, and Vyasa tells Yudhishthira to gather the same gold and sacrifice; Yudhishthira consults his ministers.
Krishna, seeing Yudhishthira grieving, begins a speech and recounts Indra's war with Vritra as a lesson about hidden enemies.
Krishna explains the causes of illness, lists the troubles Yudhishthira has faced, and tells him to face his own mind and then rule the kingdom.

Krishna teaches that death and eternal Brahman are the two forces within every creature; he recites the Kamagita, in which Desire boasts of its disguises, and then urges Yudhishthira to turn his desires to virtue and sacrifice.
The sages comfort Yudhishthira; he performs funeral rites, gives gifts, returns to Hastinapura with Dhritarashtra, and goes on ruling with his brothers.

Janamejaya asks what Krishna and Arjuna did; Vaisampayana describes their travels and Krishna's consolation of Arjuna; Krishna asks Arjuna to tell Yudhishthira he will leave for Dwaravati, and Arjuna agrees.
Janamejaya asks about Krishna and Arjuna's talk; Arjuna says he forgot Krishna's teaching and asks for it again, and Krishna offers to tell an older story instead.
Kasyapa serves an emancipated Brahmana, who tells him of the many sorrows he endured across lives and of how he gave up the world for the Formless.
Kasyapa asks how the body dies and how the soul is freed; the sage explains how harmful habits lead to death, how the soul leaves the body, and what afterlife follows.
The sage explains how deeds carry over into new bodies, lists the virtues of the good, describes creation, and closes with a teaching on crossing the ocean of rebirth.
The sage lists the marks of the liberated, teaches Yoga and its meditative method, answers the disciple's questions about the body, and Vasudeva closes by praising the teaching as a rare mystery.
Vasudeva introduces a Brahmana couple; the wife asks what will become of her, and the husband describes the soul's seat, the breaths, and the seven-flamed inner fire.
The Brahmana describes the inner sacrifice of ten priests and libations, his wife asks about the origin of Word and Mind, and he recounts the old dispute between them.
The Brahmana explains how Word moves through the breaths and why Mind is fixed while Word is moving.
The Brahmana names seven inner priests that cannot perceive one another's qualities; his wife asks why, and he recounts the argument between the senses and the mind.
The Brahmana introduces the five breaths as inner priests, and their first claim to supremacy is made by Prana.
Each breath in turn claims to be foremost, until Brahma says that none is superior and each has its own role.
Devamata asks Narada which breath arises first in a new creature; Narada explains the breaths' pairing and their link to fire, desire and calm.
The Brahmana presents the four-part inner sacrifice, with the breaths as its chants and renunciation as its fee, and closes by naming Narayana as the soul of all.
The Brahmana teaches that one inner ruler, preceptor and enemy each dwell in the heart; the Lord of creatures answers the beings with the word Om, and each group takes a different disposition.
The Brahmana describes crossing the dangerous worldly forest and entering the forest of Brahman; his wife asks about it, and he describes its trees, fruits, rivers and the sages who dwell there.
The Brahmana describes his detachment and tells of the Yati's protest against the goat sacrifice, the priest's defence, and the Yati's view that the soul is beyond destruction.
The Brahmana concludes that the Yati fell silent and the priest completed the sacrifice free of delusion.
The Brahmana tells of Kartaviryarjuna shooting at the ocean; the ocean sends him to Rama, Rama kills the king, destroys the Kshatriyas, and is told by heaven and his ancestors to stop.
The Pitris introduce Alarka, who first aims arrows at the mind and then at the nose, which each reply that the arrows cannot harm them.
Alarka aims at the tongue, the skin, and the ear; each sense answers that his arrows will only pierce his own vital parts.
Alarka aims at the eye and then at the understanding; each again warns him that his arrows are useless.
Alarka turns to Yoga and slays the senses through concentration; the Pitris tell Rama to stop killing Kshatriyas and take up penance, which he does.
The Brahmana names the inner foes and the qualities linked to each; he then quotes King Amvarisha, who names craving as the greatest foe and says the soul is the true king.
Janaka threatens to banish a Brahmana, who asks where he may go; the king is struck silent, then explains his detachment, and the Brahmana reveals he is Dharma.
The Brahmana presents himself as a liberated man of many roles, says knowledge is his wealth, describes the one path, and reassures his wife.
The Brahmana's wife asks how knowledge is gained; the Brahmana describes the fire-sticks of knowledge and the way to perceive the Kshetrajna, and she reaches beyond it.
Arjuna asks where the Brahmana and his wife are; Krishna says that the mind is the Brahmana, the understanding is the wife, and that he is the Kshetrajna.

Arjuna asks to hear about Brahma; Krishna introduces a preceptor-disciple dialogue, in which the disciple asks questions and the preceptor answers that knowledge and renunciation are the highest, and tells how sages approached Brahma with the same questions.
Brahma answers the sages' questions, teaching that all things come from Truth, that the stages of life form the path, and that understanding the elements frees a person from sin.
Brahma describes the body as a city governed by the three qualities, lists the faults of Darkness and their consequences, and shows how those ruled by it can rise again.
Brahma lists the many forms of the quality of Passion, describes the people it drives, and says that understanding it frees a person from it.
Brahma describes the qualities of Goodness, the virtues of those who practise it, and their rise to heaven and freedom from attachment.
Brahma explains that the three qualities are always combined, shows how each dominates in different creatures and castes, and says that the wise who understand them gain freedom.
Brahma names the Great Soul as the first creation from the unmanifest, describes its nature, and says that knowing it frees one from delusion.

Brahma says that the Great Soul gives rise to Egoism, the second creation, which is the source of beings and feels that it is all this, and that consciousness of the self leads to enjoyment of the qualities.
Brahma covers the elements, the breaths and organs with their deities, the four kinds of birth, and the inward path of renunciation by which the self is seen in all beings.
Brahma names the foremost of each class of things, teaches that kings must protect good men, gives the marks of the elements and senses, and describes the Kshetrajna as pure knowledge.
Brahma names the first of many things and their order, teaches that all things end in destruction, and says that knowledge alone has no end.
Brahma describes the wheel of life and says it is freed by understanding its motion; he then sets out the householder's duties, the six acts, and the reward of heaven.
Brahma describes the duties of the student, the forest dweller and the wandering renunciant, the eight vows, and the inner self that brings release at death.
Brahma calls renunciation the best penance and knowledge the highest, uses the image of the eternal tree and the two birds, and says that understanding the field frees one from sin.
Brahma describes the many views of Brahman, links the self to Goodness, and says the self and Nature differ; the sages still have doubts and question the Grandsire again.
The Rishis list the contradictory views on duty and ask Brahma which duty is most worthy and how the knower of the field is linked to Nature; Brahma answers them.
Brahma teaches harmlessness and knowledge, explains the knower and Nature as enjoyer and enjoyed, lists the qualities of the five elements, and places Purusha above them all.

Brahma describes the mind's rule over the elements, the chariot image, the power of penance, and the immortal self; the sages act on his words, and Vasudeva reveals he was the preceptor and asks leave to visit his father.
Arjuna agrees to go to the elephant-named city, meet Yudhishthira and inform him of Krishna's plan to depart.
Krishna and Arjuna arrive at Hastinapura, visit the family, and the next morning Arjuna asks Yudhishthira's leave for Krishna to go to Dvaraka, which is granted with gifts.
Yudhishthira gives Krishna leave to depart; Krishna takes leave of Kunti and sets out with his company toward the city of the Anarttas.
Krishna meets Utanka in the desert; Utanka asks about peace with the Kurus, Krishna explains the war's outcome, and Utanka threatens a curse, which Krishna answers with a plea.
Utanka asks for the teaching; Krishna says he is the source of all beings and qualities, takes many forms to protect righteousness, and explains that the Kauravas fell through their own wrong.

Utanka praises Krishna and asks for a vision of his form; Krishna shows his cosmic form, grants a boon, and in the desert Utanka refuses water from a hunter; Krishna explains that the hunter was Indra with nectar, and promises the Utanka-clouds.
Utanka's devotion to Gautama, his old age and tears, Gautama's kindness and offer of his daughter, and Utanka's gratitude.
Utanka restored to youth marries Gautama's daughter, Ahalya asks him to fetch the ear-rings of Saudasa's queen, Gautama warns of danger, and Utanka meets Saudasa in the forest.
Saudasa, a man-eater under a curse, prepares to eat Utanka, who pleads that he is on his teacher's errand and promises to return; Saudasa asks what he seeks.
Utanka asks for the ear-rings; Saudasa sends him to his queen, and Utanka insists on the request.
Saudasa sends Utanka to Madayanti, who asks for a sign from her husband and describes the ear-rings' powers.
Saudasa gives a sign, Madayanti gives the ear-rings, and Saudasa explains his reasons and reminds Utanka of his promise.
Utanka asks whether to return to the cannibal king, Saudasa advises him not to, and the ear-rings are lost to a Naga in the forest.
Indra opens the way to the Naga world, a fire-steed fills it with smoke, the Nagas return the ear-rings, and Utanka brings them to Ahalya.
Janamejaya asks what Krishna did next; Vaisampayana describes Krishna's return to Dvaraka during the festival, his welcome by the Vrishnis and his parents, and his account of the battle.
Vasudeva asks Krishna to describe the battle; Krishna lists the commanders and their falls from Bhishma to Duryodhana, and the night slaughter, and the Vrishnis grieve.
Krishna's account of the battle omits Abhimanyu's death; Subhadra asks for it and faints, Vasudeva falls too, Krishna describes Abhimanyu's death, and Kunti comforts the mourners and arranges rites.
Vasudeva holds Abhimanyu's rites and gives generously; Vyasa comforts the mourners and promises a grandson for Arjuna, then urges Yudhishthira to fetch wealth for the horse sacrifice.
Janamejaya asks how the buried wealth was obtained; Yudhishthira consults his brothers, Bhima proposes worshipping Shiva, and the Pandavas set out after offerings.
The army marches cheerfully to the buried treasure; Yudhishthira makes camp under the guidance of Brahmanas, and the brothers fast and listen to learned talk through the night.
Offerings are made to Shiva, his attendants and the Yakshas; the treasure is excavated and loaded onto animals and vehicles; the Pandavas return to the city with it.
Vasudeva returns to Hastinapura, where the child is found stillborn after Ashvatthama's weapon; Kunti begs Krishna to revive him, and collapses until Krishna comforts her.
Subhadra grieves over the dead child, pleads with Krishna to fulfil his earlier promise to revive him, and says that she will die if he does not.
Krishna agrees to act, enters the prepared lying-in room, and Uttara, with Draupadi, begs him to revive her child, blaming Ashvatthama's cruelty and her own wish to die.
Uttara faints, revives, begs Krishna to save her son, and Krishna withdraws the weapon with a vow on his truthfulness; the child begins to move.
Krishna withdraws the weapon, the child revives and is named Parikshit, and the Pandavas return with wealth to a city decked for celebration.

Vasudeva greets the Pandavas, who enter the city with the treasure and honour the elders; Vyasa grants leave for the horse sacrifice; Yudhishthira asks Krishna to take part, and Krishna agrees to help.
Vyasa agrees to perform the initiation and prepares the horse; Krishna names Arjuna to guard it, with Bhima, Nakula and Sahadeva given other duties.
Yudhishthira charges Arjuna to guard the horse and seek friendship rather than battle; Bhima and Nakula guard the city, and Sahadeva looks after the guests.
The initiation is completed; the horse is released; Arjuna follows it with Gandiva, and the horse roams through many lands where Arjuna fights many kings.
The Trigartas attack Arjuna, who asks them to desist; they refuse, Arjuna defeats their leaders, Gandiva falls after a wound, and the Trigartas submit.
Vajradatta seizes the horse and is driven off by Arjuna; he returns on an elephant, and Arjuna cuts through his arrows and wounds him and his beast.
On the fourth day Vajradatta taunts Arjuna and charges, Arjuna fells the elephant, spares the defeated king on Yudhishthira's instruction, and sends him to the sacrifice.
The Saindhavas surround and wound Arjuna, omens appear, Arjuna falls senseless, the gods pray, and Arjuna recovers and routs his enemies with Gandiva.
Arjuna fights the Saindhavas but spares those who yield; Dussala brings her grandson, Arjuna makes peace, and the horse moves on to Manipura.
Vabhruvahana comes out with gifts, Arjuna rebukes him, Ulupi urges him to fight, and father and son battle until both fall; Chitrangada arrives and finds her husband slain.
Chitrangada reproaches Ulupi and asks for Arjuna's life; Vabhruvahana grieves and vows to die; Ulupi brings a gem, reveals the illusion, and Arjuna is revived.
Ulupi explains that she arranged Arjuna's defeat by his son to lift the Vasus' curse; Arjuna thanks her, invites his son to the sacrifice, and declines to enter the city while his vow lasts.
The horse travels to Rajagriha, where Arjuna defeats Meghasandhi, spares him and sends him to the sacrifice, and then the horse goes on to the eastern lands, where Arjuna defeats more armies.

The horse travels through many realms, Arjuna subdues or is welcomed by their rulers, and at Dwaravati he is honoured by Ugrasena and Vasudeva before the horse moves on to Gandhara, where Sakuni's son awaits.
Sakuni's son leads the Gandharas against Arjuna, who defeats them and spares their king at his mother's request, and urges peace and attendance at the sacrifice.

Yudhishthira hears that Arjuna is returning and sets the sacrifice's date; Bhima builds the grounds, invitations go out, guests arrive, and the sacrifice is ready; the sacrifice begins amid debates, and the kings marvel at the golden grounds, animals and feasts.
Yudhishthira asks Bhima to honour the kings; Krishna arrives and reports Arjuna's message about honouring the kings, avoiding bloodshed, and welcoming Vabhruvahana, and Yudhishthira agrees.

Yudhishthira asks why Arjuna suffers; Krishna names a minor flaw; Draupadi objects; Arjuna's envoy announces his return, and Arjuna is welcomed; Vabhruvahana arrives with his mothers and goes to Kunti.

Vabhruvahana is welcomed and honoured; Vyasa tells Yudhishthira to begin the sacrifice and pay threefold; the rites are performed, the altar and stakes are set up, and animals are bound, with heavenly beings attending.

The horse is sacrificed; Yudhishthira gives the earth to Vyasa, who returns it, and Krishna returns it to Yudhishthira, who pays for it with millions of coins; the wealth is divided, the guests depart, and Yudhishthira returns to his capital.
Janamejaya asks about a wonder at the sacrifice; a golden-half mongoose says the sacrifice is worth less than a small gift of barley, and the Brahmanas ask him to explain.

The mongoose recounts how the poor Brahmana and his family each gave their share of barley to a guest, who was the god of righteousness; the mongoose's body was made gold by the barley dust, and Vaisampayana closes by praising gifts and penance over sacrifice.

Janamejaya asks why the mongoose belittled the sacrifice; Vaisampayana tells of the dispute at Indra's sacrifice, King Vasu's false judgment, and the lesson that lawful and sincere giving is what brings merit.

Janamejaya asks how the reward of lawful wealth compares with sacrifice; Vaisampayana tells of Agastya's long sacrifice, Indra's withheld rain, and the sages' call for harmless, lawful offerings, then explains who the golden mongoose was.

Jamadagni sends Anger away, the Pitris tell it how to end its curse by disparaging Dharma, and the mongoose ends its curse at Yudhishthira's sacrifice; the Parva closes and the translator's notes begin.

Janamejaya's question and Vaisampayana's account of how the Pandavas honoured Dhritarashtra as their ruling elder, with Bhima's lingering resentment.
The Pandavas serve Dhritarashtra and Gandhari with care, and Yudhishthira's gentle conduct wins the old king's trust while Bhima stays reluctant.
Bhima's outburst, Dhritarashtra's confession and request to retire to the forest, and Yudhishthira's distressed reply.
Dhritarashtra collapses, Yudhishthira's grief and touch revive him, and he asks again to eat and to leave, just as Vyasa arrives.
Vyasa urges Yudhishthira to let Dhritarashtra retire to the forest, and Yudhishthira agrees and asks him to eat first.
Dhritarashtra goes home, takes his meal, and then gives Yudhishthira detailed advice on governing.
Dhritarashtra explains the circles of allies and foes, the six policies, and how a king should act when stronger or weaker than his rival.
Dhritarashtra advises when to make war or peace, the kinds of power a king should keep, and how to prepare an army.
Yudhishthira agrees to the advice, Dhritarashtra plans his gifts and departure with Gandhari, and he tells the assembled people that he will retire to the forest.
Dhritarashtra asks the people's forgiveness, commends Yudhishthira to them, and they respond only in silent tears.
Dhritarashtra asks the citizens' leave, Samba speaks for them and blames fate for the war, and the old king dismisses the assembly.
Vidura brings Dhritarashtra's request for funeral wealth, Yudhishthira and Arjuna accept, and Bhima's angry objection is silenced.
Arjuna urges Bhima to honour the old king, and Yudhishthira offers Dhritarashtra wealth from the treasury and from the brothers' houses.
Vidura reports Yudhishthira's and Arjuna's consent, Bhima's reluctant acceptance and the charities proposed, and Dhritarashtra resolves to proceed.
Dhritarashtra makes lavish gifts and feeds the guests for ten days, in memory of the dead, with Yudhishthira's approval.
Dhritarashtra leaves the palace for the forest, Yudhishthira collapses in grief, and the whole city follows in lamentation.
Dhritarashtra leaves the city, Yudhishthira is left behind, and Kunti refuses all pleas to turn back and follows Gandhari into the forest.
Kunti explains why she roused her sons, declines any share of the kingdom, and tells them to go back.
The Pandavas turn back, Kunti stays, and the old king's party camps by the Bhagirathi for the night, with the city left in mourning.
Dhritarashtra settles by the Bhagirathi, moves to Kurukshetra under Satayupa, is initiated by Vyasa, and his household takes up severe penance.
The sages visit Dhritarashtra, Narada tells of the forest-penance heroes and foretells the old king's end, and the assembly leaves in good spirits.
The Brahmins and citizens fret over the elders in the forest, the Pandavas grieve for their losses, and Parikshit gives them some comfort.
The Pandavas, grieving, resolve to visit the forest, and Yudhishthira orders the army and supplies prepared for the journey.
The great procession sets out, with each Pandava described in his conveyance, and Yudhishthira catches sight of the old king's hermitage across the Yamuna.
The Pandavas reach the hermitage on foot, reunite with Dhritarashtra, Gandhari and Kunti, and present the court to the old king.
The ascetics ask who is who, Sanjaya points out and describes each Pandava and wife, and the old king greets the company.
Dhritarashtra and Yudhishthira exchange questions, then Vidura appears and passes into Yudhishthira's body, and his own body is not to be cremated.
The Pandavas spend the night in the hermitage, tour the sacred retreats, and gather round the old king for the arrival of Vyasa.
Vyasa asks after the family's welfare, explains the divine parentage of Vidura and Yudhishthira, and offers to grant a wish.
Janamejaya asks his questions, Vyasa offers a boon, Dhritarashtra laments his sons, Gandhari asks for a sight of the dead, and Kunti prepares to speak.
Kunti tells Vyasa how she came to bear Karna, and Vyasa absolves her and promises to grant her wish.
Vyasa tells the women they will see their dead and explains the divine origins of the heroes, and the company goes to the Bhagirathi to wait for night.
Vyasa calls the dead from the Bhagirathi, the warriors of both sides rise, and Dhritarashtra and Gandhari see them with the sight Vyasa gives.
The living and the dead are reconciled and then dismissed, the widows join their husbands, and the chapter closes with praise for hearing the story.
Janamejaya asks how the dead can reappear, and Vaisampayana answers with a discourse on deeds, the soul and the body.
Dhritarashtra gains sight, Janamejaya sees his father Parikshit brought back, Astika speaks in praise, and Janamejaya asks for the sequel.
The old king dismisses Yudhishthira and his household to return to the capital, after Yudhishthira's and Gandhari's protests and Kunti's farewell.
Narada visits Yudhishthira, who asks about his father, and Narada describes the old king's penance and death in a forest fire.
The Pandavas, the palace and the citizens hear of the death and weep, and Yudhishthira speaks after his cries.
Yudhishthira mourns his father, Gandhari and especially Kunti, blames the fire and his own brothers, and the household wails in grief.
Narada explains the cause of Dhritarashtra's death, Yudhishthira performs the funeral rites and gifts, and the parva closes with a benediction.

The author attribution line for the Mahabharata.
Yudhishthira sees omens in the thirty-sixth year and learns of the Vrishni destruction, and Janamejaya asks how and by whose curse it happened.
Samva is disguised as a woman and tricks the sages, who curse him to bear an iron bolt, and the king has the bolt ground to powder and bans liquor.
A long catalogue of omens and Time's visits to Vrishni houses, followed by Krishna's reading of the signs and his order for a pilgrimage to the sea.
The Vrishnis go to Prabhasa, drink and quarrel, and kill one another in a frenzy, and Krishna and Daruka then set out to find Rama.
Krishna sends Daruka for Arjuna, has Vabhru guard the women and sees Vabhru killed, visits his father, finds Rama's soul departing as a serpent, and lies down in yoga.
The hunter Jara wounds Krishna by mistake, and Krishna rises to heaven and is honoured by the gods.
Daruka brings the news to the Pandavas, Arjuna goes to Dwaraka and finds the city in mourning, and he comforts the women before seeing his uncle.
Arjuna comes to his uncle, who weeps over the dead and passes on Krishna's last instructions, then announces he will give up his life.
Arjuna prepares the people to leave, Krishna and the dead are cremated, Dwaraka is flooded, the widows are robbed on the road, and Arjuna settles the survivors before visiting Vyasa.
Arjuna pours out his grief to Vyasa, who explains that the Vrishni fall and Krishna's death were fated and that the Pandavas' task is complete.
Janamejaya asks what the Pandavas did after the Vrishni disaster, and Yudhishthira resolves to renounce the world. He settles the kingdom and makes offerings and gifts before leaving.

The citizens object, the Pandavas strip off their finery and fire rites, and the party sets out with a dog. At the sea, the fire god asks Arjuna to surrender Gandiva, and the travellers then turn north after circling the western coast.
On the northward journey Draupadi falls, followed by Sahadeva and Nakula. Yudhishthira explains each fall by a fault, and Bhima keeps asking why.
Arjuna then falls, and Yudhishthira blames his boasting. Bhima falls next and begins to ask why, and the king walks on.
Bhima, still lying on the ground, asks the king why he has fallen. Yudhishthira says it is his greed and boasting, and he walks on with only the dog.
Shakra invites Yudhishthira to his chariot, and Yudhishthira refuses to go without his brothers and asks that the dog be allowed to come.
Shakra argues that dogs bar a man from heaven, and Yudhishthira refuses to abandon a devoted follower. The dog is revealed as Dharma, who praises Yudhishthira and recalls his earlier test at Dwaita.
The gods carry Yudhishthira up to heaven, where Narada praises him. He declines to stay and says he will go wherever his brothers and Draupadi are.
The title and author line of the Mahabharata, attributed to Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa.
Yudhishthira sees Duryodhana seated in glory in heaven, rejects sharing that place, and Narada reminds him that enmities end there.
Narada urges Yudhishthira to forget old wrongs and greet Duryodhana properly, and Yudhishthira asks where his fallen kin and allies are.
Yudhishthira says heaven is empty without his brothers and allies, and the gods agree to show him where they are.
The messenger leads Yudhishthira along a hellish path until he stops, and Yudhishthira, disgusted, starts to turn back.
Pleading voices surround Yudhishthira and each names a dead hero or Draupadi.
Yudhishthira wonders what sin could have brought these righteous people to hell, then curses the gods and resolves to stay with them.
The gods arrive and the hellish scene disappears. Indra and Dharma explain the hell vision was a test and an illusion, and Dharma praises his son.
Yudhishthira bathes in the Ganga, takes a celestial form, and goes on with the gods to the place where the heroes are.
Yudhishthira finds his kin and allies in heaven, and Indra explains the identity and place of each one he sees.
Janamejaya asks about the fate of the heroes, and Vaishampayana explains where each one went after death, then the snake sacrifice ends and Janamejaya returns home.
Sauti describes the work's composer, its purpose, and the merits of reciting or hearing it, including the reason for its name.
The narrator recalls Vyasa's verses on the transience of life and the eternity of righteousness, and closes with praise of the work.
Janamejaya asks about rites, rewards and gifts, and Vaishampayana introduces the work's scope, the merit of listening, and the gifts owed to honored persons and Brahmanas.
The manner of reciting is described, and the first four parvas of recitation each bring rewards equal to great sacrifices.
The fifth through tenth parvas bring richer heavenly rewards, with cars, Apsaras and time spent with the gods.
The listener's heavenly life and the gifts due to the reciter are described, followed by the first feasts to give at the early parvas.
The gifts for the parvas from Arani through Karna are listed, mostly food, robes, water pots and weapons.
The gifts for the parvas from Shalya through Asramvasika are listed, mostly food and gems.
The gifts for the last parvas are listed, followed by worship of the complete book and the final gifts and feasts.
The closing praise says the work is sacred and leads to liberation and Vishnu, and the Svargarohanika parva and the whole work are declared complete.
